service.text: When LisainCA's son mentioned he wanted an early run, the staff gave him directions and had his running shoes set out at the entrance before he woke. You choose your dinner and breakfast times, both come to the room (they served all four of her family in one room on request), an evening snack of inari appeared after the kaiseki, and the massage she booked through the inn was thorough and reasonably priced. Smiley90 calls the service excellent.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms strike a balance between rustic and luxurious, each with its own open-air onsen bath, and they are air-conditioned in summer. LisainCA recommends Yama no Ashita, on the second floor, over the ground-floor Yama no Yube, which ran a bit humid because its bath is more enclosed. Smiley90 calls the rooms excellent, and FlyingTurk1 found the place a tad dated but loved it anyway.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yama no Chaya sits in a narrow forested valley, and the rooms look onto the valley and the trees, which Smiley90 says is peaceful without being what he would call a view. LisainCA loved watching the rain on the trees from the sitting room and calls the stay a fantastic respite from Tokyo. KI-NRT notes it is not quite as centrally located as Gora Kadan, Ginyu or Gora Hanaougi, and LisainCA says not to miss the Hakone Open Air Museum nearby.

cities.text: Odakyu Romancecar Shinjuku→Hakone-Yumoto (~85 min), Tozan railway→Kōwakudani (~35 min), 5-min inn shuttle (reserve).

Reverse of: Direct Tozan BUS Gōra/Sengokuhara→Odawara (~45 min — one seat; Tozan rail adds a Hakone-Yumoto change), then Tōkaidō Shinkansen→Kyoto (~1h50 on the ~2-hourly Odawara-calling 'Hikari'; 'Kodama'+change or ~2h40 all-Kodama otherwise).

Midōsuji hop Umeda→Shin-Osaka, Tōkaidō 'Hikari' Shin-Osaka→Odawara (~2h05 — the same ~2-hourly Odawara-calling 'Hikari' the hakone>kyoto leg uses at ~1h50 to Kyoto, plus the ~15-min Kyoto–Shin-Osaka segment; 'Nozomi' skips Odawara and all-'Kodama' is ~2h40), then the direct Tozan BUS Odawara→Gōra/Sengokuhara (~45 min, one seat; the Tozan rail adds a Hakone-Yumoto change).

inns.name: Yamado
inns.summary: A 12-room hot-spring retreat in the Iwate mountains with free-flowing source onsen in every room, a private bath suspended over the stream that is worth the trip on its own, and Iwate-proud staff whose hospitality stood out most for KI-NRT. The kitchen does regional fusion led by chicken and pork, which he admires without calling it destination dining. He has stayed once, and calls it well worth the journey for a quiet retreat with authentic hot springs.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is a Japanese-European fusion built on Iwate ingredients, led by Ginsetsu chicken, a breed Yamado developed (as shabu-shabu and Sichuan-style sweet and sour), and Hakkinton pork as a fusilli and a low-temperature chop, with foraged plants in most dishes and an inventive shidoke cheesecake. KI-NRT admires the commitment to Iwate's larder even though chicken and pork are not his picks for fine dining, and homemade breakfast toast is superb.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The onsen is gensen kakenagashi, straight from the source and never recirculated, and every one of the 12 rooms has its own (Katsura's sits on an outdoor terrace nearer the river). The best soak is Yu-ba Issun, a private rental bath suspended over the stream and hugged by foliage, booked ahead in 30-minute slots. The water is tuned to the season, KI-NRT watched a yamame trout glide below, and they came back at night to soak under starlight.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is what stood out most for KI-NRT. Most staff are Iwate locals with visible pride in the region, and his room attendant Hitomi Kamata was exceptional: noticing his wife's cast, and knowing she usually writes furigana over difficult kanji so he can study each dish later, Hitomi handwrote furigana over every kanji on the menu. Brandt, the one English speaker, was just as gracious and caring, and he is confident you will be in good hands.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT's Luxury Suite Buna was 52 square metres with a separate living area, a bedroom and an indoor onsen that becomes semi-open-air when the large sliding windows are pushed back, done in subdued, calming colors; the view was so good they spent hours gazing at it. It has no desk. Buna is the second-best room, so book Katsura if you can: the same layout, closer to the river, with an outdoor terrace onsen (it was already taken on his dates).

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yamado sits beside a forested hill and a stream in western Iwate, and instead of a manicured garden it embraces its remote location, with all 12 rooms facing the hillside and river. The main building holds reception, a cozy lounge and the restaurant Fukuzenbo, hung with photos and paintings made by the staff. There is little to explore on site, and what is there is deeply peaceful; KI-NRT calls it a quiet retreat far off the tourist trail.

cities.text: Tōhoku Shinkansen Tokyo→Kitakami (~2h50), change to the JR Kitakami line→Hottoyuda (~50 min, sparse), then a ~6-min inn taxi. ⚠ deep-snow branch line off the main spine — build in a connection buffer.
Hokuriku Shinkansen Kanazawa→Ōmiya, cross to a 'Hayabusa'→Kitakami, then the Kitakami-line local→Hottoyuda + shuttle. ⚠ long, ending on a deep-snow single-track branch.
Tōhoku Shinkansen Sendai→Kitakami (~40 min), change to the JR Kitakami line→Hottoyuda (~50 min, sparse), then a ~6-min inn taxi — the region-hub leg.

inns.name: Fuji Seiran
inns.summary: Fuji Seiran is a five-suite newcomer on the west coast of Izu built around the view of Mt. Fuji across Suruga Bay, with spectacular cooking from its opening week. At $2,400–2,900 a night KI-NRT called it Asaba prices without the pedigree, and the trucked-in bath water, the shared walls and the lounge terrace that faces away from the mountain are where the near-perfection those rates demand falls short. It is best on a clear day between late fall and early spring, and if you have two nights he suggests pairing it with Asaba.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The cooking was spectacular even in opening week, built on Suruga Bay seafood from the local fishermen and produce from the inn's own farm, and every serving was artful and expertly balanced. KI-NRT's standouts were the salt-grilled unagi shirayaki, the grilled Ise spiny lobster sauced with its own liver, and a lightly seared bonito in soy dashi with fried garlic, a simple dish he called simply sublime.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no hot-spring source here: the only onsen in the Heda area is brought in daily by truck, heated and dispensed into each bath, a recirculated system and not water flowing from the source. Every room has a private onsen tub and a sauna on its deck facing Fuji, which KI-NRT still found enjoyable, but he says this would not be the best choice for a true onsen experience. In Souten the smoked-glass screens block the view from the tub.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT and his party were the only guests two days after opening, and with the GM on sick leave the assistant GM, Takara Sato, welcomed them with enthusiasm at the head of a young, cheerful team from Japan, Myanmar, Taiwan and Vietnam. He came away calling the hospitality warm. Small touches included heated towel racks, complimentary electric toothbrushes and personalized chopsticks engraved with their names and the date.

room.label: Room
room.text: The five suites are identical apart from small differences in decor, and each faces Mt. Fuji with a private onsen tub and a sauna on the deck. Despite the claimed 150 square meters the real living space is closer to 100, generous but more like an Aman junior suite than a full suite, and the rooms share walls instead of standing as detached villas, which KI-NRT found odd. Avoid Souten, which sits lower on the hill and screens its deck.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The inn stands near Cape Osezaki, a kilometer-long strip of virgin juniper forest reaching into Suruga Bay, and the view of Mt. Fuji rising across the water is the whole reason for the place. The best months are late fall through early spring, and if clouds hide the mountain KI-NRT is not sure he would recommend it, since unlike Hakone there is little else to do in Heda. The Yuhimi Terrace lounge is angled so that it has no view of Fuji.

cities.text: 'Kodama'/'Hikari' Tokyo→Mishima (~45-55 min, every ~30 min), then the flat-rate cab into the Shuzenji valley (~40-50 min, book with the room). No self-handled change. Rail alt: Izuhakone Sunzu line→Shuzenji (~35 min) + short taxi, +1 change.

Reverse of: The inn-bookable flat-rate cab Shuzenji valley→Mishima (~40-50 min; Asaba ¥12-15k, book with the room — Asaba runs NO shuttle), then the direct Mishima-calling 'Hikari'→Kyoto (1h50, ~2-hourly, dep Mishima :58 — reserve; hourly 'Kodama'+change fallback). No self-handled change. Rail alt: Sunzu line→Mishima (~35 min), +1 change.

inns.name: Hanamurasaki
inns.summary: A large, modern luxury ryokan above the Kakusenkei gorge, and the food (spectacular winter snow crab above all) is the main reason anyone comes; source-fed bathing reaches only its top suites. KI-NRT's reservations (restaurant-only dining, a view-less private bath, baffling ordering) kept it at 'merely one of the top choices in Hokuriku' for him in 2018; the 2024 renovation and simplified set menu have since answered some of that, and a 2025 guest called it the perfect choice for a food-first stay.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Food is the main reason anyone comes, and in winter that means Zuwai-gani snow crab, which KI-NRT says blows away any other crab, best of all as sashimi. In 2018 dinner was ordered from a huge points-based menu (crab sashimi had to be asked for), but a 2025 guest got a set kaiseki with no choices and found dinner and breakfast exquisite. Meals are never served in the room, and on his crab yardstick Nishimuraya and Matsusaki rank higher.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Only the top Comfort Suites get onsen direct from the source; most of Kaga Onsen does not have pure onsen at all. KI-NRT's Comfort Suite Haru had its own onsen bath and sauna, but no view and no open air, his main wish. The public baths are a main indoor bath and a smaller open-air one on the top floor; he found the open-air one very nice though much like other properties', and a 2025 guest thought it lovely to sit under cover watching the rain.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is polished and attentive, and KI-NRT found the whole stay hosted to a very high standard, with staff gracious and unwavering about ensuring a great stay. LisainCA, in 2025, was met inside Kaga Onsen station by the hotel driver, welcomed with sweets and tea, and had food sensitivities accommodated without complaint. Despite the property's surprising size she found it attentive and personal, and calls the service impeccable.

room.label: Room
room.text: The top room, Comfort Suite Haru, is 170 square metres, with a huge living room and a small bedroom, but it has no view and no private garden, so KI-NRT called it a very nice room to laze away in, though not idyllic. Several rooms became Art Suites in 2024, and from photos he thought the humongous Natsu suite had much empty space. A 2025 guest's standard room was large and traditional, with a sitting area on the gorge, which every room faces.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Hanamurasaki stands above the Kakusenkei gorge in Yamanaka, which KI-NRT calls the best of the Kaga onsen towns, and its famous footpath is close by; a 2025 guest found the morning walk along it incredibly beautiful. Arrival tea comes in a tea room looking over the green above the gorge. The property is far bigger than most luxury ryokans and the public areas are modern, so anyone after an intimate, very traditional inn should look elsewhere.

cities.text: Kanazawa→Kaga-Onsen (~25 min), then ~25-min taxi up to Yamanaka (inn can arrange).
Hokuriku Shinkansen direct Tokyo→Kaga-Onsen (~2h50, 'Kagayaki'/'Hakutaka' since 2024), then taxi up to Yamanaka Onsen (~25 min). No self-change.
Reverse of: Kaga-Onsen→Tsuruga (~30 min), 'Thunderbird' Ltd Exp→Kyoto (~1h25).
Reverse of: ~25-min taxi from Yamanaka Onsen to Komatsu Airport, the KMQ→Fukuoka hop (~1h40, ~4 daily ANA/ORC), then the subway 2 stops into Hakata (~5 min). ~3.75h door-to-door.
Reverse of: ~25-min taxi to Komatsu + KMQ→Fukuoka (~1h40) into Hakata, then Nishi-Kyushu relay→Nagasaki via Takeo-Onsen (~2h). ~5.75h door-to-door.
Reverse of: ~25-min taxi to Komatsu + KMQ→Fukuoka (~1h40) into Hakata, then Kyushu Shinkansen 'Mizuho'→Kagoshima-Chūō (~1h17). ~5.25h door-to-door.

inns.name: Kinsuikan
inns.summary: A 39-room Miyajima ryokan that won KI-NRT back to the island after a disappointing stay at Iwaso, provided you book one of the six renovated special rooms, because the regional kaiseki served there (conger eel, fugu, Hiroshima oysters) is the reason to stay. The kitchen has to carry a large operation, since nobody in the thread has written about the service and the in-room baths are not true onsen, so the inn ends up below what the plates alone would suggest. It is near the bottom of its price class and KI-NRT's choice for a night on the island.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: KI-NRT called the kaiseki dinner and the breakfast sublime, and the meal is built on Hiroshima's seafood: raw conger eel with its liver, fugu, abalone and stonefish sashimi, then oyster hot pot and grilled Hiroshima oysters. The bilingual omakase menus are among the most extensive he has seen, naming the farm or port behind each ingredient. These meals are for the six special rooms; others can pay to upgrade dinner but cannot get that breakfast.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The communal gender-segregated baths are honest-to-goodness onsen and reportedly the only ones on Miyajima. The in-room baths of the special rooms are not onsen, though: the water picks up some calcium and magnesium from the rocks in the tub, and KI-NRT, a big fan of jumping in and out of an in-room onsen, counted this as his one disappointment. The top-floor room 403 has its bath in the open air.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here. Guests in the six special rooms have both dinner and breakfast served in the room.

room.label: Room
room.text: The six Tokubetsu-shitsu special rooms were completely redone in 2021 or 2022 and are new and modern, with sea views, heated floors, a free-flowing bath by the window and both meals served in the room. They are small at 42 square metres, while the upper traditional suites run over 100, but KI-NRT says their advantages are too great to ignore unless you travel as a family. The toiletry kits are a level above even good Japanese inns.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Kinsuikan is a short walk from the Miyajima ferry terminal and around the corner from the main tourist strip, with a rooftop terrace where you look across at Itsukushima Shrine and the torii gate. The building is nondescript and there is no garden to speak of, but the special rooms look out at the Seto Inland Sea. KI-NRT urges you to stay overnight: the landmarks are lit at night, the morning is quiet, and 99% of visitors are daytrippers.

cities.text: Reverse of: Ferry + JR back to Hiroshima (~50 min).
Shinkansen Kyoto→Hiroshima (~1h40), JR to Miyajimaguchi + ferry (~40 min), then ~3-min walk.
Sanyo Shinkansen Nozomi Hakata→Hiroshima (~1h), JR Sanyo Main Line→Miyajimaguchi (~25 min), then the ~10-min ferry to Miyajima + short walk.

inns.name: Otogi no Yado Yoneya
inns.summary: Otogi no Yado Yoneya is a 17-room fairy-tale-themed onsen ryokan deep in rural Fukushima near Sukagawa, its rooms and seasonal 'Otogi Kaiseki' dinner built on a playful (but not gimmicky) storytelling concept, with a six-room Hanare 88 annex added in 2021. The bathing stands out most, with source water in every room plus communal rock baths, and KI-NRT counts it among the best onsen he has found. The remote setting has nothing famous nearby and the food drew real reservations, but he left calling it a place that stands out.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is the 'Otogi Kaiseki', themed each season on a fairy tale, and KI-NRT's ran on The Three Little Pigs. He found it an enjoyable conversation piece that never upstaged the flavours, built on pesticide-free, largely wild ingredients. The wild Fukushima flounder sashimi was his standout, but the shorthorn beef came as a hamburger-style haché and the breakfast fish was plain salmon. Ikyu guests call the vegetables the best of any inn.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The onsen is one of the best KI-NRT has found. The water enters each bath from the bottom to limit contact with air and felt exceptionally smooth, like a silky skin lotion, so staff advise you not to rinse off afterwards. Every room has a bath flowing straight from the source (his was on a deck over the forest), plus communal indoor and outdoor rock baths and a mist sauna. It runs so hot he stopped the flow 30 minutes before bathing.

service.label: Service
service.text: The hospitality is heartfelt and graceful, and the staff were warm, charming and eager to please. KI-NRT's private dinner server, Ms. Arima, born and raised in the area, explained each course and its fairy-tale link with an enthusiasm he called infectious, and he left full of smiles and gratitude. It sees about one overseas guest a month yet stays fully booked year-round. Some Ikyu guests find the narrated dinner too long (7 PM to near 9:30).

room.label: Room
room.text: The 17 rooms are split between the 11 in the main building and the six-room Hanare 88 annex, considered the more desirable, though KI-NRT thinks they differ little. He picked Suite #887 (54 square metres) over the 80-square-metre flagship Nazumu at the same price, for its expansive patio with a dazzling open-air bath over the forest, where Nazumu has only an ordinary indoor bath. Both are junior suites. The main rooms were redone in 2024.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yoneya sits in south-central Fukushima about an hour east of Aizuwakamatsu, near nothing noteworthy, and almost no foreigner has heard of it. Inside it is rural-modern Japanese with a streak of eccentricity, which KI-NRT calls quirky without overwhelming the senses: Alice in Wonderland porcelain by Lladró, a Hobbit-house wine cellar and a Gaudí-inspired installation in front of the communal baths, and a lounge with free drinks and snacks.

cities.text: Tōhoku Shinkansen Tokyo→Kōriyama (~80 min), change to a JR Tōhoku Main Line local→Sukagawa (~10 min), then the ~10-min inn shuttle (reserve).
Hokuriku Shinkansen Kanazawa→Ōmiya, cross to a 'Yamabiko'→Kōriyama, then a Tōhoku local→Sukagawa + shuttle. Reliable Shinkansen the whole way to the branch.
Reverse of: Tōhoku Main Line local Sukagawa→Kōriyama (~10 min), transfer to Tōhoku Shinkansen→Sendai (~40 min), plus the ~10-min inn shuttle (reserve).

inns.name: Sui Suwako
inns.summary: A new-ish, modern 8-room ryokan on Lake Suwa that KI-NRT has now stayed at three times and calls his go-to in the area, definitely the top luxury inn near Matsumoto, with excellent local-smelt kaiseki and a rooftop mixed-gender bath looking across the lake to the Alps. The rooms are the modest part, comfortable and functional but not opulent. It is a reliable anchor for the Matsumoto and Nakasendo corridor and not a destination in itself.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Meals are served in the room, and KI-NRT found them excellent, including the wakasagi tempura, which they prepared specifically for his party (he had learned beforehand that wakasagi, Japanese smelt, is a delicacy, a small fish caught in Lake Suwa but not in large volumes). The Japanese breakfast was delightful, and on his third stay in 2023 the food was still great, as solid as on his two earlier visits.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The rooftop communal onsen, which KI-NRT calls incredible, looks out over Lake Suwa to the Japan Alps in the distance. It is mixed-gender and bathing suits are required, so families and men and women can enjoy the open-air bath together (the inn lends onsen wear free of charge). On a later visit he noticed a faint smell of chlorine, which was unfortunate but understandable. The top room type also has its own open-air hot spring bath.

service.label: Service
service.text: The service was polished on KI-NRT's third stay, as it had been on his earlier two, and on an earlier visit they prepared the wakasagi tempura specifically for his party.

room.label: Room
room.text: There are only two room types among the eight rooms of the five-story building, and the top type is the Wide Japanese/Western-style room with open-air hot spring bath. KI-NRT calls the rooms simple, functional, comfortable and sufficient, though not supremely opulent. He stayed in Room 501 on the top floor, which is likely the best room with the best view of the lake and mountains, and found the accommodations comfortable again on his third stay.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Sui Suwako sits on the banks of Lake Suwa in Shimosuwa-shuku, a post town on the Nakasendo, and from the rooftop bath the view sweeps over the lake, the surrounding town and some of Nagano's famous mountains, with the Japan Alps in the distance. KI-NRT uses the inn as a first night on the way to Matsumoto Castle and calls it an excellent choice for anyone walking the Nakasendo.

cities.text: Reverse of: Ltd Exp 'Azusa' Kamisuwa/Shimosuwa→Shinjuku (~2h13–2h22, direct), plus the ~5–10-min inn car. Suwa's real advantage: the Azusa reaches it ~25 min before Matsumoto, so it is the closest north inn to Tokyo after the Gunma pair. Azusa timetable: Shinjuku→Kamisuwa 2h13–2h22, Kamisuwa→Matsumoto 24–25 min. Kamisuwa (Sui Suwako, ~10-min car) and Shimosuwa (Iwanoyu, ~5-min car) are one stop apart, so they share this loc.

Reverse of: Via Matsumoto: 'Shinano'→Nagano (~50 min), change to the Hokuriku Shinkansen→Kanazawa (~65–70 min). Getting to Matsumoto from Suwa (inn car + the 24–25-min 'Azusa', then a self-handled change onto the onward train) costs one MORE transfer and ~20 min vs the Matsumoto counterpart — priced in here; the onward rail is identical and already researched.

inns.name: THE YUKAWA Ichijoh Branch
inns.summary: An eleven-suite modern ryokan opened in September 2025 in a forested valley on the Yukawa River outside Shiroishi, the flagship of the Ichijo family, twenty generations of innkeepers since 1428, with a private open-air onsen bath and a fully private dining room for every party. KI-NRT gives the kitchen the edge over its venerable neighbor Michinokuan, and the top suite ranks among the nicest modern ryokan rooms of his many stays; the one drawback is that it costs noticeably more than Michinokuan for comparable rooms.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner leans on Miyagi itself: sea urchin in the shell and conger eel from the Sanriku coast, Zao wagyu and nodagamo duck from local farms, and Zao's Tsuyahime rice, which KI-NRT says rivals Niigata's famous varieties. His favourites were a horsehair-crab clear soup and conger eel with foie gras and balsamic sansho, which worked surprisingly well. Nothing is avant-garde, but every dish was well prepared, and he gives it the edge over Michinokuan.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every one of the eleven suites has its own open-air onsen bath on the balcony looking onto the Yukawa River, fed by Yukawa Onsen, a source newly drilled along the riverbank whose minerals are similar to the famed Kamasaki Onsen next door, which supplies the family's Yunishi Ichijo. Two private baths can be reserved free of charge; they are a bit larger and even closer to the river than the suite bath, but KI-NRT would not call them a must-do.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT and his party were wonderfully looked after by a caring and friendly staff, especially Mr. Shigeta, their dinner server and bartender, and Ms. Hamada, who speaks good English after a homestay in California. They were the only guests in the house that night, so he could not see the service under a full house, though he imagines it would remain exemplary, and the three Rakuten guests so far mark service a full 5.0.

room.label: Room
room.text: All eleven accommodations are suites with their own open-air hot-spring bath. KI-NRT took the River View Yukawa Suite, the top category at 90 m², elegantly appointed with a balcony of lounge chairs beside the onsen bath, and calls it easily one of the nicest rooms of the many modern ryokans he has stayed at. Nine are standalone villa suites, and he found the 80 m² River View Villa Suite excellent too, with vaulted ceilings, closer to the river.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The Yukawa is a modern retreat tucked into a valley of lush forest with the Yukawa River flowing directly in front, and the view from the suite balcony is mesmerizing; the Zao range, with its Okama crater and late-winter snow monsters, is just north. Shiroishi itself does not have a ton to offer and is usually a stop on a Tohoku road trip, with Michinokuan less than a kilometre away. The architecture is strikingly contemporary.

cities.text: Tōhoku Shinkansen 'Yamabiko' Tokyo→Shiroishi-Zaō (~1h50; the fast 'Hayabusa' does NOT stop there), then the inn's free shuttle (~15–20 min).

Hokuriku Shinkansen Kanazawa→Ōmiya (~2h01), cross to a Shiroishi-Zaō-calling 'Yamabiko' (~12–13/day, roughly hourly; Ōmiya→Shiroishi-Zaō ~1h23) + inn shuttle (~18 min). One change at Ōmiya — the 4.4h prices the wait for the select Yamabiko; off-peak an added Fukushima/Sendai change can beat waiting (→2 changes).
Reverse of: Inn shuttle to Shiroishi-Zaō (~15 min), Tōhoku Shinkansen 'Yamabiko'→Sendai (~13 min).

inns.name: Taiza Onsen Sumihei
inns.summary: A 23-room inn from 1868 on the Tango Peninsula that exists for Taiza-gani, the 'phantom crab' that only five local boats bring in. The crab kaiseki is inventive and outstanding, the service is impeccable and the silk-art rooms are handsome. The onsen in the name is trucked, heated, chlorinated water with a noticeable chlorine smell in every bath, and KI-NRT says this is not the inn to book if bathing is a priority. The crab is why you go.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The Kiwame course is the only one with Taiza-gani, the 'phantom crab' that five local boats bring in, and it is capped at eight guests, so book months ahead. Every dish was outstanding: yubiki body meat barely scalded, legs swished in the dashi pot until they open like a flower, and tomalley fresh enough to eat raw. KI-NRT puts the crab cooking slightly ahead of Bouyourou's, but a loud table in the semi-private dining room drowned out the server.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The spring water is trucked in, circulated, heated and chlorine-sterilized, and the chlorine smell was pronounced in every bath KI-NRT tried, in the room and in the six private rental baths alike (five are free to use). Lower room categories have no bath of their own and there is no large communal bath. He says this is definitely not the ryokan to visit if onsen is a high priority.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was impeccable from start to finish. Mr. Wada looked after Mrs. KI-NRT's mother's wheelchair and guided the party throughout, and the young dinner and breakfast servers, Aoi Yamada and Kou Kamataki, were enthusiastic and knowledgeable. Mr. Kamataki is decent in English, so if you don't speak Japanese he would be a good choice as your server.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms are modern Japanese, light and airy with high ceilings, and the standout is the Oshie raised-cloth artwork in Tango Chirimen silk on the bedroom walls, with snow crabs, stars, cosmos or moon depending on the room. Kinean runs 60m² and the Sanzenhou special room 78.6m² with an open-air terrace bath, a minor step up. KI-NRT finds the higher-end rooms nicer and roomier than Bouyourou's, but the lower categories have no onsen.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Sumihei sits off the beaten path on the rugged Tango Peninsula, steps from the tiny port where the five Taiza-gani boats come in, and that closeness to the water gives every room an ocean view and a sunset, partly obscured by power lines. A separate 2017 lounge building has a library and a terrace with panoramic sea views and the same silk art as the rooms. It is also the only luxury inn here that takes children under 13.

cities.text: Ltd Exp 'Hashidate' Kyoto→Amino direct (~2h30). Snow-risk in January.
Reverse of: Amino→Kyoto (~2h30) + Shinkansen→Tokyo (~2h15) — a full travel day.

inns.name: Tsukihitei
inns.summary: Tsukihitei is a five-room 1902 hideaway inside Nara's primeval forest, rescued from datedness by the Miyako Hotel Group's 2023–25 renovations, and it is now KI-NRT's clear answer to where luxury travelers should sleep in Nara, with first-rate creative kaiseki and a superb rebuilt villa in a setting nothing nearby matches. There is no onsen, and only the three refurbished rooms deliver the full experience.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki is creative and plated with great care, and the standout was local: a clear soup of Yamato duck coated in kuzu with fried Miwa somen and yuzu, simple-looking with remarkable depth. Hokkaido abalone and sea urchin were both outstanding. KI-NRT notes the kitchen sources from across Japan instead of the region, which he does not hold against it, though it feels different from regional ryokans that proudly detail their provenance.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at Tsukihitei, so the baths are ordinary heated water: the Sakura Villa has its own hinoki tub, and two indoor private baths in the main building can be used whenever they are free. Nobody has written more about the bathing than that.

service.label: Service
service.text: The three renovated rooms (Sakura, Wakaba and Take no Ma) have meals served in the room, and Hagi and Yanagi eat in private rooms a few steps away, so everyone dines privately. The one lapse KI-NRT mentions is that the dinner server did not elaborate much on the menu, beyond saying the abalone and sea urchin came from Hokkaido. Beyond that, nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Sakura Villa, rebuilt in April 2023, is a 90-square-meter suite in a modern rural Japanese style: a tatami room with a recessed floor under the table, heated floors, Western beds, a hinoki bath, fast internet and no television, a sensible omission in KI-NRT's view. Sakura, Wakaba and Take no Ma were all refurbished between 2023 and early 2025 and he recommends one of those three; Hagi and Yanagi are unrenovated and noticeably simpler.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Tsukihitei stands inside the Kasugayama Primeval Forest, a UNESCO-listed stretch of ancient cedar, and the grounds are an extension of the forest, with a stone lantern, a small bridge over a creek and covered wooden walkways linking the buildings. They are small but wonderfully atmospheric, and the trailheads are minutes from Nara Park, Todaiji and Kasuga Taisha. For somewhere central yet secluded, KI-NRT says Tsukihitei has no equal.

cities.text: Kintetsu Kyoto→Kintetsu-Nara (~45 min), ~5-min taxi.
Reverse of: Kintetsu Nara Line Rapid Express Kintetsu-Nara→Osaka-Namba (~36 min, direct, ~every 15 min).

inns.name: Auberge Suzukane
inns.summary: Suzukane is a corporate-owned ryokan in the center of Bandai Atami run by a former wedding coordinator, with a full suit of knight's armor at the entrance, and the reasons to stay are the food, the warmth of the staff and the big renovated rooms with source-fed in-room onsen. KI-NRT loved it and regretted nothing, but was plain that nearby Atamiso is on a slightly higher plane, because Suzukane is in town with only a courtyard for outdoor space and its dining is half-private. It is the one to pick when creativity at the table matters more to you than the view out the window.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kitchen does creative kaiseki with subtle European accents (it cooked French until about eight years ago), and KI-NRT called the dinner exceptional: onion mousse with caviar as a dip for raw purple asparagus, Miyagi oysters he found sublime, and portions bigger than at the other inns on the trip. The one miss was the carpaccio-style abalone, which they would rather have had cooked. Breakfast was among the top five he has ever had at a ryokan.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every room has its own bath of free-flowing, direct-source Bandai Atami spring water (a favorite of KI-NRT's), and the VIP room Kinu adds an open-air onsen and a ganban-yoku, a dry sauna where you lie on heated stones. He found the private onsen delightful but a bit snug for two. The two private rental baths, Kane-no-yu and Suzu-no-yu, each have both a hot and a cold spring pool, which makes them enjoyable in summer as well.

service.label: Service
service.text: The staff were outstanding, and the okami Mayumi Suzuki, a former wedding coordinator who took the role in 2020, served dinner in a tag-team with the nakai Ms. Amitou, who was professional, attentive and always available. When KI-NRT mentioned going on to Nanyo the next day, the okami came back with a binder of maps, route options and printouts of the attractions, and he said she bent over backwards to ensure a wonderful stay.

room.label: Room
room.text: Every room is 90 square meters with a Western living area, a tatami room and a bedroom with proper beds. Kinu, the VIP room, was renovated in October 2024 in a low-key modern Japanese style with the latest technology and artistic touches, and it is the one with the open-air bath and the hot-stone spa. Next to Atamiso's traditional rooms, which show slight signs of age, KI-NRT found these the more modern and better equipped.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Suzukane is in the town center of Bandai Atami, and its only outdoor space is an inner courtyard leading to the guest rooms, so there is no garden and none of the seclusion of Atamiso ten minutes away, whose manicured grounds KI-NRT calls spectacular. This is where Atamiso holds the edge for him: a more tranquil setting, and private dining where Suzukane's half-koshitsu arrangement lets the sound of neighboring guests intrude.

cities.text: Ban'etsu West line from Koriyama to Bandai-Atami Station is about 15 min, then a short taxi to Auberge Suzukane.
Tohoku Shinkansen Yamabiko Tokyo to Koriyama is about 1h20-1h30, then the 15 min Ban'etsu West local to Bandai-Atami plus a short taxi.

transit.note: This is Bandai-Atami in Fukushima (not Shizuoka Atami); reached via Koriyama on the Tohoku Shinkansen.

inns.name: Gora Kadan Fuji
inns.summary: Gora Kadan opened its second-ever property in July 2025, a 42-room ryokan-hotel hybrid facing Fuji and big enough for a gym, a pool and three dining rooms. The one guest who has written it up found the stay exceeded his expectations and immediately rebooked a villa; KI-NRT, who has not stayed, expects at worst a Hoshino resort done right, and a 2026 guest called that very accurate. Only the Open-air Bath Suites and up have spring water in the room, so check the room grade before booking, and book the sushi or teppanyaki counter over the included kaiseki.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: There are three ways to eat: the included kaiseki, the teppanyaki counter Fuji Kanda and a sushi counter run by Sushi Sho. Fc912 found the selection varied and enjoyed Fuji Kanda, and a June 2026 guest called the food outstanding. Web reports say the kaiseki is the weak point for a Gora Kadan and the counters are where the kitchen is strongest, so the sensible pattern is kaiseki one night and a counter the next.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The property drilled its own spring 1,500 meters down, and the onsen feeds a bath building with indoor and open-air baths, saunas, an indoor pool and a Fuji-facing infinity pool, plus in-room baths in every suite. Which grades get spring water in the room is not published, and KI-NRT had heard the standard suites' view baths are plain well water, so ask. Nobody has described a soak here, though Fc912 rebooked the hare villa for its onsen pool.

service.label: Service
service.text: Fc912, who stayed a few months after the July 2025 opening, hit some service issues, though in his view none significant enough to complain about and the kind of thing a new ryokan irons out within a few months. Nobody who has stayed since has written about the service.

room.label: Room
room.text: The build quality struck Fc912 as top notch, and a June 2026 guest called the rooms beautiful. The ground-floor rooms with stone baths have lovely garden views but no sight of Mt. Fuji, so if the mountain is what you came for, avoid them and book upstairs. The hare villa, which Fc912 rebooked for a return in April, is essentially a two-bedroom suite with a large onsen pool, and the Open-air Bath Suites run 136 to 139 square metres.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: All 42 rooms look at Mt. Fuji, 12 km away, at Subashiri just south of Lake Yamanaka, with a Gora Kadan golf course next door. Fc912 found the views spectacular, though KI-NRT, who has not stayed, is not a huge fan of Fuji from this angle compared with Lake Kawaguchi's. Fuji is a daily coin flip: a June 2026 guest got only a glimpse through cloud, and the first winter's guests had no view one day and a glorious one the next, so book two nights.

cities.text: Shinkansen Tokyo→Mishima (~50 min 'Kodama'/'Hikari'), then a SELF-BOOKED taxi ~40 min (the inn's published route — it is not a hotel car; pre-book, Mishima's rank is shallow). Free alt: the inn's call-on-arrival shuttle from Gotemba Stn (~20 min, per the inn FAQ; limited vehicles) via the Odakyu 'Fujisan'/hourly Shinjuku highway bus. Direct HND private transfer ~1h30 on arrival day.
Reverse of: Hotel car back to Mishima (~40 min), Tōkaidō Shinkansen→Kyoto (~2h).
San'yō 'Nozomi' Hiroshima→Nagoya (~2h05), 'Hikari'/'Kodama'→Mishima (~1h–1h15), then the hotel car ~40 min (car-only access — arrange the transfer).

inns.name: Yado Shiontei
inns.summary: A 10-room crab ryokan that opened in 2021 in Kaike Onsen, with modern hardware built to a very high quality, all-suite rooms on the area's saltwater spring and service Fc912 called pretty perfect, but the crab itself ranked below Nishimuraya and Bouyourou for the two parties who tried it, at roughly double Nishimuraya's per-person rate. The building and the rare water justify a stay; if the Matsuba-gani course is what matters most, both reviewers point you elsewhere.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is a Matsuba-gani (snow crab) course served in one of five private dining rooms: sashimi, charcoal-grilled crab, shabu-shabu and the Koura Zake, where the crab head is grilled in its shell and cooked with sake poured inside, which KI-NRT found amazing. The kitchen brought the best out of the crab and the non-crab dishes were delightful, but he could not get Nishimuraya Honkan out of his mind, and Fc912 preferred the crab at Bouyourou.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The water is Kaike Onsen's rare saltwater hot spring, found in the early 1900s by a fisherman who saw bubbles rising 200 metres offshore, and the area is considered a pioneer of thalassotherapy. Every room has its own onsen bath, there is no communal bath, and the single private rental bath was no bigger than the bath in KI-NRT's room and no more impressive. Fc912 was glad of it, because the baths in his room Kuon felt a bit cramped.

service.label: Service
service.text: Fc912 found the service pretty perfect, and surprisingly flexible for a ryokan in a region that sees few Western guests. KI-NRT's own review says nothing about the service either way.

room.label: Room
room.text: All ten rooms are true suites with in-room onsen, in a modern Japanese build of very high quality (impeccable, Fc912 said). The two Kihinshitsu (special rooms), Reirou and Kuon, are 150 square metres with indoor and outdoor baths and no shared walls. KI-NRT preferred Reirou, because Kuon is slightly less contemporary and has an Edwardian-style couch, and Reirou is at the end of the corridor, so he never heard a footstep.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The inn is on a main street in central Yonago among bland buildings, and from outside nothing says luxury. Inside it is an oasis of tranquility, with ikebana, small dry rock gardens, a little tea room where two corridors meet and a gallery of works by living National Treasures, though the grounds are not expansive. Matsue Castle, Izumo Taisha and the Adachi Museum garden are nearby, and Fc912 found the region peaceful with few tourists.

cities.text: Okayama to Yonago ~2h on Yakumo LEX, then ~15 min car to Kaike Onsen.
~30 min by car from Yonago/Miho Airport to Kaike Onsen.

inns.name: Bettei Amafuru Oka
inns.summary: Bettei Amafuru Oka is a 15-room annex on a hill over Kagoshima Bay, the most upscale stay in Ibusuki, taking just four groups a day and grafted onto a half-dormant resort complex, but it has onsen in every room, the sunaburo-and-ceramic-spa circuit, warm Nepali-staffed hospitality and chef Kanemasa Matsumoto's serious French cooking. The bathing culture and the bay views make the stay, and the surrounding complex feels eerie, dated and underused.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is a choice of French, kaiseki or teppanyaki, and KI-NRT took the French at Céleste, where chef Kanemasa Matsumoto cooks with Kagoshima ingredients (Osumi eel, Yakushima tuna, Kuroge wagyu). There are fewer courses than a kaiseki but the execution was superb: foie gras and grilled unagi over scrambled eggs, kanpachi carpaccio with caviar and mango, and Ibusuki beef grilled over Sakurajima lava rocks. Breakfast is Western only.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every room has its own onsen, and in the Amafuru Suite it is a hinoki tub on the balcony with killer views over the bay, and KI-NRT found the water wonderfully silky. The rest is reached through the Bay Hills wing: several private onsens, Ibusuki's sunaburo (buried to the neck in heated volcanic sand for ten to fifteen minutes) and a ceramic spa where you soak among radiostone beads heated by spring water, which he found a striking detox.

service.label: Service
service.text: Most of the staff are from Nepal, living in Japan with their families and fluent in Japanese, and KI-NRT did not miss native staff: Bichitra, Sunik and Sita served his meals with exceptional knowledge of each dish, and everyone was sweet, professional and eager to please. The GM says the property would not be viable without foreign help, and it takes only four groups a day, so he calls the whole thing a superb, hospitality-driven experience.

room.label: Room
room.text: The 112 square metre Amafuru Suite is spacious and airy with natural light, a sunrise view over the bay from the balcony (where the onsen sits) and a complimentary minibar stocked with Krug, and the interiors were refreshed when the annex opened in late 2020. KI-NRT's reservation is that it feels more like a hotel room than a luxury ryokan, with mostly carpeted floors and furnishings that could sit comfortably in a four-star hotel.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The annex sits on a hill over Kagoshima Bay, with a Steinway in reception, and on its own side it is serene and soothing. It is grafted onto the former Greenpia Ibusuki, whose surgeon owner made part a cancer hospital and the rest the 103-room Bay Hills hotel, nearly empty when KI-NRT stayed, so the vast, dated public areas you cross to the spa and restaurants feel eerie and underused, though they hold a library, a golf simulator and a theater.

cities.text: Ibusuki no Tamatebako / JR from Kagoshima-Chuo (~50 min) or ~50 min by car to the inn.
Shinkansen Hakata to Kagoshima-Chuo (~1h20), then local train/car ~50 min down to Ibusuki.

inns.name: Fufu Kawaguchiko
inns.summary: Fufu Kawaguchiko is the Fufu group's flagship, a modern, youthful hotel-ryokan hybrid that KI-NRT calls the only choice for luxury travelers in the Fuji Five Lakes, though a slight notch below Fufu Nikko in most aspects. Everyone likes it and nobody is blown away. His reservations center on the noisy, crowded dinner room and on service that is polished but impersonal for 32 rooms, and the famous view is partially blocked by trees. Book the highest floor you can, ideally one of the two top suites with the open-air onsen bath.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kitchen does innovative modern kaiseki that stays Japanese: udon made partly from charcoal so the noodles are black, several courses of Fujinosuke (a salmon and trout cross), and KI-NRT found it mostly successful in balancing creativity with flavor. The champagne and Bordeaux list is deep, and Morita-san's fruit cocktails match Tokyo's best bars. The one drawback is the dining room, where two seatings pack the tables and it gets noisy.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The two 136 m² Luxury Premium Suites, the rooms KI-NRT tells you to book, have their own open-air bath of natural hot-spring water and a large balcony with a panoramic view of Mt. Fuji. Beyond noting that the bath is there, nobody who has stayed has written anything about the bathing itself.

service.label: Service
service.text: The staff are mostly young, which gives the place a casual, energetic feel without any snobbery, and the service is attentive and well coordinated: a 2024 couple got a warm welcome and a visit from the GM during dinner. KI-NRT found it lacks the personal touch of the finer family-owned ryokans and is unbefitting a property of only 32 rooms, decent service but not the memorable kind; he also wanted the waiters trained to explain each dish.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms are contemporary and bright, with greenery everywhere, and the ones to get are the two 136 m² Luxury Premium Suites, with a separate living room, an open-air onsen bath and a balcony facing Mt. Fuji. KI-NRT loved his but felt it lived more like 90–100 m², with a slightly claustrophobic bedroom. A 2024 guest's Comfort Suite showed some wear but was tasteful and comfortable. Ask for the third floor, which sees the lake and Fuji.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The hotel sits on a slight rise about a mile back from Lake Kawaguchi, with a good but not exceptional view of Mt. Fuji on a clear day: tall pines on a neighbor's property block the left side (the owner declined to have them cut), so the higher floors see more. The shore is a five-minute ride on one of the hotel's e-bikes, and KI-NRT says nothing beats the Lake Kawaguchi area, with Chureito Pagoda nearby, for the most picturesque views of Fuji.

cities.text: Reverse of: JR 'Fuji Excursion' Ltd Exp Kawaguchiko→Shinjuku direct (~2h, ~4/day). Miss it → Fujikyu→Ōtsuki + Chūō Ltd Exp = ~2h25, 1 change.

Round the south side of Fuji rather than back through Tokyo: Fujikyu 'Mishima·Kawaguchiko Liner' bus Kawaguchiko→Mishima (~1h30–1h40, roughly hourly, ¥2,700 — japan-guide, Oct 2025), one change at Mishima, then the Tōkaidō Shinkansen Mishima→Kyoto (~1h51 on a Hikari that calls at Mishima, ~2h27 on the all-stations Kodama — ekitan). ~4h15 door-to-door with the inn shuttle and the change. (Via Tokyo — 'Fuji Excursion'→Shinjuku, cross to Tokyo Station, 'Nozomi'→Kyoto — is ~4h30 and two changes, and the Fuji Excursion runs only ~4/day.)

inns.name: Hotel Iyaonsen
inns.summary: A 20-room hotel perched over Shikoku's remote Iya Valley that KI-NRT calls a great experience even though, as luxury ryokans go, it is on the lower end of the scale: the incredible gorge setting (astonishingly gorgeous in fall foliage season) and the cable-car ride down to the riverside baths on the valley floor more than make up for the minor shortcomings, and both the service and the kitchen impressed him more than he expected. He would return. Try for Tamayura (Room #505), the only room with an en-suite open-air onsen bath.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kitchen focuses on local ingredients and recipes. The first dinner blew KI-NRT away, with salt-grilled amago (a river trout) that was full of flavour and edible from head to tail, Iya soba made from 100% buckwheat, pike conger, and raw konjac and raw yuba served like sashimi, which he called sublime. The second dinner dipped, with a frozen-tasting udon, and he suspects most guests stay one night so the kitchen has few Plan B dishes.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The baths to use are down on the valley floor, reached by cable car: separate men's and women's communal onsen plus private rental baths, all on natural hot-spring water that KI-NRT found amazing, soft and slippery, with the river flowing right in front of you. The open-air bath on the deck of the top room Tamayura is not free-flowing, so you fill it from scratch each time, and the shower is outside too, painful in the dead of winter.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT came away impressed by the level of service over a two-night stay, which more than met his expectations for a hotel this remote, though he does not single out any one gesture or member of staff.

room.label: Room
room.text: Of the 20 rooms, the one to try for is Tamayura, a top-floor corner suite and the only room with an en-suite open-air onsen bath. At 47 square metres it is not massive and smaller than top rooms elsewhere, but the open layout (living room, a nook for the valley view and the sleeping area) made it feel bigger than the number suggests. The decor is Japanese but modern, in earthy tones with plenty of natural light, and it seemed fresh and new.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The hotel is perched over the Iya Valley, a remote mountainous part of rural Shikoku, and the view down the gorge is incredible, astonishingly gorgeous in fall foliage season. Getting there is part of the adventure: the road in is twisty and in places only one car wide, and you need a rental car, since nothing except the Peeing Boy statue is within walking distance. KI-NRT found the hassle added to the charm of being somewhere so remote.

cities.text: Limited Express Nanpu from Okayama to Oboke Station runs about 1h40 via the Seto bridge and Dosan line, then roughly 30 min by car into the Iya Valley.
Limited Express from Tokushima to Oboke via the Dosan line is about 1h20, then roughly 30 min by car to the onsen.

inns.name: Kagaya Bettei Matsunomidori
inns.summary: The 31-room luxury annex of the giant Kagaya, which KI-NRT calls the top ryokan in Wakura Onsen hands down, with museum-grade art in the public areas, gracious staff and fine Noto seafood. His December 2023 return did not live up to the fond memories of 2016, because the push-button in-room bath is a real flaw at this level, and he now places it a step below some of his other recent top luxury stays. For now the point is moot, because Matsunomidori is being demolished after the 2024 Noto quake and Kagaya is consolidating it into a new building of about 40 rooms due at the end of FY2027.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Noto seafood is what the kitchen does best, and both meals are served in a private dining room. The sashimi, the amaebi sweet shrimp above all, was sublime on KI-NRT's 2023 stay, and so was the boiled kano-gani snow crab, though not every dish was exceptional and the breakfast portions ran small. In crab season you can choose a standard kaiseki instead of an all-crab menu, and he doubts the crab course would match Nishimuraya Honkan or Bouyourou.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The in-room bath is the biggest shortcoming. Onsen does not flow into it continuously; you push a button to fill it with hot-spring water, the temperature is not regulated, and once it goes lukewarm you drain it and start again, so get in the moment it is full. KI-NRT calls this a real hassle and unacceptable at a luxury onsen ryokan, and not all rooms have an onsen bath. The communal open-air bath gets around it.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT describes the service as incredible, competent, gentle and graceful, and the polish he found in 2016 still held on his December 2023 return. Everything in the minibar is free, and the lounge serves coffee, tea and manju all day at no charge. Only guests aged 13 and older are allowed, so it stays tranquil for couples. Make sure you book Matsunomidori and not the main Kagaya next door, which is the normal version run by the same owner.

room.label: Room
room.text: The top room, the 140m² Special Room with Open-Air Bath, has a living room, a tatami room and a separate bedroom, and apart from the tatami room it is carpeted and furnished Western-style, with beds instead of futons. Everything was in tip-top shape on KI-NRT's 2023 stay, but the room felt a tad dated to him, the shower tiles among the elements that have not aged well. The standard rooms have the checkerboard tatami Matsunomidori is known for.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The public areas are massive and amount to an indoor museum of ceramics and Wajima-nuri lacquerware, the work of the craftsman Kado Isaburo above all. Outside is the renowned garden of manicured pines, fronted by Tokuryoan, a historic tea house built by the Maeda clan and moved here when the ryokan opened, with stupendous views across the sea to Noto Island; book the tea ceremony early. Wakura Onsen itself never became a walkable onsen town.

inns.name: Nakanobo Zuien
inns.summary: A 47-room adults-only inn from 1868 in the heart of Arima Onsen, run as a polished hybrid hotel with carpeted halls, a public cafe and a gift shop, and nothing like an intimate ryokan. Its 2023-renovated VIP rooms have their own Kinsen and Ginsen stone baths, a twin-water combination no one else in town offers, and in one of those rooms KI-NRT calls it possibly the best choice in Arima. Across two visits a decade apart his verdict is warm but measured, a solid luxury pick when you are already in Kansai, though he is not sure he would go out of his way for Arima.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner was fantastic, particularly the teppanyaki. The cold chawanmushi, the sashimi platter and the seared Kobe beef nigiri were standouts, and the scallops, romaine and shimeji mushrooms cooked in butter were surprisingly delicious. The Kobe filet was excellent but not the top grade they offer, so KI-NRT would order the Chateaubriand every time. He preferred the food here to Gosho Bessho's, and breakfast was hearty but drew no wow.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The VIP rooms have both of Arima's waters on the deck, a Kinsen (the golden spring, iron-rich water that turns reddish-brown in the air) and a Ginsen (the clear silver spring) in stone tubs, and no other inn in town offers the pair. The water is 100% pure onsen but recirculated (junkan) and not continually fed kakenagashi, which KI-NRT suspects is true of every luxury inn in supply-limited Arima, and the temperature was right for long soaks.

service.label: Service
service.text: Ms. Kominami, who took care of the meals, was a highlight of the stay, enthusiastic, patient with KI-NRT's many questions about the dishes, and attentive, serving a refill of sake within minutes of the request. The property runs more like a hotel than a ryokan, with shoes staying on until you reach your room, and it is adults-only (guests must be at least 13).

room.label: Room
room.text: The VIP rooms are the ones to book. Wako, 119 m², has a Western-style living room, a tatami room, a separate bedroom with two double beds, two toilets and a deck with the Kinsen and Ginsen stone tubs; Atago, 99 m², combines the living and tatami areas into one space and has one toilet, but the tubs are the same size and the experience the same. Both were renovated in 2023 and have modern comforts without the musty smell of older properties.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The location is the main advantage, in the heart of Arima Onsen adjacent to the main street, with the shops, restaurants, cafes, temples and museums at your doorstep, a convenience KI-NRT says cannot be overstated. Arima is one of Japan's top three hot-spring towns, though KI-NRT has never been particularly fond of the town itself. The inn has its own garden, lit at night, but with 47 rooms and carpeted floors it has the feel of a hotel.

cities.text: Osaka Stn/Umeda to Arima Onsen ~60 min direct highway bus, then ~5 min to inn.
Shin-Kobe/Sannomiya to Arima ~30 min by bus or Kobe Electric Rly, then ~5 min.

inns.name: Yoyokaku
inns.summary: A 19-room inn in Karatsu, Saga, formed in 1893, with museum-grade Meiji-era architecture, a magnificent old-pine garden, a Karatsu pottery gallery and excellent in-room kaiseki from the local catch, at prices near the very bottom of the high-end range. The retired chairman lives on site and will happily host guests for hours in good English. KI-NRT calls it one of his most authentic ryokan stays ever, and Michaeljinnyc pronounced it sublime. The one drawback is that there is no onsen anywhere on site.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is kaiseki from the waters around Saga, served in your own room. KI-NRT called it excellent: okoze came as sashimi and battered and deep-fried, and there was ikejime grouper ara-ni, the fatty meat around the bones, simmered. It was not the best kaiseki he has ever had, though local delicacies are part of the appeal of rural Japan. Breakfast was creative too, with a firm, dashi-infused tofu the highlight.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen anywhere at Yoyokaku, and the tub in the room and even the communal bath run ordinary heated water. KI-NRT calls that a bit of a downer, and says an onsen would be especially welcome for a stay in the colder months.

service.label: Service
service.text: The retired chairman, Akihito Okouchi, still lives on site and hosted KI-NRT for several hours with tea and sweets, then walked him through the property explaining its craftsmanship and history in good English. Ask to meet him, because he loves interacting with guests. The okami, his daughter-in-law, is a former English teacher and fluent, and KI-NRT found the staff throughout charming, elegant and sophisticated.

room.label: Room
room.text: Tonbo (room 211) is a ground-floor corner room with an awesome view of the garden, tatami with a low table and zabuton cushions and no sofa, chairs or beds, and the futons go down after dinner in the room's second section, so the table stays put. KI-NRT found none of the usual old-inn compromises (creaky floors, thin insulation, slow internet), and the WiFi was lightning fast. The bathroom has a single sink and a plain, non-onsen tub.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yoyokaku was formed in 1893, and each step down its wooden corridors made KI-NRT feel he was slipping back to the Meiji era. The magnificent garden is dominated by old matsu pines, which give the inn its sense of place, and the ground-floor rooms open onto it. A small gallery shows Karatsu-yaki pottery by local artisans. It is a few blocks from the sea (you can sometimes hear the waves) and from Karatsu Castle, which is not visible from the inn.

cities.text: Fukuoka City Subway Kūkō Line through-running onto the JR Chikuhi Line, Hakata→Karatsu (~75 min, no change on through services; the subway segment isn't JR-Pass-covered), then a short taxi to Yoyokaku. By car ~55 km / ~1h via the Nishi-Kyushu Expwy free sections — lowland, winter-trivial.
Reverse of: Chikuhi-line through-train Karatsu→Hakata (~1h25, ~every 30 min), then 'Sakura'→Kagoshima-Chūō (~1h35; 'Mizuho' 1h16).
Reverse of: Chikuhi through-train→Hakata (~1h25), 'Relay Kamome'→Takeo-Onsen + 'Kamome'→Nagasaki (~1.4h). (The Matsuura-railway coastal route is lovely and ~6h — a day out, not a transfer.)
Reverse of: Chikuhi through-train→Hakata (~1h20), 'Sakura'/'Mizuho'→Kumamoto (~38 min).
Airport bus Kanazawa→Komatsu + KMQ→Fukuoka (~1h40) into Hakata, then the subway/JR Chikuhi through-service Hakata→Karatsu (~75 min). ~5h door-to-door.

inns.name: Zaborin
inns.summary: Zaborin has been Niseko's established luxury ryokan since 2015, with fantastic hardware, two onsen baths in every room and a loyal following, and the three guests who reviewed it here enjoyed it, one calling it a contender for KI-NRT's top ten. But the food and service reports have turned mixed, founder Shouya Grigg now calls neighbouring Shiguchi the ryokan he always wanted to make, and the most recent visitor, who did both back-to-back, would give a single Niseko night to Shiguchi.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is mostly traditional kaiseki, and there is a private meal at an irori hearth that cristmh found very unique. Reports differ by year. cristmh had incredible food in 2019, Fliar excellent food in autumn 2024, and mattjp in 2025 got a meal that was perfectly fine and not particularly memorable next to the terrific modern tasting menu at Shiguchi next door. KI-NRT has heard mixed reports on the food from Japanese travellers.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every room has two gensen kakenagashi onsen baths, real source-fed hot spring water flowing through, one indoors and one outside on the spacious deck, so you bathe without leaving your room. cristmh called the rooms with their indoor and outdoor onsens amazing, and Fliar singled the two baths out as well.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is the weak point. Fliar found the staff very good and mattjp had no particular misses, but housekeeping did not impress Fliar, and mattjp found the service at Shiguchi next door meaningfully better. luckypeach skipped a planned 2020 stay after Japanese reviewers reported a service drop with pandemic staff turnover, and says it was never celebrated for service anyway, with check-in at a lobby counter and nobody walking you to your room.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms are the strongest thing here, amazing in cristmh's words and very spacious at around 120 square metres with a large deck, and mattjp, who stayed at Zaborin and Shiguchi on consecutive nights, gave Zaborin a slight edge on hard product. Fliar's one gripe was a living room too sparse even by minimalist Japanese standards, where some ikebana or a few art works would not have gone amiss. luckypeach calls the hardware fantastic.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Zaborin is a very modern build in the Niseko countryside at Kutchan, designed by the Sapporo architect Makoto Nakayama with founder Shouya Grigg, understated and beautiful, though mattjp found it quite hotel-like beside Shiguchi, which looks as if it had stood there for 50 years. The location is beautiful, and the approach from Chitose passes through the national park, which Fliar enjoyed for the autumn colours even though the road was very busy.

cities.text: ~2 hr by car/private transfer from New Chitose Airport (CTS) due west to Niseko.
~2.5 hr by car from Sapporo (or rail to Kutchan + 15 min drive).

inns.name: Akan Tsuruga Besso Hinanoza
inns.summary: A 25-room ryokan that is the top (and probably only) luxury option on Lake Akan, with terrific Hokkaido kaiseki, a free-flowing onsen bath in every room and an interesting corner of eastern Hokkaido with Ainu culture and marimo on the doorstep. Service is the weak point, corporate and unpolished on both stays in the thread. KI-NRT called it a great, memorable stay, though two years later he summed it up as really nice, with nothing that knocked their socks off.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki is terrific, and the kitchen does a wonderful job with Hokkaido ingredients: okra, butterbur, sweet corn and bamboo shoots, plus salmon, whelk and sea urchin. KI-NRT put the charcoal-grilled Kuroge wagyu almost at Hida and Matsusaka level, unusual for Hokkaido beef. Breakfast is equally inspiring, with never-frozen ikura so plump he had two helpings of rice heaped with it and called it sublime. A 2024 guest found the food superb.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every one of the 25 rooms has its own onsen bath, and in the suites it sits out on the deck, free-flowing and not recirculated, which KI-NRT called perfect. There is also a communal daiyokujo, but because every room has its own bath it was empty every time he went in. A 2024 guest called the bath facilities excellent and singled out the stone sauna, where you put on a towel dress and lie on the stone on another towel.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is the weak point on both stays. KI-NRT found it fine but formulaic and less personalized than at top ryokans, which he puts down to the inn not being family owned, and the meal servers kept having to check with the kitchen on questions he expects answered on the spot. Michaeljinnyc had it worse in 2024 and called it the worst service of his ten-plus stays, with cold, aloof local staff and foreign staff who misunderstood requests.

room.label: Room
room.text: Four of the 25 rooms are 110-square-metre Tokubetsu-shitsu (the Ama no Za suites), and KI-NRT's, the Hina no Za, had a living room, a tatami room and a separate bedroom in high-quality Japanese-contemporary decor, with the onsen bath on the deck and two toilets (but curiously only one sink). He thought the suite was really nice. A 2024 guest found the standard rooms spacious and well maintained, down to tower speakers and a stack of jazz CDs.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Hinanoza is a nondescript seven-story building steps from the Lake Akan shore, with Ainu wood carvings through the common areas. Almost everything is a short walk away: the Ainu Kotan village with its craft shops and museum, lake cruises, forest hikes and the marimo, ball-shaped green algae. In February the frozen lake hosts a nightly festival with fireworks and Ainu dances. The town is one main street, and a 2024 guest found most of it closed.

cities.text: ~70 min by car/shuttle from Kushiro Airport to Lake Akan Onsen.
~4.5 hr by car from Sapporo across eastern Hokkaido (most fly Sapporo-Kushiro then drive).

inns.name: Arcana Izu
inns.summary: A 16-suite auberge above the Kano River whose French-Japanese kitchen KI-NRT ranks with the best restaurants of Tokyo and Paris. Everything else trails the food, since the rooms are comfortable but dated, and an October 2025 guest found the room tired and the service transactional. With Asaba fifteen minutes away, it works best as a one-night fusion interlude between traditional ryokans, and KI-NRT is not sure it is worth going out of your way for on its own.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The French-Japanese cooking is why you stay, and KI-NRT puts it with the best restaurants of Tokyo, Paris and Rome. The sauces are fused with dashi, so even cream or tomato sauces carry umami, and many dishes are created for one season and never made again. Breakfast is nearly as noteworthy, with wasabi you grate yourself and a hearty lettuce-and-whitebait soup. Even Fc912, whose October 2025 stay was a letdown, found the food excellent.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every suite has its own free-flowing kakenagashi onsen bath on a terrace over the Kano River. In The Suite it is a massive and wonderful open-air bath on the deck with views of the river and the forest beyond, which KI-NRT found a great place to unwind. There is no communal bath, and no lobby or common area either, since the property is a few room buildings and a separate restaurant.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is the weak point. KI-NRT's two 2021 stays passed without complaint, but Fc912, who stayed in October 2025, found it transactional: the wooden plate holding the amuse-bouche was covered in spider webs, and when he pointed it out the waitstaff simply said sorry and neither the manager nor the chef followed up, which was not a language issue since he speaks Japanese fluently. Ikyu's guests are warmer and give it 4.69 over 51 reviews.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms are comfortable, airy and tasteful, with large windows and river views, but the property shows its age. The Suite, the top category, is 86.4 square metres and open-plan, which KI-NRT found not quite wow-inducing next to rooms well over 100 square metres, and the bathroom tiles look like they are from the turn of the century. The lower categories are far less spacious and darker, so book a top suite. Fc912 found the room tired in 2025.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Arcana sits above the Kano River in Yugashima, and all sixteen suites face the river and valley below with the mountains and forest beyond, a setting KI-NRT says will lower anyone's heart rate by a few notches and should be stunning in autumn. There is no lobby, common area or grounds, only the room buildings and the restaurant, and he found it all good but nothing that stands out against Japan's top ryokans. Asaba is fifteen minutes away.

cities.text: Shinkansen Tokyo→Mishima (~50 min), Izuhakone Sunzu line→Shuzenji (~35 min), then the free inn shuttle ~25 min (Ochiairo includes it — reserve; Arcana is a sparse Tokai bus or ~20-min taxi).
Reverse of: Inn shuttle back to Shuzenji (~25 min), then Izuhakone Sunzu line + Tōkaidō Shinkansen Shuzenji→Kyoto door-to-door ~2h38 (Google Maps live routing, confirms the Mishima change).

inns.name: Bettei Oborozukiyo
inns.summary: A 19-room inn five minutes' walk from Dogo Onsen Honkan, built in 2015 with a classic look but a fresh, modern feel, and KI-NRT calls it far and away the top luxury option in the town. Every room has its own open-air onsen fed by the same spring as the Honkan, and an Iyo beef shabu-shabu hot pot stood out in a delicious kaiseki dinner. He still routes Shikoku itineraries through it years later, as the base for a Matsuyama swing, though he does not treat it as a destination in itself.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki is locally sourced and super fresh, with awesome seafood (some of it served as sashimi) and an Iyo beef sirloin shabu-shabu hot pot that KI-NRT called a great way to enjoy the local meat. He found the meal delicious and beautifully presented, though not the best he has ever had, and meals are served in private dining rooms, where his one nitpick is that he would have preferred to eat in his own room.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every room has at least one open-air onsen bath, and the water comes from the same source as the Dogo Onsen Honkan. KI-NRT's Oborozuki Suite had two free-flowing baths, a small open-air one for a single person and a much larger one that can be enclosed or opened up with sliding glass; he kept the small one hotter for warming up and the big one cooler for a long soak, which he called pure bliss. There is also a communal bath, which he did not try.

service.label: Service
service.text: Dinner and breakfast were served by Riyo Miyauchi, a charming, engaging and enthusiastic young woman born and raised in the area, who answered a stream of questions about Ehime and its food, and KI-NRT summed the service up as friendly and attentive.

room.label: Room
room.text: The top category is the G-Type Special Room with Open-Air Bath, and KI-NRT's Oborozuki (room 307) is a 94-square-metre suite, nicely laid out and tastefully furnished, with two onsen baths, two separate toilets (a favourite of Mrs. KI-NRT) and a bedroom completely closed off from the living area, so she could nap while he took a video call.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The inn is a five-minute walk from the centre of Dogo Onsen and its Honkan, the historic bath house that was a setting in Miyazaki's Spirited Away, and KI-NRT finds Dogo one of the more charming onsen towns in Japan, its restaurants, shops and cafes giving off a Taisho-era feel, though not quite as atmospheric as Kinosaki. With 19 rooms it is a big departure from the mega hotels in the area, and he says to make sure you visit Matsuyama Castle.

cities.text: About 25 min by Iyotetsu tram from JR Matsuyama Station area to Dogo Onsen terminus, then a short walk.
Limited Express Shiokaze from Okayama to Matsuyama runs about 2h40, plus roughly 20 min by tram out to Dogo Onsen.

inns.name: Kinugawa Kanaya Hotel
inns.summary: Kinugawa Kanaya is a 41-room hotel billed as Japan's first Western-style luxury establishment, with shoes-on hotel formality, optional meals and a photogenic garden in Kinugawa Onsen near Nikko. KI-NRT put the kaiseki among the top five meals he has had at any top-flight hotel or ryokan in Japan, names the hotel among the few luxury ryokans with a teppanyaki table, and felt the service was perfect. He still gave it four stars rather than five, because the rooms run small for the exorbitant price and he would only maybe return, and that is what keeps the hotel from being an all-time great.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner was the highlight of KI-NRT's stay, among the top five meals he has had at any hotel or ryokan in Japan, with not a single dish short of incredible. The first course alone ran from chawanmushi to ayu, and nothing was old-fashioned: each course was familiar yet prepared in an unusual way, above all a white-miso bouillabaisse of sea bream, prawn and scallops, the best soup he has had. He also lists it among the top ryokans with teppanyaki.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every room category has a private in-room onsen bath, on the balcony in some and inside the room in others, which is one of the few things that differ between them. Kinugawa Onsen water, an alkaline simple spring, fills two large communal baths above the river valley with an open-air section, plus a bookable private bath and a sauna. Nobody in the thread has described the water, the temperature or the view, so the bathing itself has no verdict.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT felt the service was perfect: Kanaya manages the balance of formality and attentiveness with finesse and grace, without ever being stuffy about it. It runs as a hotel more than a ryokan, so shoes stay on at the entrance and you can book a stay without meals included.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT's one complaint is the size of the rooms. All seven categories are 66 m² (only the John Kanaya Suite is bigger), differing only by floor, lounge access, balcony size and where the in-room onsen bath sits. For the exorbitant price he expected more: not claustrophobic, yet not roomy enough to laze in all day. His junior suite, unlike the dark common areas, was bright, airy and contemporary Japanese, with not a scuff mark in sight.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The view of the Kinugawa River and valley from most rooms is one of the three things KI-NRT says make the hotel stand out (with the food and the service), and there is a photogenic garden at the back. It is a classic luxury hotel from an earlier Western era, dark brown leather in the common areas, aging but in really good shape, and keeps its historic charm while adapting to the times. Kinugawa is an onsen town 30 minutes from central Nikko.

cities.text: Tobu Spacia limited express Asakusa->Kinugawa-Onsen ~2h, then ~5 min by car.
JR to Shimo-Imaichi + Tobu to Kinugawa-Onsen ~1h15, then ~5 min by car.

inns.name: Kuramure
inns.summary: A 19-room modern retreat in Asarigawa Onsen, Otaru's only hot-spring village, five linked buildings along the Asarigawa river with a private onsen in every room. The one FlyerTalk account, an August 2025 stay before a 2026 renewal, calls the dinner, the breakfast and the river-view soaking tub excellent. Ikyu's crowd has been more mixed since then, with the bath their highest mark at 4.22 but food (3.55) and satisfaction (3.78) noticeably cooler and recurring complaints of dark rooms.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: jtrader, the one FlyerTalk member to have stayed (August 2025), thought the dinner excellent, built on excellent local ingredients, and the breakfast too, though not quite as elaborate as elsewhere. All alcoholic drinks are included, and there is a lovely bar with a good selection of Nikka whiskies, where he never saw anyone else. Since the 2026 renewal Ikyu guests put the meals near 3.55 and repeatedly find the cooking short of the price.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every room has its own onsen, and jtrader's was indoors with a window that opens onto the river. There is a public onsen as well, which he found very nice and never shared with another person, and having both public and private baths was one reason he chose Kuramure over Zaborin. Since the 2026 renewal Ikyu guests put the bath at 4.22, their highest mark.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here. Ikyu guests since the 2026 renewal put it near 4.04, their second-highest mark after the bath.

room.label: Room
room.text: jtrader's room was a suite of three rooms plus its own bath and quite large, and the in-room onsen at a window that opens onto the river, and the architecture throughout is very modern, by Makoto Nakayama. The rooms are the softest of the Ikyu marks since the 2026 renewal, near 3.91, because the kura (storehouse) concept makes them dark.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The property is very modern in its architecture and sits by a river outside Otaru, and jtrader never saw anyone else during his entire stay except a few arriving for dinner at the same time, a privacy he singled out. KI-NRT (who has not stayed) calls the immediate surroundings nicer than Ryotei Kuki's, though having been to Otaru three times he feels there is nothing else to see or do in the area. The Yoichi whisky distillery is not far away.

cities.text: ~75 min by car (official access page); or ~65 min by JR Rapid Airport to Otaru-Chikko Stn, then the hotel's reserved shuttle or a taxi.
~40 min by car to Asarigawa Onsen; by transit, JR to Otaru Stn then a local bus toward Asarigawa Onsen (~30 min, infrequent).

transit.note: Otaru Ferry Terminal is ~20 min by car (official access page).

inns.name: Osteria Sincerità
inns.summary: Osteria Sincerità is a three-room auberge ryokan on a town-centre lot in Akayu Onsen, built around chef Makoto Harada's Italian-Japanese counter cuisine and an undiluted source-fed cypress bath in every villa, 50 meters from its sister inn Yamagata The Takinami. There is no view and no garden, and KI-NRT considers the two-storey rooms more rustic-artistic than pure luxury, but the food is what brings people here, cooked from Yamagata's own ingredients by a chef who held a Michelin star in Niigata. It makes most sense as one night of a two-inn Akayu split.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is chef Makoto Harada's Italian-Japanese cooking at an open-kitchen counter (there is one private room, which KI-NRT got), built on Yamagata's wild vegetables, fungi, meat and river fish. Harada won a Michelin star at Il Riposo in Niigata before Takinami's owner gave him free rein here. KI-NRT found each dish a delight, the seared horse meat in a buckwheat galette possibly the best baniku he has tried. Ikyu guests put the food at 4.95.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Each villa has a hinoki open-air bath fed with a continuous flow of 100% pure source onsen, straight from the spring, and Alba and Monte add a private steam sauna (Grano does not). The one shared bath is a private rental carved from a single giant slab of Mt. Zao volcanic stone, bookable in 50-minute slots, and with three rooms KI-NRT expects no trouble getting a slot. Ikyu guests give the baths a perfect 5.0 and single out the water.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT found the service matched sister inn Yamagata The Takinami and then some, starting with a spread of welcome snacks.
