Foreign guests are rare and one staff member, Ms. Mamuta from Nepal, handles English. Ikyu guests put service at 4.84, their lowest mark here, and the reservation that recurs is the dinner format, which starts for all parties at once as a staged show that not every guest enjoys.

room.label: Room
room.text: The three villas, Grano, Monte and Alba, are two-storey with two bedrooms and an open-air onsen bath, and each has a screen painting from the Takinami collection and a Finn Juhl Baker sofa, different in each room. Grano (135 square metres to the others' 150) is the only one with a dry rock garden. KI-NRT took Grano for the garden and calls the rooms more rustic-artistic than pure luxury, but found it comfortable. Ikyu guests give the rooms 5.0.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Osteria Sincerità sits on a small lot in the middle of Akayu town, with the restaurant and three villas around a small courtyard, outdoor seating with a firepit and a yurt-like tent that serves as the lounge. There is no garden, no view and no large communal area, and KI-NRT's advice is to walk 50 meters to Yamagata The Takinami and use its facilities. Ikyu guests put the facilities at 4.95 all the same.

cities.text: Yamagata Shinkansen 'Tsubasa' direct Tokyo→Akayu (~2h20) — pick a train that stops at Akayu — then a short taxi/inn shuttle.

Hokuriku Shinkansen Kanazawa→Ōmiya (~2h01), Tōhoku 'Yamabiko' Ōmiya→Fukushima (~1h07), change to the 'Tsubasa' over the Itaya pass→Akayu (~52 min) + short taxi. Two changes (Ōmiya, Fukushima). ⚠ heavy January delay exposure on the final Tsubasa leg.
Reverse of: 'Tsubasa' Akayu→Tokyo (~2h19), Tōkaidō 'Nozomi'→Kyoto (~2h15) — one clean change, but the 'Tsubasa' has a winter-suspension history.

Reverse of: Yamagata Shinkansen 'Tsubasa' Akayu→Fukushima (~35 min — a SE backtrack), transfer to a northbound Tōhoku Shinkansen→Sendai (~25 min), plus a 5-min taxi/inn shuttle at the Akayu end (reserve).

inns.name: Fufu Nara
inns.summary: A sleek modern Fufu resort in Nara with in-room open-air onsen even in the base rooms, and a restaurant set in a historic tea-house garden a shuttled five-minute walk downhill. Two member stays in late 2025 loved it outright, and one guest's five-out-of-five verdict put it among the top Fufu hotels, just below Nikko, on the strength of its service. KI-NRT has never reviewed a stay here and calls it hotel-like and corporate next to Tsukihitei's intimacy, so expect polish and comfort over old-Japan atmosphere.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is kaiseki one night and teppanyaki the next, and OWHKG2016 found both equally delicious and everything of a very high standard, though he prefers the food (and the decor) at Fufu Nikko slightly. Bristom called the food very good and liked finding his name printed at the top of the menu.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Even the lowest-category rooms have their own open-air onsen tub off the bathroom, free-flowing and looking into bamboo forest, and both recent guests singled it out: Bristom for the view and easy access from the bathroom, OWHKG2016 because the outdoor bath was great. Neither has written about any shared bath.

service.label: Service
service.text: Staff come out to meet arriving cars and park them, and when OWHKG2016's party of six arrived they checked which bags went to which room, so the luggage was already in place after a private check-in in the bar area. A chauffeured Alphard runs to the restaurant, with umbrella escorts in the rain. He called Miss Lin one of the best hotel staff he has ever had, and when he left his key in the car a clerk ran out in the rain to fetch it.

room.label: Room
room.text: Modern, spacious suites with huge beds, and Bristom had the best sleep of his trip in one of the lowest-level rooms, which he still found nice. OWHKG2016's group took the lowest-category stylish suites (104 to 106), each with a different design and a sitting room that seats six adults comfortably, and his advice is that any room here is fine because there is no bad room to be had.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: A big, spread-out modern property in Nara, where the restaurant is a five-minute garden walk downhill from the rooms (slippery in rain in geta and socks) inside a historic garden with a very nice tea house, which OWHKG2016 recommends touring if it is open. KI-NRT calls it sleek and new but hotel-like and corporate, without Tsukihitei's intimacy, and notes that luxury travellers to Nara are not spoiled for choice.

cities.text: Kintetsu Kyoto→Kintetsu-Nara (~45 min), ~5-min taxi.
Reverse of: Kintetsu Nara Line Rapid Express Kintetsu-Nara→Osaka-Namba (~36 min, direct, ~every 15 min).

inns.name: Fujiiso
inns.summary: A historic Nagano inn with 240 years of pedigree and many repeat guests, which added two fresh, spacious suites in 2022 with source-fed onsen baths, so you can stay at a famous old ryokan without giving up comfort. The nakai service is stellar and the kitchen is creative with local produce. KI-NRT gladly drove the extra half hour for the experience and still recommends it in 2026, but says one night is enough unless you have a car, since off-season Yamada Onsen offers next to nothing.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Head chef Atsushi Fujimoto builds the meal on Nagano's produce and sansai (wild mountain plants), which in April meant white asparagus, bamboo shoots and nozawana at their peak. KI-NRT liked the grated white asparagus soup with uni and shiso flowers, the fried age soba-gaki, and Fujiiso's own signature dish, Ponpon Nabe, a fondue of skewers deep-fried in olive oil that looks far too heavy and turns out light. He calls the cuisine very nice.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The onsen water comes straight from the source and flows freely into the in-room baths of the two Tokubetsu suites built in 2022 (some of the older rooms have the same feature): granite in the Fuji Balcony Suite and hinoki cedar in Yamazakura. The bathing area has large windows that open right up, so the soak turns into a half open-air onsen bath. Nobody in the thread has described a communal bath here.

service.label: Service
service.text: A nakai-san (butler) is assigned to each room, and KI-NRT found both of his stellar: Mariko and Chie were elegant, charming and attentive, and they took their time deliberately explaining each feature of the rooms and each course at dinner and breakfast. Chie speaks good English and is usually assigned to foreign guests, so ask for her if your Japanese is not up to snuff. Meals are served in a private dining room (although not in your own room).

room.label: Room
room.text: Book one of the two Tokubetsu Shitsu (special) suites built in October 2022, Fuji Balcony Suite and Yamazakura, which are fresh, stylish and much larger than the other rooms while keeping traditional Japanese decor. Fuji is the one to get, with 158 square metres against Yamazakura's 110 and a very nice entrance hallway. Both have a Western-style living room, a tatami room, a bedroom with Western beds and an onsen bath.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Fujiiso is the historic inn of Yamada Onsen, a small and sleepy hot-spring town 20 to 30 minutes by car from Nagano city. The lobby lounge is enormous for a 24-room inn, with an expansive viewing area that should be picturesque in summer and fall. Nearby Matsukawa Keikoku is a gorge counted among the most beautiful in Japan, but only with leaves on the trees; otherwise there is little to do, and KI-NRT says one night is enough without a car.

cities.text: Hokuriku Shinkansen Tokyo→Nagano (~1h20–1h30), then a ~30–45-min car up to Yamada Onsen (Fujiiso arranges transport; no rail last mile — nearest is Suzaka Stn + taxi). ~2h20 door-to-door.
Hokuriku Shinkansen Kanazawa→Nagano (~65 min), then a ~30–45-min car to Yamada Onsen. ~2h door-to-door.

inns.name: Isshin
inns.summary: An eight-villa contemporary onsen ryokan (2008) at the foot of the Kirishima mountains that delivered almost everything KI-NRT hoped for: standalone villas, private dining rooms and slick source-fed water that he singled out for special mention. The one blemish was the policy of charging 440 yen for each extra bath towel, and a manager who simply said that two per guest is generally sufficient, which was enough that he would almost certainly pick Myoken Ishiharaso or Wasure no Sato Gajoen over a return visit, so it sits just under the region's established inns despite the quality of the stay.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: All meals are served in a private koshitsu dining room with floor-to-ceiling windows over the water garden. The kaiseki dinner was satisfying, with classics such as shrimp tempura, and the Kagoshima A5 wagyu shabu shabu was outstanding: KI-NRT found the beef superb and the salt-dashi and sesame ponzu dipping sauces equally impressive. Breakfast was tasty but less memorable, and he would have preferred a better grilled fish to the standard salmon.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every villa has its own source-fed onsen bath out on the patio (Kobai, the top room, has an indoor bath too), large enough for two or three people. The water is pumped from 1,200 meters directly below the property and is so slick and moisturizing that KI-NRT and his wife skipped lotion afterwards. There is no communal bath and no rental bath, but he thinks the in-room furo should satisfy the most discriminating onsen aficionados.

service.label: Service
service.text: You have dedicated servers for both dinner and breakfast, and their knowledge and engaging personalities made for easy, enjoyable conversation about the area and the food. The one real blemish was the towel policy. When KI-NRT asked for extra bath towels (his wife folds them under her back in bed), they charged 440 yen per towel, and the manager simply replied that two per guest is generally sufficient, which he found cheap and petty.

room.label: Room
room.text: Even the base rooms are standalone villas with a 70 square metre footprint, in a contemporary Japanese-modern style. KI-NRT stayed in Kobai, the top room, refurbished in 2023, with a large deck and garden off the living room, a Ryoanji-style dry rock garden by the bedroom, a sunken table, and indoor and outdoor onsen baths. It felt a bit like sleeping inside an art exhibit, and he ranks it with the top rooms at the best ryokans.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Isshin stands at the foot of the lush Kirishima mountains, about 30 minutes north of Myoken Ishiharaso and close to Kirishima's prime hiking trails, with Mt. Shimoe on the horizon. A water garden lies between the reception, lounge, dining area and villas, with a covered walkway hovering above it, and with the mountains behind it makes a charming picture, especially at night when the pool and walkways are lit. KI-NRT calls the setting serene.

cities.text: Shinkansen Hakata to Kagoshima-Chuo, then ~15 min car from Kagoshima Airport area to the inn.
~15 min by car from Kagoshima Airport to the inn.

inns.name: Lamp no Yado
inns.summary: A 14-room ryokan of old Japanese buildings in a cliffside alcove at the very tip of the Noto Peninsula, built around a long pool that runs between the buildings and the sea. KI-NRT calls it unlike any other ryokan he has stayed in, with top notch food and aged buildings that are in very good shape while still exuding rustic charm, though he says it is not Gora Kadan, Ginyu or Beniya Mukayu. The January 2024 Noto earthquake left only minor damage, but the inn was last reported closed pending structural inspections and power, so check that it has reopened before you plan around it.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Meals are taken in a communal dining area, and only guests in the top room, Nami no Rikyu, have the option of eating in their room, which is what KI-NRT did. He had not expected the food to be on par with the very best in Japan and was pleasantly surprised: everything was top notch, if not as inventive or memorable as Gora Kadan, and it contributed to an overall great experience.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: KI-NRT calls the onsen very nice, with wonderful views of the rough Sea of Japan, and the property's long pool runs between the buildings and the ocean; he found the pool area beautiful and tranquil, and it is part of what gives the place its peaceful feel. Nobody in the thread has written about the water itself.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: Most of the rooms are very traditional, in old Japanese structures, and all of them have incredible views, including of the sunrise over the sea. KI-NRT had half expected the place to be run down and in dire need of a refurbishment given its age, but it was in very good shape while still exuding rustic charm, which he calls a tough balancing act to pull off. The top room is Nami no Rikyu, the only one with the option of in-room meals.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Lamp no Yado will make you feel as if you are at the edge of the world: it sits in an alcove below the cliffs at the very tip of the Noto Peninsula, looking like a small village from above, with wonderful views of the rough Sea of Japan. Non-guests are not allowed onto the property, adding to the exclusive feel. No rail lines run nearby, so you need a car, and with one you can see the Salt Village, rice terraces and samurai-era homes.

cities.text: ~2.5h by car/limousine from Kanazawa to the tip of the Noto Peninsula (or LEX to Wakura + car).
Hokuriku Shinkansen Tokyo->Kanazawa ~2h30, then ~2.5h by car to Suzu.

inns.name: NEOLD Private House
inns.summary: A one-party kominka retreat in sacred Yoshino that offers the widest range of traditional Japanese activities KI-NRT has seen anywhere: Noh, geisha, tea ceremony, calligraphy, river fishing, and a full Shogun experience with an Osaka action cast. He calls it one-of-a-kind and a must-visit for private cultural immersion, and he is certain to return. That verdict puts it higher than the lodging alone would, since the beddings trail the top houses and the baths are heated water with no onsen.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The GM, Kimihiro Ogino, is also the chef and cooking is his true love: he is a sushi master and will make whatever you ask, sushi, tempura, kaiseki or Western dishes. KI-NRT ordered the usual omakase kaiseki and found it handsomely presented and nicely prepared, with fewer courses than top ryokan kitchens, Yamato beef and vegetables from Ogino's own garden. Lunch the next day brought incredible kuzu soba, kuzu udon and tempura, all of it light.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at NEOLD. The house has an indoor bath and an outdoor open-air bath, both heated water, plus a shower and another bathroom in the detached hanare, and KI-NRT mentions them only in passing.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT found the service friendly and attentive, as it should be for a private house. The GM, Kimihiro Ogino, runs the place with three other staff, and Ahmed, an English speaker, comes from the Osaka office when foreign guests stay. Whatever activities you choose, they bring in the specialists: for the Shogun and Ninja days a cast of five actors and producers came from Osaka, and costumed vassals welcomed KI-NRT home as their lord.

room.label: Room
room.text: The whole two-storey kominka is yours, with three bedrooms, a dining area around an irori hearth, a tea room, a counter dining room and a detached hanare with a basement bar; eight to ten people fit comfortably. The Shogun armor in the main tatami room is by the artisans behind the 2024 Shogun series, but beddings and toiletries fall a bit short of Asaba, and KI-NRT says you can do better for pure accommodation, though not in this region.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: NEOLD is about 20 minutes by car from central Mount Yoshino, in the interior of the Kii Peninsula, one of the most sacred parts of Japan and uncrowded on weekdays. Yoshino itself is a World Heritage site with Kimpusen-ji temple and over 30,000 cherry trees in April. The grounds are vast, with a gorgeous Noh stage used for private performances and a lawn big enough to film a samurai battle on. Koyasan is 90 minutes away and Kumano Hongu 2.5 hours.

cities.text: Kintetsu Kyoto→Kintetsu-Nara (~45 min), ~5-min taxi.
Reverse of: Kintetsu Nara Line Rapid Express Kintetsu-Nara→Osaka-Namba (~36 min, direct, ~every 15 min).

inns.name: Shiki no Yado Michinokuan
inns.summary: A nine-room ryokan from 1985 near Shiroishi Castle that doesn't scream opulent luxury and doesn't need to, because it is wrapped in forest, serves both meals in the room, cooks delectable local food and is elegantly staffed. KI-NRT would return without hesitation, but only for one of the three suites with in-room onsen, ideally the top Akebono suite, renovated in 2024, because the six standard rooms share the communal baths and miss the point.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: KI-NRT found the cuisine neither unique nor especially creative, but the kitchen puts great effort into local and seasonal ingredients and the result was delectable. The fava-bean tofu with dashi and soy-sauce jelly, the grilled Sendai kuroge wagyu steak and umen (a local noodle soup like somen but thicker, made without oil) were all excellent. Breakfast was standard Japanese, good but with nothing that stood out. Both meals come to your room.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The three suites each have their own onsen bath, and in Yui Suite Shinonome it is indoors, though the large glass window can be opened for a semi-open-air effect. The other six rooms have no bath of their own and use the communal, gender-segregated onsen. KI-NRT looked forward to a soak before dinner on arrival, and he would return only for one of the suites so as to have the onsen in the room.

service.label: Service
service.text: The house is elegantly staffed, with a waka-okami (proprietress-in-waiting) on hand and a nakai-san, Ms. Suzuki, attending the room and serving both dinner and breakfast there, the classic arrangement KI-NRT always seeks out. He calls it a charming and comfortable property.

room.label: Room
room.text: Yui Suite Shinonome is more of a junior suite, with the bedroom only partly separated, but there is plenty of space in a Western-style living and dining room with a fireplace and a small tatami sitting area. The nits are cheap toiletries, a water-only minibar, and a drinks fridge by the communal bath that charges even for milk and yogurt. The top suite, the 110 m² Akebono, was fully renovated in spring 2024, and KI-NRT would book it next time.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: You arrive to mountains and forest all around with no man-made object in sight, and the heart rate drops at once. Every room faces a small rear lawn surrounded by flowers, a sight to behold when the hydrangeas bloom. The exterior is traditional and the interior contemporary Japanese, simple and unpretentious with just enough style (wooden ceiling beams, paper-lantern lights) to add flavor, and Mrs. KI-NRT approved. Shiroishi Castle is close by.

cities.text: Tohoku Shinkansen Sendai to Shiroishi-Zao is about 15 min (or ~50 min by local line), then roughly 20 min by car to the inn.
Tohoku Shinkansen Yamabiko from Tokyo to Shiroishi-Zao is about 2h, then roughly 20 min by car.

inns.name: Yunohanaso
inns.summary: A modern rural-Japanese onsen ryokan perched over the Hokigawa River in Nasushiobara, remote enough that most guests come purely for the springs, the food and the hospitality. The river is the attraction, with two large private rock baths on its bank and an open-air onsen on the top suite's balcony, and the kaiseki is careful and prettily plated. KI-NRT found the stay unexpectedly compelling, while an earlier visitor thought it solid but not distinctive enough to return to, and the spring water itself is honest but unremarkable.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is top-notch and prettily presented: a magnificent konbu-cured flounder with miso-vinegar dressing, a humble grated-corn soup with egg tofu and crab that made KI-NRT's eyes pop, iwana sashimi that was quite possibly the best he has ever had, and a simmered sea-bream head (tai kabuto-ni) that was the most impressive dish of all. There are few original creations, but each dish is made with great care, and zander86 also called the food great.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The two private rock baths beside the Hokigawa River, Aoba and Momiji, are the highlight, massive and well designed with a hypnotic river view, especially after dark, and KI-NRT recommends a session even if your room has its own onsen. Seven of eleven rooms have an in-room onsen and the rest use the communal baths. The spring rises beneath the inn, but the water is neither silky nor sulfurous, and zander86 found his in-room bath a little cold.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is refined, with hospitable and charming staff in elegant silk kimonos, and KI-NRT compares the professionalism to Asaba. The welcome runs from two kinds of kuzumochi at check-in to small bites waiting in the room, and the lounge pours complimentary coffee, juice and beer, with whiskey and wine in the evening. Unusually, the same server (Ms. Watanabe) handles both dinner and breakfast, so your preferences are remembered the next morning.

room.label: Room
room.text: Izumo, one of two premium hanare suites, is 118 m² of light wood with a living room, tatami washitsu, dining area and separate bedroom, plus an indoor onsen and an open-air one on the river-facing balcony, and KI-NRT says it had everything he looks for in a top suite. Musashi, the other premium suite, is 80 m² with the open-air bath only. zander86 stayed in the renovated Owari room and found it solid, though his in-room onsen ran a little cold.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The lounge, the private baths and the rooms all overlook the Hokigawa River with nothing but forest on the far bank, a soothing, mesmerizing view, and the modern rural Japanese building blends into its surroundings. A dilapidated building downriver is an eyesore if you lean out and look for it. Nasushiobara has none of the onsen-town charm of Kurokawa or Kinosaki and little nearby, so most guests come only for the springs, food and hospitality.

cities.text: Tohoku Shinkansen Tokyo->Nasushiobara ~1h15, then ~30 min by car/bus.
Tohoku Shinkansen Utsunomiya->Nasushiobara ~13 min, then ~30 min by car/bus.

inns.name: Auberge Yusura
inns.summary: Yusura is a five-villa auberge near Ise Jingu, opened in 2018, with standalone rooms around a saltwater pond, each with an open-air bath of Sakakibara spring water trucked in from 45 minutes away, and a kaiseki kitchen led by a Kitcho-trained chef. Service is the standout, a gracious proprietress and a team wonderful with every age, while the kitchen falls short of its pedigree and the Matsusaka beef was the biggest letdown. Five rooms make a full buyout easy, and KI-NRT calls the whole setup hard to beat, so he has already booked a return visit with the same group.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki comes from a head chef who trained at Kyoto's Kitcho, and KI-NRT had high expectations that the food fell short of: nothing was bad, but several dishes felt overly simple, such as the clam tamajime, which did not feel refined. The biggest letdown was the Matsusaka beef, which did not live up to its big-three wagyu reputation. Breakfast was satisfying but not standout, and he allows he may be judging harshly after years of top ryokans.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every villa has its own open-air onsen bath behind it, surrounded by gardens and high walls for full seclusion, but the property has no hot-spring source of its own: the water is trucked in from Sakakibara Onsen, about 45 minutes away and known for its silky texture, and it is not continuously flowing, a fairly common setup. Guests are advised not to rinse off after bathing, for the skin's sake. There are no other baths, communal or reservable.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is where Yusura excelled. Led by the gracious and personable proprietress, the team was warm, attentive and professional, and especially wonderful with the children in KI-NRT's four-generation group, going out of their way for guests of every age. His group had the whole property to themselves, which likely helped, but he doubts it would change much with other guests. Staff English is limited, and they rarely host international guests.

room.label: Room
room.text: All five villas stand alone with no shared walls, facing the saltwater pond, but they are open-plan with no separate rooms, which is not KI-NRT's preference. Four are 65 square metres, adequate but a bit tight for a family; Keyaki is 80 square metres and the most private, though it feels much the same inside. A walking path runs between the pond and the three villas on the right, so if privacy matters book Keyaki or Kaede on the left.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yusura opened in 2018 with a clean, modern look, and its five villas face a saltwater pond with a dry rock garden; the grounds are small but beautifully landscaped, and the main building holds a lounge and the dining area. The location was a major reason KI-NRT chose it: Ise Jingu, Toba, its aquarium and Mikimoto Pearl Island are all within 20 minutes, Amanemu is 45 minutes away, and you need a car for anything further on the Kii Peninsula.

cities.text: Reverse of: Kintetsu Ltd Exp Iseshi/Ujiyamada→Kyoto (~2h); most change at Yamato-Yagi, a few run direct (2/hr).
Reverse of: Kintetsu Limited Express Ujiyamada/Iseshi→Kintetsu-Nagoya (~80–85 min, direct).

inns.name: Kayotei
inns.summary: A ten-room, family-run classic that delivers the traditional ryokan feeling in spades (riverside seclusion, antiques in the hallways, dinner in a private room), and KI-NRT still calls it a tad overrated, because across repeat stays it never excelled at any one thing: the food is good but not great, the rooms decent and minimalist, and the service not quite as personalized as you would expect from so small a family-run house. It is a lovely, authentic first ryokan for a traditionalist, but it is not a destination in itself, and he says the same of the whole Kaga area.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Kayotei serves traditional kaiseki, and in crab season that means a heaping helping of Zuwai-gani snow crab: sashimi, charcoal-grilled, crab meat and tomalley cooked over a lava rock, and a clear soup with crab-paste balls and yuzu that KI-NRT called simply divine. It was done very nicely, but nothing stood out as innovative, it missed his top five Japanese meals, and over repeat visits he has settled on good but not great, even in crab season.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Higashiyama Suite, the top room, has its own in-room onsen bath (hot-spring water, but indoors, with no open-air tub). Nobody in the thread has written about the shared baths.

service.label: Service
service.text: The room attendant, Ms. Terue, was charming, warm and there to meet every need, and she also served dinner. Meals are served in a private room elsewhere in the building and not in your own room, which KI-NRT would have preferred, though at least guests are not made to eat together in an open dining area. His considered verdict over repeat stays is that service is not quite as personalized as you would expect in such a small, family-run property.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Higashiyama Suite, the top room, is a spacious Japanese-style room with a wide balcony over the forest and a private onsen bath, and the furnishings are decidedly minimalist. One curious touch is a mini-room between balcony and living room with a Victorian-era table and chairs, old-school but hardly Japanese. The rooms are neither worn nor pristine, scuffed here and there, and KI-NRT says they lack the zen luxury some other ryokans convey.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Kayotei sits secluded on a beautiful stretch of serene river outside Yamanaka Onsen, and the architecture blends into the forest so well that KI-NRT calls the sense of place wonderful. The hallways are lined with antiques, hand-made pottery and traditional paintings, and the effect is of having gone back in time. Yamanaka Onsen is a sleepy little onsen town he found charming, and the Kakusenkei footpath along the river is a nice walk.

cities.text: Kanazawa→Kaga-Onsen (~25 min), then ~25-min taxi up to Yamanaka (inn can arrange).
Hokuriku Shinkansen direct Tokyo→Kaga-Onsen (~2h50, 'Kagayaki'/'Hakutaka' since 2024), then taxi up to Yamanaka Onsen (~25 min). No self-change.
Reverse of: Kaga-Onsen→Tsuruga (~30 min), 'Thunderbird' Ltd Exp→Kyoto (~1h25).
Reverse of: ~25-min taxi from Yamanaka Onsen to Komatsu Airport, the KMQ→Fukuoka hop (~1h40, ~4 daily ANA/ORC), then the subway 2 stops into Hakata (~5 min). ~3.75h door-to-door.
Reverse of: ~25-min taxi to Komatsu + KMQ→Fukuoka (~1h40) into Hakata, then Nishi-Kyushu relay→Nagasaki via Takeo-Onsen (~2h). ~5.75h door-to-door.
Reverse of: ~25-min taxi to Komatsu + KMQ→Fukuoka (~1h40) into Hakata, then Kyushu Shinkansen 'Mizuho'→Kagoshima-Chūō (~1h17). ~5.25h door-to-door.

inns.name: Kyo Yunohana Resort Suisen
inns.summary: Suisen is a real, source-fed hot-spring ryokan in the Yunohana Onsen area of Kameoka, 30 minutes from Kyoto by direct train, with an open-air onsen bath on the balcony of every one of its 13 rooms and a kitchen good enough that breakfast matched dinner. KI-NRT was plain that it is not a destination ryokan like the ones in his top ten. Given its proximity to Kyoto, legit onsen and succulent cuisine, he calls it a great option for people who want to try a ryokan without the time or energy to go farther afield, and a screaming bargain by Kansai standards, unusually cheap for what it delivers.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kitchen does kaiseki with its own twists, and KI-NRT said it did not disappoint: steamed yuba over tofu mochi in a simple yet sublime dashi, simmered vegetables prepared to perfection, and mountain-yam paste with shrimp deep-fried with somen noodles. The only letdown was the octopus clay-pot rice near the end, a wasted slot in new-rice season. Breakfast was as delightful as dinner, down to a homemade corn dressing they bought to take home.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The water is real, source-fed onsen, which is rare anywhere near Kyoto, where an "onsen" usually means water trucked in and recirculated. All 13 rooms have an open-air bath on the balcony, there is a private rental rock bath reached by an enchanting walk across the creek (paid by the hour, and worth it in KI-NRT's view), and a communal bath with indoor and outdoor tubs, which he had all to himself before dinner and called pure bliss.

service.label: Service
service.text: A courtesy shuttle meets guests at Kameoka Station, the drinks in the minibar, including beer, are free of charge, and an array of Japanese treats is laid out on the table in the room. KI-NRT raised no complaints but wrote nothing specific about the staff, and nobody else in the thread has described the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: Even the entry-level rooms are over 50 square meters, each with an open-air onsen bath on the balcony. Of the two top categories, the 113 square meter Suisen Suite adds a tatami living room, dual sinks, more storage and a bigger balcony, while the 85 square meter Semi Suite was refurbished more recently (2021 vs 2013) and feels shinier, though the Suisen Suite did not feel in need of a refresh. KI-NRT's advice is to book the best available room.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The grounds are thin and long and compact, but they make good use of the space: a small creek runs through, with a dry rock garden on one side and a forested embankment on the other, and the garden is lit up at night. Kameoka is a perpetually foggy produce-growing valley on the outskirts of Kyoto, and KI-NRT would not advise first-time visitors to spend much time touring it, though the Hozu River boat down to Arashiyama is a fun, scenic outing.

cities.text: Kyoto to Kameoka ~28 min JR Sagano Line, then ~15 min inn shuttle to Suisen.
Osaka to Kyoto ~30 min, transfer JR Sagano to Kameoka ~28 min, then ~15 min shuttle.

inns.name: Ryokan Nishiyama
inns.summary: A design-forward ryokan in suburban Onomichi, with standalone-house rooms up to 81 square metres, an all-day lounge of complimentary sake, beer and whisky, and a Japanese-French dinner with a wine pairing. The one party to review it, ten people at Christmas 2025, called it a highlight of their trip, with immaculate rooms and extremely high-level service. At $540–650 a night it is toward the affordable end for this quality; the suburban location, with no famous sights nearby, is the drawback, and that one enthusiastic stay is the only account so far.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is modern Japanese-French cooking, served to OWHKG2016's party of ten in a private room in the old wing, with a wine pairing offered and every other drink free of charge. He never saw the wine list, though he spotted Cristal, Gaja, Burgundy and Bordeaux in the cellar, so it is surprisingly well stocked. He was a big fan of the food, his wife, a pickier eater, enjoyed it less, and breakfast is a more traditional spread.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no hot spring, and the water is heated, but the top rooms have a real bath product. Kiri has a hinoki open-air bath and an indoor tub, Ume has an iron-kettle open-air bath and an indoor one, and the house bath is run as a bookable private bath for the rooms without their own. The one detailed stay was in Sakura, which has no in-room bath, and it never describes bathing, so there is no first-hand verdict.

service.label: Service
service.text: The manager, Son, received the party of ten warmly and led them to the lounge for matcha and snacks, and pre-arrival emails had always been promptly answered. OWHKG2016 called the service extremely high level, counted the stay among the highlights of a trip that also took in three Fufu hotels, and would not hesitate to return.

room.label: Room
room.text: Wara and Matsuzake are standalone houses of 81 and 63 square metres, extremely spacious and the favourite room type of OWHKG2016's wife, while Asahi and Sakura share a building with a connecting door that opens on request. He liked Asahi upstairs best, because its sitting room looks over the lovely garden, though Sakura below has the better layout and bathroom. Every room the party of ten took was in immaculate condition.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Nishiyama is in a suburban part of Onomichi with few famous sights nearby, and OWHKG2016 did not know what to expect. Inside, the design is stunning, the reception doubles as a guest lounge where sake, beer, whisky and gin are complimentary all day, there is a lovely garden that the Asahi sitting room looks onto, and dinner is served in the old wing. He recommends anyone in the area or passing through to stay at least a night.

cities.text: Reverse of: JR Sanyo local Onomichi→Fukuyama (~15 min), Sanyo Shinkansen Fukuyama→Hiroshima (~25 min) — change at Fukuyama (faster than Shin-Onomichi, 3 km out of town).

Bookend down the Sanyo Shinkansen: 'Nozomi'/'Sakura' Kyoto→Fukuyama (~1h40), then JR local Fukuyama→Onomichi into town. (Shin-Onomichi is direct but sits ~3 km out, so Fukuyama-and-local lands you at the station.)

inns.name: Yunotani Senkei
inns.summary: A nine-room cottage ryokan in remote Totsukawa, the highest-end base KI-NRT found within reach of Kumano Hongu Taisha, with fresh 2017 log cabins and a private open-air onsen he calls pure bliss, run by a loud, energetic and warm-spirited attendant. He says it is not on the same level as Gora Kadan or Wanosato, nor among the top five ryokans he has stayed at. Still, there were no service flaws to speak of, and it has a charm all its own. His stay came at the height of the pandemic in the fall of 2020, and he recommends it as a good luxury option for trekking part of the Kumano Kodo.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Meals are normally served in the main restaurant, but during KI-NRT's pandemic-era stay dinner and breakfast came to the room together on large trays left outside the door, bento-style and nicely done, though no substitute for a multi-course kaiseki. He found the food more than adequate: the meals made them happy and content and added to the stay, but not among the most memorable he has had, and he has eaten at Japan's finest ryokan kitchens.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The suites have a beautiful and soothing private open-air onsen bath right in the suite's own garden, which KI-NRT sums up as pure bliss and recommends booking (in the thread he describes it as an open-air onsen available for private use, with no onsen inside the room itself). The public baths are wonderful as well.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was great, and the proprietress is not the usual unobtrusive, discreet hostess: she moves quickly, speaks loudly and in familiar Japanese, and is full of energy, which took KI-NRT aback at first, though she was warm spirited and did all she could to make the stay memorable, asking about plans and offering advice in a caring, never nosy way. His stay was at the height of the 2020 pandemic, so service was somewhat abnormal.

room.label: Room
room.text: The nine cottages have a rural-modern feel, like a luxurious log cabin, and because the property only opened in October 2017 everything is fresh and spotlessly clean, with the amenities and technology you expect of a luxury place and a sense of place. KI-NRT stayed in Sumire, the top-category cottage suite, a relatively spacious 79 square metres with the private open-air onsen in its garden, a very comfortable place to pass the time.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yunotani Senkei is deep in the mountainous interior of the Kii Peninsula, in Totsukawa, and its remoteness is part of its charm. KI-NRT chose it as possibly the highest-end ryokan within reach of Kumano Hongu Taisha and the Nakahechi trail, though the shrine is still a 30-minute drive, so you need a car (otherwise stay in Kumano Hongu proper). He calls it an excellent rural retreat in a beautiful, isolated area and would not hesitate to return.

cities.text: ~3 hr by car from Osaka to Totsukawa via Gojo.
~2 hr by car from Gojo/Nara to Totsukawa.

inns.name: Gora Kadan
inns.summary: A 39-room modern-Japanese ryokan in Gora and one of KI-NRT's 'Hakone holy trinity', with polished omotenashi, meals served in the room and onsen baths in the first-floor rooms only. It 'just missed my top ten' for him in 2022 and is still 'always a solid choice' in 2025, but by then members were asking about the many negative reviews of its condition, and the one dedicated review is a scathing late-2023 member stay (furniture falling apart, room not clean, food just OK) that urges others to avoid it. The service and the architecture seem intact, and the worry is the aging fabric.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: KI-NRT calls the food good, and he values the ability to have meals served in your room, which few of the Hakone competitors offer. The one dedicated review, TBD's late-2023 stay, found the food just OK, and nobody in the thread has raved about this kitchen.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Only the first-floor rooms have onsen baths; rooms on the second floor get regular hot water, so the room you are assigned decides your bath. The Kadan Suite Aoi has an open-air onsen bath in its own private garden.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT calls the omotenashi first-rate and the service polished, and Gora Kadan is one of the few ryokans he knows (with Shinsen and Myoken Ishiharaso) where the nakai, your room attendant, escorts you through everything at the property instead of just serving dinner. The inn also welcomes small children, with child-sized yukata, slippers and geta. TBD, the one member with a dedicated review, found the service friendly but not personal.

room.label: Room
room.text: Some of the rooms are quite small, and KI-NRT would go with Akebono or Akatsuki if they are available, and the Kadan Suite Aoi (private garden, open-air onsen bath) as a fallback. The condition of the rooms comes up again and again: TBD found his room in OK shape but the furniture falling apart and the room itself not clean, and by 2025 members were asking about recent reviews describing areas in need of repair and maintenance.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The architecture is modern Japanese, centrally located in Gora, and KI-NRT says it is exactly this architecture and ambiance that give Gora Kadan a slight edge over the plethora of competitors in the area; he groups it with Ginyu and Yama no Chaya as the Hakone holy trinity, and Hakone itself has plenty to do, with Mt. Fuji views from Lake Ashi and Owakudani. TBD found the atmosphere not very private.

cities.text: Odawara Shinkansen + Hakone Tozan line/bus toward Gora ~2h12.
Tokaido Shinkansen to Odawara + Hakone Tozan line/bus ~2h15.

inns.name: Fuefukigawa Onsen Zabou
inns.summary: A winery-owned Koshu ryokan that gave KI-NRT a "fairy tale-like" stay, with mesmerizing pond-and-garden grounds and glorious bathing, let down by middling cha-kaiseki, the one flaw he wished away. Both reviewers agree the magic lives in the Kotogawa and Tsuzumigawa suites, and in a lesser room it is a different inn. At $450–650 a night it is near the bottom of this collection's range, which makes the food an easy flaw to accept.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is cha-kaiseki in a restored kominka farmhouse, with Maruki wines and a pairing option. KI-NRT found the food the weakest point of his stay: the clear soup with a chicken-stuffed lily-bulb manju and abalone was delicious and the handmade soba delightful, but the grilled amberjack was nothing special, the cedar-grilled Koshu beef tough and short on flavor, and the portions small. A 2024 guest also called it decent but not outstanding.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The outdoor communal bath is a massive hybrid of pool and river that you can swim in, with a cave at the far end reached by wading up the onsen stream, and at night the whole area is lit up and hauntingly beautiful, so KI-NRT called it one of the most atmospheric onsen he has ever seen. Its water ran a bit lukewarm for him. Indoors is a large onsen, and the two top suites have a hinoki hot-spring tub on the balcony above the koi pond.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is elegant and graceful, and many of the staff were born and raised locally, take pride in their work and know the area in depth. KI-NRT spoke Japanese with them, so he cannot say how it goes in English, but a 2024 couple who spoke none found the language gap no problem at all because the staff tried so hard, and their winery tour was well organized, with a detailed translation of the Japanese-language guide.

room.label: Room
room.text: Kotogawa and Tsuzumigawa, the two 73-square-metre suites, are the only rooms of 23 with the garden and lake view, each with a hinoki onsen tub on the balcony. The room itself does the job, tastefully furnished in muted tones, but has one sink, an older washlet and a deck shower with the head low on the railing, so KI-NRT crouched to rinse (a 2024 guest found that no chore). Entry rooms are not special in any way, so book a suite if you can.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: A manicured garden and small koi lake, home to a pair of ducks, is the centre of the property, seen from the lounge and best of all from the two top suites, and all around are Yamanashi mountains and hills that are lush and rugged at once. The grounds are compact but artfully crafted, and KI-NRT found them mesmerizing and the inn unique and mystical. The salon pours unlimited free Maruki wine with wagashi, and the inn runs a winery tour.

cities.text: Ltd Exp 'Kaiji' Shinjuku→Enzan (~1h30), then ~10-min drive — inn pickup from Enzan Station (reserve).
Reverse of: The long way round: Ltd Exp 'Shinano' route west via Kōfu to Nagoya (~2.5h), Tōkaidō Shinkansen→Kyoto (~1h) — a genuine transit day.

inns.name: Kumano Bettei Nakanoshima
inns.summary: Kumano Bettei Nakanoshima is an island ryokan off Nachikatsuura, a five-minute boat ride from shore and the only luxury option near Kumano Nachi Taisha and Nachi Falls, built around a seaside onsen that KI-NRT calls really nice and, at its best, spectacular and mystical. Ultra-fresh Katsuura seafood and personable service are real strengths, but only one of the 44 rooms has an in-room onsen and the view is partly marred by oil tanks across the strait. KI-NRT calls it a good, relaxing base for exploring the area, and says to book Kihinshitsu, the top room, if you can.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kitchen has its pick of Katsuura port: nama maguro, the local tuna that is never frozen before serving, served cutlet-style, and grilled abalone in the shell with butter. KI-NRT found the food really good and thoroughly enjoyed it, and while it was not the most creative of meals, it did not need to be. Meals are in the main restaurant, and the private dining rooms have no ceiling, so drunk guests were audible at dinner. Whale has appeared.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The onsen is a seaside one, and KI-NRT calls it spectacular and mystical. Only one of the 44 rooms, the top-category Kihinshitsu in the Chomontei building, has an in-room onsen, and the bath in the other rooms is not spring water, so everyone else uses the communal baths or rents the private open-air onsen bath by the hour, which he found really nice with good views from the water and used twice in a one-night stay.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is a strong point. Everyone from the manager to the front desk to the wait staff was courteous, warm and personable, seemed to care about the stay, and was eager to explain the area, its history and the ingredients in each dinner course, and they allowed a late checkout, which KI-NRT notes cannot be taken for granted at Japanese ryokans. He was impressed that a hotel with this many rooms pulls off the personal touch.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT's Luxury Deluxe Ocean View Room, the second category from the top, was modern and reasonably stylish with a good view of the ocean and the peninsula across the way. It had no separate bedroom and living room, which he prefers, and no large closet, so the rollerboard luggage sat on the living-room floor. The top category is a single room, Kihinshitsu, the only one of 44 with an in-room onsen, and it was not available when he booked.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Nakanoshima is a private island off the Kii Peninsula coast, a short boat ride from the mainland, and the only high-end choice near Kumano Nachi Taisha and Nachi Falls. The view across the strait is partly marred by two large green oil-reserve tanks on the facing peninsula, which the property can do nothing about. Take the short, easy hike from the roof of the building to the hilltop for a panoramic view, with a foot bath along the trail.

cities.text: Shin-Osaka to Kii-Katsuura ~4h on Kuroshio LEX, then ~7 min walk + ~5 min shuttle boat.
Nagoya to Kii-Katsuura ~3h20 on Nanki LEX, then walk + shuttle boat.

inns.name: Amakusa Tenku no Fune
inns.summary: A 15-room contemporary-Western property above Amakusa bay, closer to a hotel than a ryokan, that KI-NRT found outstanding overall in 2021: incredible Italian-leaning cuisine, first-rate service and mesmerizing island-sea views, let down only by a dated build and no onsen. He would only maybe return, because the same owners opened Amanojyaku in 2023, which he expects 'likely outshines it in every way,' and that is where he now points people.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The cuisine was the highlight of KI-NRT's two-night stay in 2021, scrumptious high-end Italian fare built on Amakusa's famous seafood, and the uni pasta made with the local purple sea urchin is the dish he names: if you have never had uni pasta in Japan, you must try it. Four years later he still recalled the food as incredible, and he expects the same owners' newer Amanojyaku to be as wonderful, or even better if that is possible.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen here, which KI-NRT names as one of the two things that let the property down. The same owners' newer Amanojyaku nearby has onsen straight from the source in every room, which he calls a huge advantage, and that is part of why he now points people there instead.

service.label: Service
service.text: The service was first-rate on KI-NRT's 2021 stay, and he still called it that when he looked back on the visit four years later. The property runs more like a hotel than a ryokan (shoes stay on except in your own room, and nobody really polices even that), and he had no complaints about the service.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Island View Villa is generous at about 74 m² plus a 34 m² balcony, and most rooms are in a building behind the reception and restaurant with great views. The architecture and decor are thoroughly Western contemporary, but the build was already dated in 2021, the one flaw KI-NRT names besides the missing onsen, and the fresher, more luxurious sister property Amanojyaku is where he would stay now.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The ryokan sits on a commanding hilltop over Amakusa bay with sweeping views of the sea and the many small islands dotting it, and KI-NRT calls Amakusa breathtakingly scenic and puts it above the more famous Matsushima. He came through on a road trip around the Hidden Christian sites and the UNESCO World Heritage churches of Nagasaki. The same owners' newer Amanojyaku nearby has the same mesmerizing views of island-dotted sea.

cities.text: Shinkansen Hakata to Kumamoto (~45 min), then ~90 min by car/rental to Kami-Amakusa.
Shinkansen to Kumamoto side, then ~90 min by car south to Amakusa.

inns.name: Asan Kotonami
inns.summary: A 28-room modern onsen resort in rural Kagawa whose one extraordinary asset is a vast, exuberant bathing complex, the place KI-NRT calls the Disneyland of onsens, and the rooms have private outdoor onsen of their own besides. Rooms are new, cosy and very well kept, the service warm and the food decent, and at roughly 40,000 yen a head it is among the cheapest nights in this company. It is an onsen destination before it is a luxury one.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is cooked over an irori hearth: salted grilled ayu (sweetfish), miso-glazed tofu, and satoimo taro and konjac roasted over the coals. Meals are served in a semi-private room shared with two other tables, and OWHKG2016 found the food decent but nothing to write home about.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The communal baths are what brings people here, and KI-NRT calls them the Disneyland of onsens: huge, indoor and outdoor, one the size of a small pool and another shallow enough to sleep in, with a fixed water pillow so your face stays above the water. The water is natural hot spring and there is plenty of it, flowing along the ground on the walk from the changing room. OWHKG2016 loved the baths here more than any on an eleven-night ryokan trip.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was very friendly and attentive on OWHKG2016's one-night stay, and the building, which opened in 2017, is new and kept in excellent condition.

room.label: Room
room.text: The type-A rooms are relatively small but extremely cosy, functional and tastefully designed, each with a private outdoor onsen that OWHKG2016 particularly loved, and they sit to the side of the building so they get a private mountain view and more privacy. Type A is ideal for two people. The whole place opened in 2017 with a tasteful modern-Japanese look and is very new and very well maintained.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Asan Kotonami is a stylish mountain-hut-style resort on the outskirts of Manno, in rural Kagawa on Shikoku. The surroundings are quiet Shikoku countryside, and the side-facing type-A rooms get a private mountain view.

cities.text: JR Dosan/Yosan line Takamatsu to Kotohira runs about 40-60 min, then the inn's free pickup is roughly 30 min by car from JR Kotohira Station.
Hourly Limited Express Nanpu covers Okayama to Kotohira in about 1h across the Seto bridge, then roughly 30 min by the inn's car from Kotohira Station.

transit.note: Asan Kotonami sits well south of Kotohira Station; times include the ~30 min inn pickup.

inns.name: Hatago Wakatsu
inns.summary: A restored two-room former tatami shop on Omihachiman's canal, and a strong argument for staying the night in a town most visitors day-trip from Kyoto. The stepping-back-in-time setting and the straw-grilled Omi beef are the strengths, but the service was reserved and sometimes brusque and the bathing is in-room tubs only, which makes this a fine night out of Kyoto and no more than that. Book Ki-no-ma, which KI-NRT calls the clear winner of the two rooms.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is at a counter in front of an open kitchen, and Omi beef is the star: straw-grilled in front of you (incredible aroma), then miso-marinated, then in a tender dashi shabu-shabu. The lake fish are handled just as well (Biwa masu sashimi, tenaga ebi tempura, grilled hamaguri), though KI-NRT missed ayu and the duck course did not win him over. Breakfast (homegrown rice, homemade dashi) is careful but lighter on variety than the top kitchens.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen (Shiga has few hot-spring sources), so bathing means the in-room tubs, plain heated water, and they are the rooms' namesakes. Ishi-no-ma's bath is carved from a single massive stone from Kyoto's Kurama area, and Ki-no-ma's is a Koya-maki wooden tub made by an artisan who also crafts soy-sauce barrels. Member jiajin was instantly reminded of the stone bath here on seeing the in-room stone baths at Yamagata The Takinami.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was a mixed bag. The head chef explained each dish at lightning speed and disappeared before anyone could ask a question, and the other staff were polite but reserved and not especially proactive. Breakfast was a different experience thanks to Ms. Kawanishi, a Shiga local with solid English who is normally the main point of contact but was off on KI-NRT's check-in day, so it is worth checking that she will be around.

room.label: Room
room.text: There are just two rooms in a restored 200-year-old sukiya residence, and the restoration never feels overdesigned. KI-NRT's party booked both and compared them directly. Ki-no-ma is a 96 m² detached villa with futons and an upstairs view over the Hachiman-bori canal, sakura trees at the windows. Ishi-no-ma (42 m², Western-style bed, garden view, no canal view) suits anyone who dislikes futons, but otherwise Ki-no-ma is the clear winner.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: A gated back entrance opens straight onto the Hachiman-bori canal, and stepping out there the first time was a wow moment, with preserved buildings along the water and a real sense of the Edo period. KI-NRT loved the silent pre-breakfast walk to Himure Hachimangu Shrine. Omihachiman is one of the nicer heritage towns in Kansai, easier to reach than Tsumago or Magome and less crowded, though he ranks those two higher for atmosphere.

cities.text: Kyoto to Omihachiman ~35 min JR Biwako Line, then ~5 min car/taxi.
Osaka to Omihachiman ~55 min JR, then ~5 min car/taxi.

inns.name: Ryokan Suiranrou
inns.summary: Ryokan Suiranrou is the flagship of Hitoyoshi Onsen and the birthplace of the town's hot-spring culture, largely destroyed by Kumagawa River flooding and rebuilt in 2021 as a clean, modern 30-room inn. KI-NRT would not rank it among Japan's most luxurious ryokans, and he calls it exceptional value and a memorable onsen experience, with three distinct springs making up for décor that cuts corners. He found it a rewarding overnight for anyone routing through southern Kumamoto, though not a destination in itself.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner at Dining Soho is a restrained kaiseki built on garden produce and Kumamoto ingredients: chawanmushi with eel and fine soba strands, a salt-grilled yamame trout and a hot pot of Miyazaki chicken. Nothing is extravagant, but KI-NRT thought the regional flavors came through well, and the slightly smaller portions were a blessing. The one drawback is the half-walled dining rooms, where a loud party next door carries through.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The onsen is the highlight here, with three spring sources on one site, and guests can try all of them. Mikage-no-yu, the original bath from 1910, has the softest, skin-beautifying water, and its uneven Matsuyama granite gives it a retro feel; the two large communal baths, Suizan-no-yu and Suiga-no-yu, each have a sauna. Midori-no-yu has two private moor-water baths, rentable by the 50 minutes, which KI-NRT says are definitely worth paying for.

service.label: Service
service.text: Ms. Yayoi, a 20-year veteran of Suiranrou, served KI-NRT's dinner and was one of the highlights of his stay: attentive, with deep knowledge of the cuisine, and she explained every dish down to where the nori came from (the Ariake Sea) with genuine enthusiasm. Nobody has written about the rest of the staff.

room.label: Room
room.text: The top room is the 86 m² Luxury Japanese-Western Room, a junior suite with a free-flowing private onsen looking over the Kumagawa River, spacious and with lovely views. The décor felt a bit on the cheap side to KI-NRT, with faux wood paneling on the counters, plastic furniture disguised with wood trim and thin towels (the ones in the baths were little more than hand towels). He recommends a Deluxe or Luxury room, which have their own bath.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Suiranrou stands on the bank of the Kumagawa River in Hitoyoshi Onsen, a small onsen town in southern Kumamoto where few travelers go. The building was largely destroyed by the river's flooding and rebuilt in 2021, and KI-NRT found the reconstruction clean and pleasant, if lacking a bit of character; the quality touches are a terrace with a small water garden, a lounge with floor-to-ceiling glass facing the river and excellent ikebana throughout.

cities.text: Shinkansen Hakata to Kumamoto (~45 min), then highway bus to Hitoyoshi (~1.5 hr); Hisatsu rail still severed since 2020 floods.
Highway bus Kagoshima to Hitoyoshi (~1.3-1.5 hr), then ~10 min car; inn offers pickup at the terminal.

transit.note: A-tier Suiranrou; Hisatsu Line Yatsushiro-Yoshimatsu section not restored, access by bus.

inns.name: Takayamaso Hanano
inns.summary: Takayamaso Hanano is a family-run inn in Arima, Japan's oldest hot-spring town, and its flagship room, the 100 m² Oyama Renge suite rebuilt in 2025 with its own kinsen and ginsen baths and a panoramic view over the town, approaches true luxury. KI-NRT came with modest expectations and left won over: the stay was quiet, comfortable and memorable, and the cooking was better than the house's station suggests. Only the top rooms are this good, and the entry level is plain. At $360–550 a night the suite is a bargain.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is a kaiseki that KI-NRT found carefully prepared, well plated and distinct from typical ryokan fare, and it exceeded his expectations. The standouts were a cold cod milt shinjo in clear broth (shinjo is usually made with shrimp or crab) and a kuwai manju under a buckwheat-husk ankake sauce. Kobe beef can be added, from shabu-shabu up to chateaubriand, and the Sanda rice at breakfast was so fragrant he took a second bowl.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Oyama Renge suite has both of Arima's waters, a kinsen (gold) bath and a ginsen (silver) bath, and bathing with the sliding glass open, three of Arima's seven spring sources in view below, gave KI-NRT a true open-air sensation. As at most ryokans in Arima the water is not fed from the source: it arrives by truck and is filtered and heated (kinsen) or cooled (ginsen), though no tap water is added to the ginsen. The communal bath is modest.

service.label: Service
service.text: The owning family are fully engaged, and the daughter who now runs the inn was attentive and efficient, with a warmth KI-NRT felt throughout the stay, while her earnest younger brother seemed less at ease with guests. The attendant who served dinner and breakfast, a polite, reserved young woman, answered questions without elaboration; she is a longtime weekend part-timer, which explains the matter-of-fact manner.

room.label: Room
room.text: The flagship 100 m² Oyama Renge suite, rebuilt in January 2025, is a fresh, modern take on Japanese aesthetics that KI-NRT says surpasses what some high-end ryokans attempt, with its own kinsen and ginsen baths and a balcony with a panoramic view over the town. Room choice makes all the difference here: the entry-level rooms are simple, with futon laid out after dinner, and only the top suites approach true luxury.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The inn is on a compact site overlooking Arima's streets, with no garden and 20 stone steps up to the lobby, but the interiors are tasteful and serene, finished in warm beige with fine ikebana and kusamono arrangements by artisans from across Japan, and there is a cozy lounge and bar. Arima itself, Japan's oldest recorded hot spring, is a delight for strolls, browsing the shops and carbonated onsen rice crackers.

cities.text: Kyoto→Shin-Osaka, change toward Sannomiya, then Arima Express bus (~1h45).
Reverse of: Direct Hankyu/JR expressway bus Arima Onsen→Osaka-Umeda (~60 min, 1–2/hr).

inns.name: Tokachigawa Onsen Sanyoan
inns.summary: An 11-room traditional ryokan in sleepy Tokachigawa Onsen near Obihiro, built around its water: Japan's only Moor onsen (plant-derived, reddish-brown once it meets the air, and silky on the skin) feeds an en-suite bath in every room, two of them open-air. The kitchen over-delivers for such a rural address and the room under-delivers (KI-NRT later summed the stay up as 'while not super luxurious, a place we enjoyed'), and the town is asleep. He recommends it as a one-night stay for the water and the cool Hokkaido summer air, and warns not to expect great luxury.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner does a terrific job with the best of Hokkaido's seafood, produce and beef, and KI-NRT found the flavors and presentation more creative and sophisticated than he expected in such a rural place. The highlights were grated mountain yam with bafun uni under a bonito-dashi jelly (turning the dashi into a jelly he called genius) and a clear soup of uni-stuffed tofu with red snow crab and junsai. Breakfast was equally delightful.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The water is Japan's only Moor onsen, a plant-derived spring that turns reddish brown once it meets the air and is silky smooth on the skin, and it flows free and never recirculated into the bath on the room's deck. All 11 rooms have their own en-suite onsen, though only two are open-air, so the gender-segregated outdoor communal bath was empty when KI-NRT visited. Guests can also use the communal onsen at the sister Daiichi Hotel next door.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here, beyond KI-NRT noting that the ryokan runs a shuttle from Tokachi-Obihiro Airport and that a private dining room was reserved for them on request.

room.label: Room
room.text: The two-story Haru no Umi special room (97 square metres, one of only two rooms with an open-air bath) is more of a country home than a design piece, which KI-NRT knew going in, but the first floor was drabber than he anticipated: two beds and a small living room with a little yellow sofa that felt constricting. The second floor was far more inviting, with a living room, a tatami room and a big patio holding the onsen bath, and they lived there.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The grounds are pretty and peaceful, manicured grass with a smattering of tall cedars (the lawn was a park golf course until recently), and the ryokan sits just off the main strip of Tokachigawa Onsen, a sleepy place with little to do nearby. The nearest establishment is the much larger and less luxurious sister Daiichi Hotel, connected by a covered walkway. KI-NRT went in July, when Hokkaido's cool days make it Japan's best region for onsen.

cities.text: ~20 min by car from JR Obihiro Station / Tokachi-Obihiro Airport to Tokachigawa Onsen.
~2.5 hr by car (or limited express to Obihiro) from Sapporo across the Tokachi plain.

inns.name: Amane Resort Gahama
inns.summary: A 2016-vintage 31-room luxury ryokan on Beppu Bay, every room with its own onsen, sharing restaurants and facilities with sister property Seikai next door. KI-NRT found it polished and serene and unusually family-friendly (Beppu's ryokans skip the age restrictions of the top family-run inns) and worthy of an adult stay. He adds a reservation of his own, which is that for a tranquil, intimate onsen experience he would skip Beppu altogether for Yufuin or Kurokawa.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Meals were of very high quality, though KI-NRT puts them below Ishiharaso or Asaba, and still very satisfying. Kaiseki is at Gahama's Kappou Matsuhide and French at sister property Seikai, and both draw on Oita's waters and the produce of its volcanic soil. The lobster sashimi and steamed local abalone, both caught near Beppu, were absolutely amazing. Breakfast is a Japanese set at Gahama or a wonderful buffet at Seikai that the children loved.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: All 31 rooms have their own free-flowing onsen, and the tower rooms pair an indoor onsen with an open-air one. The exception is the two 10F Special rooms, where the outdoor tub is a plain jacuzzi with no spring water, which KI-NRT counts as a big demerit because that is not what you come to Beppu for. Large communal baths are only at sister property Seikai, a short walk or a complimentary golf-cart ride away, which children find great fun.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT found the service polished and the atmosphere serene, even with his family party of eleven including four small children. Every meal was served in a private room (only the buffet breakfast at Seikai was not), a complimentary golf cart runs on demand to the sister property, and the children were looked after down to pint-sized Pokemon slippers, yukata and samue that fit a two-year-old, and a kids' meal they all scarfed down.

room.label: Room
room.text: The 14 tower rooms are all very spacious (a nominal 90 m²) with in-room onsen, and the difference is the view, slightly obstructed by villa roofs on 3F and clear from 5F up. KI-NRT preferred 3F and 5F to the two 10F Special rooms, which are junior-suite in layout and swap the open-air onsen for a jacuzzi; if you want a separate bedroom, skip them and save money. The other 17 rooms are villas, and only the maisonettes (with stairs) have a view.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Once inside, the building shuts out the city and its noise completely and the views of the sea are calming. The arrival is another matter, because the entrance faces a large, busy boulevard with a Nitori furniture store and a KFC as the eyesores as you pull up. Beppu is the most productive hot-spring area in Japan, with steam rising from every pore of the city, but the main attractions such as the Beppu Hells are about a ten-minute drive away.

cities.text: Ltd exp Sonic Hakata to Beppu (~2h10), then ~15 min taxi to the inn.
Shinkansen to Kokura, Sonic down to Beppu, then ~15 min taxi; no direct link.

inns.name: Fufu Kyoto
inns.summary: A 40-room ryokan-hotel hybrid that mostly pulls the straddle off, with an in-room onsen bath in every room in an onsen-poor city, a superb creative breakfast, and a prime Higashiyama base for temples and foliage. KI-NRT enjoyed it without being blown away (the Nikko sibling is the one he adores), and the rough edges are on the foreigner-facing side (hard to reach by phone or email in English), with a steep drop-off in the rooms below the top suites.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: KI-NRT booked without dinner, an option most ryokans refuse and a welcome one in Kyoto, and had the Japanese breakfast in his suite, which he calls among the best he has had in a ryokan: a white miso soup with yuba in place of the usual red (very tasty, and he generally does not like white miso) and a sweet and tangy fruit jelly for dessert. Dinner he has not tried, and a member who stayed bed-and-breakfast found the food decent.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: All 40 rooms have their own onsen bath, which KI-NRT calls a huge advantage in Kyoto, where most rivals offer no onsen and the few that do (Suiran, Aman) limit it to top rooms or a communal bath. The water is not kakenagashi though, since it is trucked in daily from the Fushimi area and reaches the rooms by circulation filtration, disinfected and reused. For a pure gensen kakenagashi soak he points you to Arima, Kurama, Kinosaki or Kaga.

service.label: Service
service.text: Reaching the hotel from abroad is where it falls short. There is no published direct phone line, and central reservations has no English option, which KI-NRT called woefully inadequate; a member's email went unanswered for over a week. Another member found no one at the door on arrival, his group's luggage randomly distributed among the rooms and a staff member showing the room who could not understand English. There is no laundry service.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT's 91 m² Luxury Premium Suite had a separate bedroom and living room, a view of the nearby mountains, Western beds and minimalist modern-Japanese decor. Room category matters a lot here: the 42 m² Comfort Twin had the onsen bath but no view (it faces the next building), and a member who took the cheapest suites found them dark and low-ceilinged, since the first floor is underground. He recommends at least the 73 m² Luxury Corner Suite.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Fufu Kyoto is a modern boutique hotel as much as a ryokan, and the pretty garden is not a central feature as at the top ryokans. The address in Higashiyama is within spitting distance of Nanzenji, Eikando (a 10 minute walk, and among the top spots in Kyoto for autumn leaves), Heian Jingu and the Philosopher's Path, and under 10 minutes by taxi from Kiyomizu-dera and Gion, which KI-NRT finds decent for a Kyoto base. There is no gym or pool.

cities.text: ~20 min by taxi from JR Kyoto Stn to Okazaki.
Osaka to Kyoto ~30 min, then ~20 min taxi to Okazaki.

inns.name: Fukudaya
inns.summary: A one-group-at-a-time renovated merchant inn on Lake Biwa's western shore, opened in 2023, which fills a real gap because high-end options in Shiga are few and far between. Its strengths are Yamada's Aman-honed cooking and the private lakeside house. Against that, there is no onsen, and the staff are so reserved that KI-NRT named it the stay's one shortcoming. It works best as a well-fed quiet night between Kansai and the Sea of Japan, and the bath is plain heated water.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Mr. Yamada, the chef and general manager, spent a decade in Kyoto kaiseki and then cooked at Amanpuri, Amanemu and Azumi Setoda, and he works closely with local farmers. KI-NRT found the food excellent overall: the Lake Biwa trout with eggplant purée was superb, so was the homemade sabazushi (pressed mackerel sushi, a Shiga specialty), and the grilled Ōmi beef sirloin was the equal of Matsusaka or Kobe. Breakfast is smaller but hearty.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at Fukudaya. The indoor bath with deck access is ordinary heated water, and KI-NRT warns that if hot springs are a priority this house does not have them. There are three bathrooms for the single group staying in it.

service.label: Service
service.text: Two people look after you, the attendant Ms. Numata and the chef Mr. Yamada. Both were kind and attentive, but KI-NRT found them extremely reserved even by Japanese standards, with conversation brief and quickly over. He noticed it most at dinner, where there is no written menu and each dish got a one-word introduction. In a house where the staff serve only your group, he thinks a warmer approach would improve the stay considerably.

room.label: Room
room.text: You have the whole house to yourselves, a two-storey traditional building that was once part of a large merchant inn founded over 140 years ago and reopened in 2022 after extensive renovations. There is a bedroom with two double beds, two tatami rooms that sleep up to four more on futons, and three bathrooms. The original irori (sunken hearth) is intact and gives the place a warm, nostalgic atmosphere, and the rest is rustic yet refined.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Fukudaya is on the western shore of Lake Biwa in Imazu, once a post town where merchants carried mackerel from the Sea of Japan to Kyoto, and with no other guests on site you hear only the waves and the waterfowl. The lake is in view from the upstairs tatami room, the dining room and the deck. Imazu village is a short walk away, with three buildings by the architect William Merrell Vories, and KI-NRT enjoyed the tour of Harie's kabata streams.

cities.text: Kyoto to Omi-Imazu ~1h15 on JR Kosei Line, then short taxi to Fukudaya.
Osaka to Omi-Imazu ~1h30 via New Rapid/Kosei Line, then short taxi.

inns.name: Hakone Gora Byakudan
inns.summary: A welcoming, English-comfortable Hakone inn in Gora that Japanese regulars return to two or three times a year, and the one member who has stayed calls it an excellent stay if not a luxury one. That single first-hand account loved it (hearty meals, top-floor foliage views, in-room onsen, a fire at night) while conceding the fabric is tired, with wood rot on the decks and a guest crowd that can break the hush.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: brownoarsman found the meals excellent, some of the most hearty and tasty he has had in Japan, though he says himself he is a casual ryokan stayer and this was his first ryokan, so nobody has measured this kitchen against the top houses. After dinner a bar and snack cart is rolled out for a couple of drinks.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The rooms have private onsen baths, and brownoarsman, who had asked for the top floor when booking, found his wonderful looking out over the late-November foliage, with a hot soak before dinner the start of his best evenings there. Nobody in the thread has written about the communal baths or the water itself.

service.label: Service
service.text: The okami speaks English very well and so do many of the staff, and the house has a great reputation for being welcoming to non-Japanese guests. Nobody in the thread has written more about the service than that, though Japanese guests like it a lot: a mother and daughter brownoarsman met had been coming two or three times a year for several years, and on Ikyu it averages 4.75 over 224 reviews.

room.label: Room
room.text: Views from the main room are excellent, and you can request the top floor when booking, as brownoarsman did for the foliage; the main room also has a great wood fire they light at night, which he found easy to fall asleep in front of after a hot soak and some sake at dinner. The interior is very nice, but the building is a bit tired and he saw wood rot on some of the outside decks and balconies.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: A hillside house in Gora with fine foliage views from the rooms, still lovely but a bit tired, and without the sculpted gardens and other amenities of Hakone's luxury inns, which is why brownoarsman does not claim luxury status for it. Its welcome to overseas guests cuts both ways: on his stay there were kids running around willy-nilly and someone taking a loud business call in the lounge at night, which he has never met at another ryokan.

cities.text: Odawara Shinkansen + Hakone Tozan line/bus to Gora ~2h12.
Tokaido Shinkansen to Odawara + Hakone Tozan line/bus to Gora ~2h15.

inns.name: Takimotokan Yukinosato
inns.summary: An 11-room mountainside onsen ryokan above Yoro Falls, an hour from Nagoya, known for in-room open-air baths and its Hida beef chateaubriand, and it caters mainly to a domestic crowd and bans children under 13. KI-NRT and one member had great stays, but a second member found everything mediocre and vastly preferred Shogetsu in Gero, so opinion splits between love it and shrug. It is awkward without a car, and the shuttle from tiny Yoro station is near-mandatory.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki dinner comes with an optional A5 Hida beef chateaubriand at extra charge, and KI-NRT found the dinner wonderful and the succulent, perfectly marbled steak well worth the additional cost; buggy51 agreed that the dinner was excellent, especially that chateaubriand, which he called fantastic. A member who stayed two nights in 2024 found the food mediocre to disappointing, along with everything else.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The two suites, Kazahana and Kangetsu, have open-air onsen baths with great views, Kazahana's in its own yard and Kangetsu's on a balcony a floor up, and even a standard 20 m² room comes with a little outdoor bath. The public onsen is quite nice, and with only 11 rooms buggy51 had it to himself for the time he was there. The member who found the inn disappointing was unimpressed by the onsen as well.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written warmly about the staff. A shuttle picked buggy51 up at Yoro station, but the couple who stayed two nights in 2024 called the service mediocre to disappointing, and the website lists a phone number and no email.

room.label: Room
room.text: Rooms are Japanese-style with tatami, and the two suites are Kazahana and Kangetsu; KI-NRT says Kazahana is the choice, because it has its own yard and a more serene setting, whereas Kangetsu is on a higher floor. buggy51 was happy in a standard 20 m² room with a little outdoor bath, and the couple who stayed two nights in 2024 found the rooms mediocre.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yukinosato is perched halfway up a mountain in Yoro, Gifu, a 3-minute walk from lovely Yoro Falls, with a commanding view of the landscape below, especially from the reception area. buggy51 loved walking the falls area and Yoro Park with its quirky Site of Reversible Destiny, while a couple who stayed in 2024 found the park underwhelming and had to trek half an hour downhill along a highway just to get lunch.

cities.text: JR/Yoro Railway to Yoro ~1h, then ~15 min by car.
Yoro Railway Ogaki->Yoro ~25 min, then ~15 min by car.

inns.name: Bourou Noguchi Toya
inns.summary: Bourou Noguchi Toya is a new-build lakeside ryokan on Lake Toya, opened in late 2024, whose top rooms pair an in-room hot-spring bath with a private sauna and a fixed rotation of three included dinner menus. The two members who have stayed disagree. A Premium Suite guest calls the food inventive and the service excellent and cannot wait to return, while a 2025 guest in a lesser room got a worn-out mattress and fire-pit smoke and would not go back. The top room is the one to book, and you will want a car.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner and breakfast are both included, and HaleiwaFlyer found the food delicious and inventive, with a decent wine list that runs to Haut-Brion.
