The kitchen rotates three dinner menus and two breakfasts, so it gets old on a long stay, and glenny84, who stayed two nights in May 2025, found both meals had their highs and lows, though the food was generally good.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The top room has its own onsen bath and a private sauna, both with temperatures you control yourself, and an all-you-can-drink dispenser in the room to go with them, which HaleiwaFlyer found well worth it. Nobody in the thread has written about the communal baths or where the water comes from.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is excellent by HaleiwaFlyer's account, friendly and professional, with everyone doing everything to answer questions and get things done, though they did not find it as polished as Aman and did not expect it to be. The inn also charters a free tour bus for guests in the afternoon.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Premium Suite, the top room, is the one to book, with its own onsen bath, private sauna and drinks dispenser, and HaleiwaFlyer called it well worth it. glenny84's lesser room in May 2025 looked stylish at first glance, but the mattress was extremely worn with no support or firmness (surprising in a property this new) and smoke from the ground-floor fire pit drifted in all evening with the windows closed, and they would not return.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Bourou stands on Lake Toya in Hokkaido, and HaleiwaFlyer recommends renting a car there because the things to do around the lake require driving or riding a bike. It opened in late 2024 with great fanfare and has a decent-sized gym, but nobody in the thread has described the grounds, the building or the views.

cities.text: ~1 hr 40 min by car from New Chitose Airport (CTS) to Lake Toya.
~2 hr by car from Sapporo southwest to the caldera lake.

inns.name: Goto Retreat Ray
inns.summary: Goto Retreat Ray is the only luxury property on Fukue, the Goto Islands' main island: a fresh new-build with sea-view rooms and an excellent locally sourced kitchen (kue sashimi, kue shabu-shabu and a sauteed kue steak in season, its own take on Goto udon), but no onsen anywhere on site and a rental car as a requirement. Both first-hand stays were pleased, and KI-NRT's advice is still not to go out of your way to stay here unless you have a reason to visit Goto, namely the empty UNESCO churches and a chartered boat to the smaller islands.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The cooking is excellent and locally sourced, and kue (longtooth grouper) was in season during KI-NRT's two nights: kue sashimi, kue shabu-shabu and a wonderfully prepared sauteed kue steak, plus abalone with a sauce made from its liver and the house take on Goto udon. He picked two nits. The paid upgraded meal adds two extra dishes to each dinner instead of better ingredients, so they were bloated, and the Goto beef was a hard, chewy rump steak.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen anywhere on site, because the only spring area on Fukue is elsewhere on the island, so bathing is the heated bath on your room's balcony. KI-NRT called the lack a significant drawback and sorely missed it after the in-room hot springs at Iki Kairi Murakami, though Nagasaki Joe loves the balcony bath.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms are fresh and new with great sea views, and each has a bath on its balcony, which Nagasaki Joe loves. KI-NRT stayed in the 70m² Deluxe Twin Room with Sea View, the top category, and found it a junior-suite layout not much different from the 58m² Superior Rooms that make up most of the inn: the differences are a vanity with two sinks instead of one and extra lounge chairs and a coffee table, which he judged not entirely necessary.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Fukue is remote and low-key, and there is little to do at the hotel itself: the activities it lines up for guests are almost all paid outside excursions, and a rental car is a requirement. The hotel calls itself a retreat, with churchy influences and a meditation room, and Nagasaki Joe found the atmosphere almost monastic. The point of Fukue is its empty UNESCO hidden-Christian churches: KI-NRT drove to Dozaki and took a boat to Egami and Gorin.

cities.text: Jetfoil from Nagasaki port to Fukue (~1.5 hr), then ~10 min car to the inn.
ORC flight Fukuoka to Goto-Fukue (~40 min) plus airport access, then ~10 min car.

transit.note: Goto convention: Nagasaki + Fukuoka; island reached by air/ferry.

inns.name: Seryo
inns.summary: The only luxury ryokan in Ohara, thirty minutes by car from Kyoto, and really a one-room inn, because you need to book the Sakura no Ma with its open-air onsen bath or you are staying in an ordinary inn. You stay for the setting, with temples on foot and the Kurama–Kibune trail nearby, while the food is good but not gourmet and the service standard. KI-NRT gave it five stars and would recommend it for the Ohara tour more than as a trip to return for.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The food is good, and the kitchen leans on the local produce that many of Kyoto's finer restaurants (Kitcho among them) buy from Ohara. The dish KI-NRT remembers is the local Jidori chicken, steamed (an unusual method he has doubts about) and done amazingly well. He puts the food short of the top kitchens in Hakone or Kaga Onsen. Breakfast is a spartan affair, thin on variety and quantity, so if you are hungry be ready to eat plenty of rice.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Only one room has its own hot-spring bath, the Sakura no Ma Japanese Suite with open-air bath, and KI-NRT calls that bath pure bliss and recommends you snag the room quickly if it is available. For the purposes of the thread the inn only counts as luxury if you are in that room, because there is no onsen anywhere else.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is typical ryokan service, courteous and helpful, and KI-NRT found the comfort and service match what this small family-run inn charges. Meal times are a bit inflexible, dinner strictly at 6PM and breakfast at 8AM, but when he said they might skip breakfast for an early start on the Kurama hike, the staff offered 7:30 instead, which he found a surprisingly gracious gesture for a small ryokan with a rigid schedule.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Sakura no Ma Japanese Suite with open-air bath is the best room in the house and the one to book, though KI-NRT notes it is not really a suite. It is fresh and clean and reasonably spacious (not gargantuan by luxury ryokan standards, and he would gladly have paid more for a higher category if one existed), well appointed with toiletries, yukata, free WiFi and even a free minibar, and a nice room to spend your down time in.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Seryo sits atop a small mountain in Ohara, a rural farmland area thirty minutes by car from Kyoto, with impressive views over the valley below. Sanzen-in is right next door, and Jikko-in, Hosen-in and Shorin-in are a few minutes' walk away, all worth visiting. Kurama and Kibune are about 15 minutes by car, and the hike between them through Kurama-dera's grounds is what brought KI-NRT here, and he calls it one of the best side trips from Kyoto.

cities.text: ~1 hr by bus from Kyoto Stn to Ohara, then short walk to Seryo.
Osaka to Kyoto ~30 min, then ~1 hr bus to Ohara.

inns.name: Tawaraya
inns.summary: An 18-room Kyoto institution founded in 1707 that KI-NRT names the one to try among the city's inns, and the top choice if you cannot leave the cities. The appeal is in the depth, the layers of detail, history and omotenashi that reveal themselves the closer you look, while plenty of other inns offer better views, baths and food. You stay for the cultural experience, knowing that the kaiseki is good and no more, that there is no onsen, and that a first visit will probably get you the base room.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Both kaiseki dinner and breakfast are still served in your own room by your attendant, as many inns no longer do. KI-NRT, comparing it with the top ryokans he has eaten at, found the cooking above average but not exceptional, with flavors on the bland side (Kyoto flavors are subtle), neither creative nor memorable, and a breakfast spread not as varied as at other top inns. Some dishes are superb, but he would not stay here for the food.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at Tawaraya. Your room has a wooden bathtub, and that is the extent of the bathing here; KI-NRT counts onsen baths among the things many other inns offer that Tawaraya does not, and says it is mostly for culture and not for bathing.

service.label: Service
service.text: The service is elegant, dignified and personal, and the staff are not particularly chatty, a plus or a minus depending on what you want; for KI-NRT it was just right. He had braced for some snobbery as a first-timer and met none, and few properties in his experience rival Tawaraya's omotenashi. Your attendant serves both meals in your room and, if you ask, will explain the history and meaning of everything on display. Valet parking is free.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT's first-visit room, Kotobuki, was meticulously kept and big enough for two, but a dual-purpose all-tatami room like a lesser ryokan's (futons replace the table and chairs at night), with one sink, nowhere to hide the luggage and only a tiny study; he would have paid for a better one. Room details are published nowhere and the best rooms go to repeat guests, though first-timers can now pick their own. Ground-floor rooms have a small garden.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Tawaraya has stood in central Kyoto since 1707, with no grand entrance or big lobby and no view beyond its immaculate gardens. The narrow doorway opens onto a wooden maze of corridors that whisks you back to the Edo era, past hanging scrolls, Muromachi-period screens, old books and ikebana, and the artwork changes monthly with the seasons. KI-NRT did not see a speck of dust anywhere, so old here never means shabby. Hiiragiya is across the street.

cities.text: ~15 min by taxi from JR Kyoto Stn to central Nakagyo.
Osaka to Kyoto ~30 min Shinkansen/special rapid, then ~15 min taxi.

inns.name: Ryotei Kuki
inns.summary: A seven-room modern build by Zaborin's architect, put up in 2009 to revitalize old Esashi, and the only high-end option there. The kitchen delivers and the town is worth the wander, but the walled-in rooms waste the seaside site, and KI-NRT puts it a notch below the top ryokans in Japan, a high-quality stop where he didn't expect to find one and not a destination in itself.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is in private koshitsu rooms, and the kitchen cooks southern Hokkaido ingredients simply and extremely well: sashimi as good as it gets, a marvelous grilled herring caught just offshore and basted with a sweet sauce, and a crisp, light abalone and maitake tempura. The one letdown was the lamb from the owner's own farm, tough and short on umami. Breakfast was plain, and the quality of everything, down to the Assabu-cho rice, was incredible.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Each of the seven rooms has its own indoor onsen bath, straight from the source and not recirculated, from the spring chairman Tanada drilled more than 1,400 metres to find, having agreed to build only if there was onsen under the land. That indoor tub is all there is, though: no large public bath, no private or rental baths, and no open-air bath, which KI-NRT regrets with the ocean right there.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here, beyond KI-NRT learning the inn's origins from a conversation with Mr. Tanada, its chairman, who had run an electronics store and a farm and went to a university to learn the hospitality business before opening it.

room.label: Room
room.text: All seven rooms are the same 63 m² Japanese-Western suite: a small tatami room, a larger living area with a leather sofa, a bedroom with Western beds and the indoor onsen bath, in a muted, minimalist modern Japanese style. There is only one sink, the Toto toilet is an older model, and the concrete privacy wall cuts off the lower half of the view, so you see the sky and parts of the ocean and marina only if you stand up.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Kuki is a seaside property in Esashi, one of the oldest towns in Hokkaido, with the Kaiyo Maru warship replica on one side and the preserved Inishie Kaido street on the other, and the historic port is very walkable. Large rocks and a concrete perimeter wall with no tall vegetation ring the property, stylish but leaving an inn beside the ocean with hardly any view of it, which KI-NRT regrets. Inside there is little beyond the lounge.

cities.text: ~90 min by car from Hakodate Airport/Station to Esashi on the southwest coast.
~3.5 hr by car from New Chitose Airport (CTS) around the Oshima Peninsula.

inns.name: Taketoritei Maruyama
inns.summary: A modern-Japanese ryokan in Arima Onsen with silver-water (Ginsen) baths in the rooms and eight rentable private baths that cover both of Arima's spring types, gold included. KI-NRT suggests it as a good Arima option, and Buster CT1K, who stayed on that suggestion, found the silver water really great and the gold pretty good too. Nobody in the thread has written a word about the food, and everything either reviewer says about the place concerns the baths.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the food here; neither KI-NRT nor Buster CT1K says a word about dinner or breakfast.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Both of Arima's waters are under one roof. The in-room baths run the silver (Ginsen) spring, a rare radium type that Buster CT1K found really great, and eight private baths, rentable in 45-minute increments, cover both the silver and the famous gold (Kinsui) water, which he thought pretty good too, so you can go back and forth between the two. The one drawback for KI-NRT is that the in-room baths are silver and not gold.

service.label: Service
service.text: Buster CT1K reports very good service, and that is all anyone in the thread has said about it.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT describes the rooms as modern Japanese and quite comfortable, and each has an in-room bath fed by the silver (Ginsen) spring. Nobody in the thread has described a particular room.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The ryokan is in Arima Onsen, and nobody in the thread has written about the property's grounds or its surroundings.

cities.text: Osaka Stn/Umeda to Arima Onsen ~60 min direct highway bus, then ~5 min to inn.
Shin-Kobe/Sannomiya to Arima ~30 min by bus or Kobe Electric Rly, then ~5 min.

inns.name: Bettei Itsuki
inns.summary: Bettei Itsuki is a Yufuin ryokan that one family in the thread has stayed at, with very good food and free sake at dinner, indoor and outdoor onsen in the room and a somewhat self-service style that still produced considerate touches for a toddler. Bristom liked it and found the value good, but said he would have picked Gekkoju Yufuin had he not overlooked it when planning, in a town stacked with strong rivals. KI-NRT names it among the area's top contenders without having stayed.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Bristom called the food very good, and the dinner menu has a free alcohol section with sake and more. Breakfast is served in a private room in the restaurant with a view. He named no individual dishes.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Karin room has its own indoor and outdoor onsen baths, set right next to each other, and Bristom enjoyed them on his family's stay. Nobody in the thread has written about any shared baths or the water here.

service.label: Service
service.text: The inn runs a bit self-service by design, but the staff think ahead: they pushed the two separate beds together so Bristom's baby could sleep in the middle without being asked, and like the other Kyushu inns on his trip it welcomes children and provides yukata, utensils, meals, chairs and even gifts for them.

room.label: Room
room.text: Bristom stayed in the Karin room, which has two separate beds (pushed together for his baby) and its own indoor and outdoor onsen baths. Nobody in the thread has described the room beyond that.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Bettei Itsuki is in Yufuin, which KI-NRT calls a very crowded field of top properties (Sanso Murata, Enowa, Yufuin Rikka, Gekkoju Yufuin and Kamenoi Besso among them). Breakfast is served in a private room in the restaurant with a view, and the Hells of Beppu are nearby.

cities.text: Direct highway bus Fukuoka to Kurokawa Onsen (~2.7 hr).
Shinkansen toward Kumamoto, then ~2 hr by car up to Kurokawa Onsen.

inns.name: Takinoya
inns.summary: The top luxury name in Noboribetsu, and KI-NRT keeps recommending it as exactly that: a very solid property with superb pure source-fed water and wonderful forest-facing communal baths. He repeats every time, though, that nothing beyond the onsen blew him away, with food that was only good, no uni served, and a nakai who refused simple requests. The water alone makes it worth a stay, and the rest is solid without being transcendent.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner was good and some of it great, but for Hokkaido, which KI-NRT calls one of the world's top seafood locales, it did not stand out from the pack. The buri (amberjack) seemed to have come previously frozen, creativity ran to minor novelties like a foam soy sauce, and no uni was served in two nights, which sorely disappointed him. He has repeated the letdown for years, while allowing that his 2020 stay may have caught a bad time.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The water is the one thing that blew KI-NRT away: 100% pure Noboribetsu hot spring water fed straight into the open-air bath on the DW suite, so you will not feel cheated as at ryokans that dilute their onsen. The communal baths are wonderful and face a scenic forest, and he rates them more expansive and better-viewed than Chalet Ivy's. He adds that Noboribetsu has awesome onsen everywhere, so every ryokan in town likely has the same quality.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was a mixed bag, without the vaunted omotenashi. The nakai was never rude but robotic and formulaic, showing experience without warmth. When KI-NRT asked her to set dinner in the Japanese-style room she answered 'that is not possible', and when he arranged dishes for a photo she told him that is not how it is done in Japan, which he found snide and petty. The front desk would not help with a booking at the new Upopoy Ainu museum either.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Japanese Suite DW type is a hybrid of Western and Japanese, with a dining room with table and chairs, a Japanese-style room and a bedroom with real Western beds, and at 92 square metres it is reasonably spacious. Meals are served in the room. There is no Presidential Suite or equivalent for anyone wanting the ultimate bling factor, but KI-NRT says the DW should satisfy even the most demanding luxury traveller. Book one of the DW suites.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Takinoya sits steps from Jigokudani (Hell's Valley), the top sight in Noboribetsu, with Oyunuma Pond, Oku no Yu and a natural foot bath close by and worth the hike, and you can smell the sulfur as soon as you arrive. The grounds are not as expansive as at other world-class ryokans, though what is there is pretty nice, including a beautiful small water garden. KI-NRT lists Takinoya among the traditional ryokans with great forest and garden views.

cities.text: ~1 hr by car from New Chitose Airport (CTS) to Noboribetsu Onsen.
~1.5 hr by car from Sapporo down the coast to Noboribetsu.

inns.name: Yoshikawa
inns.summary: A small Kyoto inn wrapped around a famed tempura restaurant, and the tempura kaiseki dinner is the event, served in a private room with the owner okami-san among the servers. The one member who has stayed recommends it but found it not quite as special as Nishimuraya in Kinosaki, missing the hot springs and village feel a city inn can't offer. It is best thought of as a dinner with a lovely garden-view room attached.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The tempura is what the inn is known for, and the member who stayed found it wonderful, very light, crispy and flavorful, with a sauce or two he had never had with tempura before. His Tempura Kaiseki with Chiya beef was served in a private room and the quality was high throughout, and the chef came in first to present the ingredients on a huge platter (for all the guests, it turned out). KI-NRT has dined at the famed restaurant but never stayed.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen and no bathhouse. Each of the seven rooms has a hinoki indoor tub of plain heated water, and according to the inn's own room list that is the whole of the bathing here. The one member who has stayed never mentions it.

service.label: Service
service.text: Welcome and service were warm and personable, and there were two servers at dinner, one of them the owner okami-san.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Wagtail (Sekirei) room was spacious with a lovely view of the garden, and that is all the one member who has stayed had to say about it.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yoshikawa is in downtown Kyoto near some shopping centers, about a 20 minute walk from Nijo Castle and close by the famed Hiiragiya and Tawaraya ryokans. The reception area is small next to Nishimuraya's much larger one with amenities, and the member who stayed missed the village feel he had enjoyed in Kinosaki.

cities.text: ~15 min by taxi from JR Kyoto Stn to central Nakagyo.
Osaka to Kyoto ~30 min Shinkansen/special rapid, then ~15 min taxi.

inns.name: Yufuin Rikka
inns.summary: A six-room Yufuin inn with a private onsen bath in every room that the one member who stayed found unbeatable for the money; it runs far less per night than neighbours like Enowa, Gekkoju or Sanso Murata, and Japanese reviewers think extremely highly of it. He would call it quality and high-end and is not sure it qualifies as luxury. KI-NRT has not stayed himself, so the account comes from that single visit and from acquaintances of his, and with six rooms it is tough to book.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: All meals are served in private dining rooms, and zander86, the one member who has stayed, enjoyed the breakfast spread here most of the three Kyushu ryokans on his trip (Amanosato and Sanso Tensui were the others). Nobody in the thread has written about dinner from their own table, but KI-NRT relays that several acquaintances who stayed recently called the fusion cuisine top-notch.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Each of the six rooms has its own onsen bath, and from some of them you look at Mt. Yufu while from others you do not. KI-NRT hears that Ichiban has the most unobstructed view of the mountain, so ask for that room if the view matters to you.

service.label: Service
service.text: Meals are served in private dining rooms, and otherwise nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: There are only six rooms, each with an onsen bath; zander86 called the inn quality and high-end but did not describe his room, and nobody else in the thread has.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Rikka is in Yufuin with Mt. Yufu as the backdrop, on what KI-NRT calls a very crowded list of top properties in the area (Sanso Murata, Zakuro, Enowa, Gekkoju Yufuin, Bettei Itsuki and others), and whether you see the mountain depends on which of the six rooms you get. Nobody in the thread has described the grounds.

cities.text: Reverse of: Ltd Exp back toward Hakata (~2h10).
Kyushu Shinkansen Kagoshima-Chūō→Hakata (~1h20), ~4-min platform transfer, then the JR 'Yufu' Ltd Exp Hakata→Yufuin (~2h15). ~3h11 total, all-rail.

Reverse of: By car (~210 km, raw ~2h25 per NAVITIME; budget ~3h): Yufuin IC → Oita Expwy → Tosu JCT → Nagasaki Expwy → Nagasaki IC (~¥5,060). Budget 3h+ in January — the Yufuin IC–Hita IC stretch (~45 km) is an official winter-tire-regulation zone (last winter: 7 days of regulation, 2 of closure); past Hita it's plains, and the Nagasaki Expwy has no regulated section at all. (Transit: Ltd Exp 'Yufu'→Hakata ~2h15 + 'Relay Kamome'/'Kamome' via Takeo, ~3.5h total, 2 changes — 2026-07 audit; rare January snow on the Kyudai line's pass.)

Reverse of: Ltd Exp 'Yufu'/'Yufuin-no-Mori' Yufuin→Kurume (~1h40, ~5/day), Shinkansen Kurume→Kumamoto (~25 min). Scenic alt: the Kyushu Ōdan bus through Kurokawa/Aso, one seat, ~4h15, 3/day. By car ~2.5h via the Yamanami Highway.

Fly to Yufuin: Tokyo→Haneda (~30 min), HND→Oita (OIT) ~1h30 nonstop (frequent ANA/JAL/Solaseed; 2026-07 audit vs flightsfrom/sakuratravel timetables), then a pre-booked FIXED-FARE taxi straight to the inn (~55 min, ¥18,320 incl. tolls — Oita Taxi Assoc., say '定額で') — no bus-schedule or shuttle sync. (Budget alt: airport bus→Yufuin Stn ~55 min, 6/day, ¥1,550pp + the inn shuttle — Enowa's needs reserving ≥3 days ahead.) Far saner than the ~5h45 all-rail haul.

Airport bus Kanazawa→Komatsu + KMQ→Fukuoka (~1h40) into Hakata, then Ltd Exp 'Yufu'/'Yufuin-no-Mori' Hakata→Yufuin (~2h10). ~6h door-to-door. (Oita is Yufuin's own airport but has no Komatsu flight — Hakata is the gateway.)

inns.name: Bettei Otozure
inns.summary: Bettei Otozure is the intimate 18-room contemporary sister to the big, aging Otani Sanso in Nagato, connected to it by a private indoor walkway, and its guests are free to dine and use the facilities at the larger property (the reverse is not allowed). KI-NRT calls it one of the top luxury ryokans in southern Honshu, not quite up to the standards of the best of the best (Gora Kadan, Asaba or Takefue), and he would not hesitate to recommend it. He found it a good base for exploring the surrounding areas by car, and the place itself is not a destination.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The food leans heavily towards seafood from the nearby Sea of Japan (fugu, tilefish, sea urchin, conger eel, stonefish), all wonderfully prepared and garnished, and KI-NRT calls the quality very high. The one drawback is that there is less of it than at other ryokans, the hassun is a single dish where most inns serve several, and on two of his three nights dessert was fruit and only fruit. Teppanyaki is available at sister Otani Sanso.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The A-Type suite has its own open-air hot-spring bath out on the massive 32 square metre balcony, with several lounge chairs to relax on around it, and KI-NRT considers an in-room open-air onsen a prerequisite for a high-category room to count as luxurious. He does not describe any communal bath, though Otozure guests can also use the facilities at the much larger Otani Sanso next door.

service.label: Service
service.text: The only service story comes from before arrival, when KI-NRT called to ask whether meals could be served in the room and was told no, it is in the restaurant; he later learned that two rooms (204, a Type B, and 206, a Type C) do allow in-room dining, both about 50 feet from his own room, and he wished they had said so even if it meant a different room category. Nobody in the thread has written about the service during the stay itself.

room.label: Room
room.text: His A-Type suite is 82 square metres with a living room, dining room and separate bedroom, plus a 32 square metre balcony, and he calls the size good but not great. The furnishings are contemporary Japanese, a plus or a minus depending on your taste. The one drawback is the semi-open plan, where the bedroom is in its own area but no wall or door separates it from the living room, which is not good if one person naps while the other works.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: There is not much to do in the immediate area, so KI-NRT treats the inn as a base for exploring western Yamaguchi by rental car. During his three nights he visited Hagi (very historic), Motonosumi Inari Shrine, Tsunoshima Bridge, Beppu Benten Pond and the incredible five-storied pagoda at Ruriko-ji Temple near Yamaguchi City, and he says it combines easily with Hiroshima and Miyajima, with the must-see Kintai-kyo Bridge at Iwakuni along the way.

cities.text: ~60 min by car/inn shuttle from Shin-Yamaguchi Stn to Otozure.
Hiroshima to Shin-Yamaguchi ~30 min Shinkansen, then ~60 min by car.

inns.name: Hanaichi
inns.summary: A seven-room inn in Tsumagoi, Gunma, founded in 2002 after the owner couple drilled 1,000 meters under the building and hit the onsen jackpot: superb source-fed water in every room plus three 24-hour private baths. The hosts are warm and unpretentious, and the cooking split the household, pretty good to KI-NRT and excellent to his wife. He is blunt that it is no destination ryokan; it works as a comfortable stop on the way to Karuizawa (45 minutes) or Kusatsu (40 minutes).

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The head chef is the owner's son, and his kitchen does a competent job with the local fish, meat and produce, all elegantly presented and nothing super fancy: salt-grilled iwana (white-spotted char), Joshu beef steak, and tuna, sweet shrimp and trout sashimi. KI-NRT remembers dinner as pretty good but not particularly memorable, while Mrs. KI-NRT recalls the meals as excellent. Breakfast was quite impressive, with a wide variety of unique dishes.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The owners decided to open a ryokan only after drilling over 1,000 meters below ground and hitting the onsen jackpot, so the water comes straight from the source directly below the property, and it is top-notch quality, with a constant flow that needs no filtration. Every room has its own onsen (not open-air, though you can open the windows), and on top of that there are three private baths open to guests 24 hours a day, first come, first served.

service.label: Service
service.text: Everyone from the room attendant to the owners to the young head chef was professional and courteous, and they do a great job of making each guest feel at home. KI-NRT felt comfortable here; it is not the type of place that intimidates you the way 'storied and glamorous' ryokans like Tawaraya or Asaba can when you first walk in.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Tsukishi room is a 75-square-metre junior suite with two beds, a living room, a dining table for two, a sitting corner with a kotatsu (a heated coffee table that keeps your feet toasty), a patio, a little work area and its own onsen, which is not open-air though the windows open. From the patio you get a bit of a view of Mt. Asama, but power lines and a cookie-cutter white building detract from it. Meals can be served in the room for a fee.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Hanaichi sits on the side of a road in the middle of nowhere in Tsumagoi, on the far side of Mt. Asama from Karuizawa, and arriving is not wow-inducing, nothing like Gosho Gekkoju: it does not scream luxury from outside, and the reception looks like a rural country home, a mishmash of furnishings that suit the owner's taste. There are barely any grounds, just a common lounge and the rental baths, and KI-NRT says it is not a destination ryokan.

cities.text: Shinkansen to Takasaki + Agatsuma Line ~2.5h, then ~40 min by car.
~50 min by car from JR Karuizawa Stn.

inns.name: Kaichoro
inns.summary: Kaichoro is an adults-only, 8-room annex of the 440-year-old, 83-room Fukuichi in Ikaho Onsen, with onsen in every room and its own entrance, lobby and staff, so you get the Ikaho onsen experience (two spring varieties, in-room open-air baths, warm staff) without the crowds of the big parent. The kitchen is the weak leg, with a few courses worthy of the setting next to izakaya-plain ones. KI-NRT found it worth doing for the golden water and an off-the-beaten-path town, and he has had better meals at cheaper ryokans.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki was a mixed bag for KI-NRT. Several servings were wonderful, the fugu in a jellied dashi broth was memorable and so was the shirako (cod milt) tempura, but other courses were unimaginative and not appropriate for a ryokan of this class; the buri daikon is a typical izakaya dish and this one did not stand out either. Breakfast was an improvement, though not enough to change his belief that he has had better meals at cheaper ryokans.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every room has onsen, and Kaichoro draws two spring varieties, Shirogane no Yu (Silver) and Kogane no Yu (Golden, reddish brown from its iron); KI-NRT's suite had the Silver in its open-air bath facing the valley. To try the Golden, book the rental bath Fuwari, which comes straight from the source. The other two rental baths, Yurari and Sarari, are Mt. Haruna tap water with no onsen in them, and the communal baths with both types are in Fukuichi.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT wondered whether the service would be watered down and corporate, given that Kaichoro is part of a much larger ryokan, but his fears were unfounded: everyone was gracious, warm, knowledgeable and professional. Kaichoro has its own dedicated staff, separate from Fukuichi, and although he does his own research and asks little of ryokan staff, he has little doubt they would do everything they could should the need arise.

room.label: Room
room.text: The 100 square metre Japanese & Western-style Suite with Open-Air Bath was modern, spacious and tastefully appointed, with a bedroom, a tatami room, a Western-style living room and two toilets (a big bonus for KI-NRT), and outside a large patio with a garden, an open-air hot-spring bath and a serene view across the valley. The one letdown is the cheap single-use, tear-open toiletries, which puzzled him at this level.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Kaichoro occupies two floors of Fukuichi's Manyo Building, and although you feel you are in a hotel in a hotel at first glance, once inside it does not feel that way. A passageway through the second Fukuichi building drops you at step 300 of Ikaho's 365 stone steps. Ikaho itself is a faded-glory, Showa-era onsen town, worth doing if you are in the area and want to be off the beaten path, though KI-NRT would not call it a bucket-list destination.

cities.text: Joetsu/Hokuriku Shinkansen to Takasaki + local to Shibukawa ~1.5h, then ~25 min by car.
Local Takasaki->Shibukawa ~20 min, then ~25 min by car to Ikaho Onsen.

inns.name: Modern Ryokan kishi-ke
inns.summary: Modern Ryokan kishi-ke is a one-group-at-a-time villa in Kamakura run by a wonderful English-speaking couple and built around on-site experiences (zazen, tea ceremonies, katana training) that KI-NRT mostly skipped in favor of the temples. He really enjoyed the stay and would love to return and do it properly, while being clear it is no one-room Aman or Asaba, since the villa layout is awkward, there is no onsen and dinner is out on the town.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Breakfast is included and is vegetarian Buddhist shojin cuisine, each dish prepared by Hitomi Kishi herself; on both days it was creative, nutritious and hearty (kabocha potage, udon in an amazing broth, marinated tofu skin made to mimic unagi), and KI-NRT never missed meat or fish. Dinner is not included, so you dine out in Kamakura, though kishi-ke can prepare anything from sushi to a shojin dinner if asked in advance.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at kishi-ke, since Kamakura is devoid of hot springs, and no special bath either; the villa's ordinary bathroom is upstairs with the bedroom.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobuyuki and Hitomi Kishi, the couple who own and run kishi-ke, host one group at a time, and KI-NRT had a delightful time with them learning about the area, how kishi-ke came to be and their plans. Nobuyuki studied English in Buffalo for a year and speaks it very well, and he doubles as a private concierge: he was extremely helpful over WhatsApp and secured a last-minute table at a popular shirasu (whitebait) restaurant.

room.label: Room
room.text: The two-story villa has 88 square metres indoors, but KI-NRT did not find it as usable as he hoped: the first floor is a tatami room used for breakfast, the bedroom and bathroom are upstairs, and the stairs between the floors are outside, a design flaw that made it too much of a hassle to use the first floor for anything but breakfast. One side faces the ocean, but the view is partially obscured by ugly electric poles and wires.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: kishi-ke is behind the main coastal road across from Yuigahama Beach, with Hasedera and the Great Buddha within walking distance and some decent restaurants nearby, though it is hemmed in by houses and businesses. A dry rock garden separates the reception, where check-in opens with a tea ceremony, from the villa. Strict zoning caps Kamakura at 980 guest rooms, so early mornings are quiet, and KI-NRT had the Great Buddha to himself at 8AM.

cities.text: JR Yokosuka Line Tokyo->Kamakura ~1h, then ~5 min by car/Enoden to Hase.
JR Yokohama->Kamakura ~30 min, then ~5 min by car/Enoden.

inns.name: Zenagi
inns.summary: A one-group-per-day villa in a restored Edo-period kominka above the rice paddies of the Kiso Valley, minutes from the Nakasendo post towns of Tsumago and Magome, with three bedrooms, a spectacular nail-less timber living hall and a wood-fired kitchen of foraged and wild-game cooking. KI-NRT found the stay memorable and completely private, but the service is casual and had its misses, there is no onsen, and the bedrooms are built for sleeping only. It makes most sense for a first Nakasendo visit or for a group taking the whole villa.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kitchen cooks the Kiso Valley, which means foraged herbs, mushrooms and chestnuts, boar, deer and river fish, much of it wood-fired with local timber and hay for a subtle smokiness. KI-NRT found the meal "prepared impeccably" if not especially fancy, and the best dishes came early, a medley of wild vegetables and an exceptional tart of smoked Shinshu trout. The boar and deer kept some gaminess, and breakfast was a plain Western spread.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no hot spring on site and none that KI-NRT knows of nearby, since the Kiso region is not blessed with onsen, so bathing means the bathroom on the ground floor of each duplex bedroom, and no more. He calls the absence a bit of a disappointment in the colder months, and his own room had no hot water at all, so they walked about thirty feet to the adjacent bathroom whenever they wanted it.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was solid, as you would expect with one party at a time, and everyone on the largely non-Japanese team (Nepalese, American and Filipino among them) was friendly and engaging. It is deliberately casual and not a traditional omotenashi experience, and with that came a slightly less attentive level of service. Several requests needed repeated reminders, including Mrs. KI-NRT's request for warm water in the bedroom, which took nearly an hour.

room.label: Room
room.text: The kominka's living floor is the show, a massive two-storey Edo timber structure joined without nails, with astonishing decoration and a table top carved from a single piece of cypress. The three duplex bedrooms (Matsu, Miya and Nori) are the weakest part, with the bathroom downstairs, steep stairs and low ceilings, and Miya is noticeably darker, so take another. KI-NRT calls this no major issue, but there was no sleepwear or toothbrush.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Zenagi is perched on a hill above a satoyama landscape of rice paddies, and Tsumago and Magome are five and fifteen minutes away by car, post towns KI-NRT calls about as magical as they come. One group has the whole place each day, and the inn arranges guided rafting, paragliding, Nakasendo Trail walks, meditation and a tea-farm visit. KI-NRT's tandem paraglide with an Asian Games gold medalist was otherworldly once airborne.

cities.text: Reverse of: Inn car to Nagiso (~10 min), JR Ltd Exp 'Shinano'→Nagoya (~60 min), then Tōkaidō Shinkansen 'Nozomi'→Tokyo (~1h40). One change at Nagoya. ⚠ Only ~4 Shinano/day stop at Nagiso — otherwise ~25–30-min inn car to Nakatsugawa, where every Shinano stops (~50 min to Nagoya, same total).

Reverse of: Inn car to Nagiso (~10 min), through 'Shinano' Nagiso→Nagano (~2h00, one seat past Matsumoto), change to Hokuriku Shinkansen 'Kagayaki'/'Hakutaka'→Kanazawa (~65–70 min). One change at Nagano — beats the Nagoya→'Shirasagi'→Tsuruga alternative (~4h, 2 changes). Sparse Nagiso stops: Nakatsugawa fallback adds ~15 min.

Reverse of: Inn car to Nagiso (~10 min), JR Ltd Exp 'Shinano'→Nagoya (~60 min), then Tōkaidō Shinkansen 'Nozomi'→Kyoto (~35 min). One change at Nagoya — the Kiso Valley sits on the natural pivot west. Sparse Nagiso stops: Nakatsugawa fallback, same total.

inns.name: Jusandi
inns.summary: A five-villa Mediterranean-white hideaway in northern Ishigaki that existed for Chef Hirose's Italian-Japanese cooking, which was good enough that KI-NRT once dined in four nights straight and which alone brought him back on a detour in December 2025. That return found the food already below what he remembered, and the chef retired at the end of March 2026 with no successor or cuisine direction announced. With no sea views, no onsen and the kitchen now an open question, he thinks booking Jusandi today means betting on an unknown.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Chef Takumi Hirose's Italian-Japanese cooking is why KI-NRT came, and in 2020 he ate dinner here four nights running: dashi in most of the sauces, and a cold capellini with tomato sauce and caviar he called divine. His December 2025 return found the menus short on imagination and heavy, though the tuskfish brandade opener was terrific and the Okinawan breakfast a high point. Hirose retired in March 2026 with no successor named.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen. Ishigaki has virtually no natural hot springs, because the geology does not favor them, and Okinawa's warm climate means bathing here leans toward showers over soaking tubs anyway, so the villa has an ordinary tub and shower at the far end of the hallway. The water feature is the private pool at each villa, pretty when lit up at night, though in a December cold spell (upper teens Celsius) lounging by it was not an option.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was outstanding on KI-NRT's 2020 stay. With only five villas the staff is small and everyone but the chef wears multiple hats, so the person who checked them in later delivered breakfast, cleaned the pool and mowed the lawn. They were professional, courteous and eager to please, and a humidifier arrived in record time. His butler from that stay, Hiroya Hayakawa, has since moved to One Suite The Grand on Kouri Island.

room.label: Room
room.text: The five villas are white minimalist concrete, each laid out slightly differently by the terrain. Maani, the one-bedroom pool villa, is long and thin, so it felt tighter than its 60 square metres, and KI-NRT would have liked more generous space. The 100-square-metre two-bedroom Yarabu is squarer, so the living room feels brighter and more open, even if much of the extra area is the second bedroom. More wood might have added warmth.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Jusandi sits on a remote plot on Ishigaki's north coast, with dense jungle all around that has been left uncleared, so although the nearest beach is a few hundred metres off there is essentially no sea view from anywhere. The white Mediterranean buildings have aged gracefully. A short jungle walk reaches a small secluded cove, the starting point for swims to the blue cave, but the north side takes fierce winds and December seas run rough.

cities.text: ~30 min by car from New Ishigaki Airport to the inn.
Flight Naha to Ishigaki (~55 min) plus airport access, then ~30 min car.

transit.note: Ishigaki reached only by air; Ishigaki Airport + Naha convention.

inns.name: Kifu No Sato
inns.summary: Kifu no Sato is the top luxury ryokan in Yunogo Onsen, one of Okayama's three famous onsen towns, and KI-NRT later called it arguably the top ryokan in Okayama Prefecture; the family that runs it went on to open Naoshima Ryokan Roka. His own impressions from a 2021 overnight are lukewarm in the details, with a drab yellow exterior in a town that has seen better days, kaiseki he called pretty darned good, and a maybe on returning. He calls it a good option if you are looking to stay somewhere between Osaka/Kyoto and Hiroshima, although it is a bit out of the way.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki was pretty darned good in KI-NRT's brief account, served in his suite's own dining room, and the one dish he describes is a clear soup of tai (red sea bream) with white hair leek, where the cheek portion of the bream was full of awesome fat and flavor and the broth was light but umami-infused.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Hiougi suite has its own open-air onsen bath, which KI-NRT called wonderful, and Yunogo is one of Okayama's three famous onsen towns (with Yubara and Okutsu). Nobody in the thread has described the water itself or the communal baths.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Hiougi suite (the name means leopard lily), where KI-NRT stayed, is a nicely appointed 75 square metres with a living room, a dining room, a separate bedroom and its own open-air onsen bath. Nobody in the thread has described the interiors beyond that.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Kifu no Sato is housed in a bland yellow building that could use a fresh coat of paint in a different colour, in a Yunogo Onsen whose postwar-boom structures were showing their age (and the town was dead during his pandemic visit), but things were better once he stepped inside, where very pretty bonsai and ikebana arrangements, including at the front entrance, help to dress things up. It is a bit out of the way between Osaka/Kyoto and Hiroshima.

cities.text: ~90 min by car from Okayama Stn to Yunogo Onsen.
Hiroshima to Okayama ~40 min Shinkansen, then ~90 min by car.

inns.name: Arimasansoh Goshobessho
inns.summary: A ten-room luxury property with French-inspired dining in Arima Onsen, its grounds thick with trees and ponds and its villas built to blend into that calming landscape, and the best KI-NRT has found in a town whose ryokans have otherwise never cut the mustard for him. The genuine hot-spring water suffers from a slow, self-fill in-room tub, and the top villa runs a little dark, but service is refined and after two nights he said the quality of it all will not make you feel cheated in any way.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is French-inspired with Japanese ingredients (bouillabaisse with fried lobster, Japanese turnip and yuzu; a spring roll of lotus root mochi and cheese), ending with rice, miso soup and pickles as a kaiseki does. KI-NRT found the food very good but just short of exceptional, and he preferred the food at Nakanobo Zuien, also in Arima. Breakfast is more Western (French toast, grilled fish) and satisfying though not memorable.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The water is the real Arima water, brackish brown and smelling of sulfur, unlike the clear water of most onsen. But the in-room bath in the Villa is not free-flowing: you fill the huge tub from a tap that trickles, 30 to 60 minutes per bath, which KI-NRT found tedious. The communal baths are indoors with no view. The Villa bathroom also has a sauna, and a new treehouse villa has an open-air kinsen (gold) bath on its deck.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is refined and a little formal, and KI-NRT could tell the staff had all been comprehensively trained in Japanese hospitality. Given the clientele that stays here, he thought discreet and unobtrusive was probably appropriate.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT's Villa Suite, the top room type, is listed at 100 square metres and felt bigger, with an enormous living room, a large bedroom, a small balcony over the ravine, high vaulted ceilings and a bathroom as big as many hotel rooms with dual vanities and the onsen tub. The dark wood and dark brown furnishings were on the dark side for his taste, and the lighting only just kept the room from feeling gloomy.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The property is at the end of the strip of hotels in Arima Onsen, quaint but a walk from the main tourist areas, and its buildings and villas blend in nicely with grounds full of trees, ponds and pretty vegetation. Stepping into the grounds will instantly reduce your blood pressure, it is that soothing a place. Arima is a stone's throw from Osaka and Kobe, and most of its other ryokans are massive pre-bubble hotels or small, run-down places.

cities.text: Osaka Stn/Umeda to Arima Onsen ~60 min direct highway bus, then ~5 min to inn.
Shin-Kobe/Sannomiya to Arima ~30 min by bus or Kobe Electric Rly, then ~5 min.

inns.name: Chikusenso Mt.Zao Onsen Resort & Spa
inns.summary: A midsize, 30-room contemporary resort in Togatta Onsen on the flank of Mt. Zao, its design blending Japanese and local elements into the surrounding landscape. KI-NRT's one detailed account calls it one of the jewels of the Tohoku region, with Chef Naoi's cooking he ranked not far off his all-time favorites. The huge Presidential Suite's outdoor bath, though, sits down a locked hallway and stairs, and he places the property among Japan's pricier stays without ranking it among the true elite.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Executive Chef Kiyokazu Naoi cooks with real skill and does not water the food down for foreign tastes. One dinner was a mostly-fugu course, and another a run of just-made tempura that Naoi-san prepared personally, which KI-NRT found innovative and delightful. He would not put the dining in his all-time top five, though it is not far off. The one drawback is that dinner cannot be served in your room, as the finer ryokans offer.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Presidential Suite's open-air onsen bath is a hassle to reach: you leave by the room's front door, go down a hallway and a flight of stairs, and unlock a door (KI-NRT's party held the only key) into a small garden. He would rather step straight from the veranda into the water. The second-highest room category avoids the problem, with its open-air bath on the balcony of an upper floor. Nobody in the thread has described the communal baths.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was courteous, friendly and attentive, but KI-NRT would not say the staff went above and beyond. When he asked them to call once the morning road report for the Zao Echo Line came through, they suggested a website, and although they asked about his plans on arrival, nobody flagged that Miyagi Fox Village would be closed the Wednesday he meant to visit. On the plus side, Chikusenso does laundry and pressing, which very few ryokans offer.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Presidential Suite, the top room of the 30, is an enormous 116 square metres with absolute privacy in all directions, so you can leave the shades open all day and night, and it has just about every modern convenience and piece of technology you could hope for. KI-NRT found the decor and furniture a bit strange and not to his taste, though it was a comfortable place to relax.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Chikusenso is a relatively new build in Togatta Onsen on the flank of Mt. Zao, and it combines contemporary design with traditional Japanese and local elements in a way that blends nicely with the serene natural surroundings. The Zao Echo Line scenic road is nearby (it closes at the slightest hint of bad weather), as is Miyagi Fox Village, and KI-NRT slots the stop into his Tohoku driving routes between Matsushima and Iizaka Onsen.

cities.text: Chikusenso is roughly 1h by car from Sendai, or shinkansen to Shiroishi-Zao (~15 min) plus about 40 min by car.
Tohoku Shinkansen Yamabiko from Tokyo to Shiroishi-Zao is about 2h, then roughly 40 min by car up to Zao Onsen.

inns.name: Hoshino Resorts Kai Unzen

features.in_room_onsen: Yes (16 of 51 rooms, private open-air balcony bath)

inns.summary: A 51-room Hoshino Resorts property built almost inside Unzen's steaming Jigoku hot-spring hells, opened in late 2022 with 16 rooms carrying a private balcony onsen. Nagasaki Joe stayed five months in on a breakfast-only plan (no dinner sampled) and found real strengths in the shared sulfur bathhouse and the breakfast kitchen, but called the room overly spartan and the exterior plain for a brand-new building. He judged it decent, though at a similar price he would pick the traditional ryokan next door instead.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Nagasaki Joe stayed on a breakfast-only plan, so dinner is untested, and his short verdict on the breakfast was good enough that he counted it among the strengths of the stay. Nobody in the thread has described the dinner here.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The shared sulfur bathhouse was the highlight of Nagasaki Joe's stay, with real Unzen hot-spring water. Some rooms have a private balcony onsen, but he has not written about them.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: Nagasaki Joe found his room spartan, and it was one of the reasons he would take the Kyushu Hotel next door at the same price.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The building stands at the edge of Unzen's Jigoku hot-spring hells, next door to the Mt.Resort Unzen Kyushu Hotel, and Nagasaki Joe called the exterior drab. Nobody has written about the grounds or the interiors in any more detail.

cities.text: Rail Hakata to Isahaya, then ~50 min bus/car up to Unzen.
Shinkansen then transfers to Isahaya, then ~50 min bus/car to Unzen.

inns.name: Kappo Ryokan Wakamatsu
inns.summary: Hakodate's most famous onsen ryokan, a 1924 inn that hosted the Emperor and came back from a years-long pandemic closure. KI-NRT's 2025 return found the kimono-clad personal service and source-fed sea-view baths as good as he remembered, but the once-revered kitchen has stood still and even the top room is dated. He thinks it may still be the best ryokan in Hakodate, but it is far from a destination property.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The November 2025 dinner was the letdown of KI-NRT's return. He once had Wakamatsu in his top-10 kaiseki experiences, but this time the zensai included matsukaze and homemade karasumi (both cheap izakaya items), a mukago yam bulb and a weird bacon-and-squid roll. He believes the chef is the same, and Mrs. KI-NRT is firm that the kitchen has stood still. Whale meat turns up in the miso soup, so tell them in advance if you object.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The hot water comes straight from Wakamatsu's own on-site source, free-flowing and never recirculated, into a gender-segregated daiyokujo with open-air sea views and one private rental bath, Azumaya, which also looks onto the sea. KI-NRT went on an unusually cold early-November day and found the dips heavenly, and Yunokawa Onsen is well regarded for its healing properties. The bath in the room is basic tap water that you fill yourself.

service.label: Service
service.text: Every room attendant and meal server wears an elegant kimono, and KI-NRT had a personal server, Ms. Sasaki, for both dinner and breakfast, a rarity these days. She had a strong command of each dish and talked about the local area. When he showed her photos from his stay two decades earlier she ran off and came back with Ms. Kobayashi, the same attendant, in tow. He calls the service exceptionally high on both visits.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms are a mixed bag. KI-NRT stayed in Yachiyo, the top room, in the original building: a 90m² reproduction of the suite where Emperor Shōwa stayed in 1954 that mixes a tatami room with a Taishō-era Western sitting area and a bedroom. He found the mix odd but acceptable for history's sake; the bathroom with its outdated toilet and a urinal is unacceptable, though, and the Wi-Fi was dial-up slow. The panoramic views made up for some of it.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Wakamatsu sits on the Tsugaru Strait at Yunokawa Onsen, five minutes from Hakodate Airport, and every room has an unobstructed view to Aomori's Shimokita Peninsula. It is a northern sea of rough water and gloomy skies most days, so you would not mistake it for Amanpulo or Amanoi. The original 1924 building is tasteful inside, but the 1994 new wing still looks like a bubble-era building in need of a fresh coat of paint.

cities.text: ~7 min by taxi from Hakodate Airport; ~15 min tram/car from Hakodate Station to Yunokawa Onsen.
~4 hr by car from New Chitose Airport (CTS); most fly CTS-Hakodate instead.

inns.name: Ryokusone
inns.summary: A seven-room traditional inn on a small hill above Kanazawa, a ten-minute drive from Kenrokuen and the Higashi Chaya district, whose top room is the Yamaboushi duplex suite, but which has no onsen and no garden. It was KI-NRT's go-to across three stays in a city where no stay had ever satisfied him, so the praise is relative to a weak field, and the kitchen slipped between 2019 and 2022. The question is moot now in any case, because the ryokan has gone out of business.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: KI-NRT found the dinner great on his 2019 stay but weaker by his 2022 visit, so the kitchen was heading the wrong way.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at Ryokusone, and KI-NRT suggests it only to travelers for whom onsen is not a requirement.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: The top room, the Yamaboushi special room, is a duplex suite with an upstairs bedroom, and it is the room KI-NRT chose to photograph for his primer entry, because he was much taken with it.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Ryokusone sits atop a small hill overlooking Kanazawa, about a ten-minute drive from the Higashi Chaya district and Kenrokuen, so it may not suit anyone who wants to be near the tourist centre. The inn is quite traditional in look and feel, which many guests will appreciate, but its footprint is very small and there is no real garden to speak of, which KI-NRT found a pity in the city of Kenrokuen, one of Japan's three most famous gardens.

cities.text: ~20 min by taxi from Kanazawa Stn.
Hokuriku Shinkansen Tokyo->Kanazawa ~2h30, then ~20 min taxi.

inns.name: Tsuruga Besso Ao no Za
inns.summary: A 25-room Tsuruga Group flagship on Lake Shikotsu with a spectacular building and interiors and a kitchen that lets them down: KI-NRT was shocked that a 2019 build at this price would serve frozen, dried-out local fish. Both 2025 stays called it overpriced even with the all-you-can-drink inclusions, and the service has a corporate feel and is patchy. He still expects anyone staying on Shikotsuko to end up here, because everything else nearby is extremely rustic by comparison and there is really no other choice.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is where Ao no Za falls down. On KI-NRT's June 2025 stay the grilled Tokishirazu salmon was hard, dry and clearly frozen, his wife's flounder was inedible, and only the opening abalone kuzu-uchi impressed, and he was shocked they served such dishes at all. Breakfast was downright pleasant by comparison. pWei, a month earlier, found the food quite solid though nothing amazing, served in private dining rooms with an included drink list.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Suite Villa's open-air onsen bath draws water from the source, but the spring is lukewarm, so the water is heated in a tank and recirculated at 41C (staff will change the temperature on request). KI-NRT puts it a step below a free-flowing source such as Myoken Ishiharaso for authenticity, but the water was still silky-smooth and soothing, and pWei also found it clear, alkaline and a great softener of the skin.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was mixed on KI-NRT's stay. Tomoko, his dinner and breakfast server, explained each dish in detail and took pride in her work and local roots, and he adored her. Other staff were less attentive: a guest relations agent never followed up on an art question, receptionists were quick when asked but not proactive, and after an outing half the staff welcomed them back while the rest ignored them. pWei found the service otherwise excellent.

room.label: Room
room.text: The 140 square metre Suite Villa is comfortable, tastefully done in modern Japanese decor with checkerboard tatami, an open-air onsen bath, two sinks and electric blinds. The one drawback is that it has no lake view, and neither does the Executive Suite Villa above it at twice the price. The GM told KI-NRT the site was chosen to be near the shops and Visitor Center, which he called a cop out. pWei's third-floor room did overlook the lake.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The interiors are grand, with ultra-high ceilings, rock and sand art, carvings of the extinct Hokkaido wolf, a wireframe owl, Ainu clothing on display and a courtyard pool with wireframe balls hovering over the water. The building tells Hokkaido's story from the Ainu to the modern age, and KI-NRT says it works beautifully. The site is Shikotsuko Onsen, the lake's tourist hub, with tour buses in the lot, though pWei found them no great bother.

cities.text: ~30-40 min by car/shuttle from New Chitose Airport (CTS) to Shikotsuko Onsen.
~60 min by car from Sapporo to the lakeside onsen.

inns.name: Yamamizuki Bettei
inns.summary: A rustic detached-villa sister to Kurokawa's renowned Yamamizuki, and the thread's standing recommendation once you accept that after Takefue and Gosho Gekkoju the area's luxury drops off steeply. KI-NRT stayed in 2016 and still recommends it, and a 2025 member couple knew it was not properly luxurious going in, liked the scenery, found the food forgettable and would only return in nicer weather. KI-NRT's advice is to get the C-type villa with its own indoor and outdoor onsen, and the village is a stronger reason to stay than the kitchen.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The food was nothing special on jpit2107's January 2025 stay, and nobody else in the thread has described a meal here.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Kurokawa is an onsen town, and the C-type room has its own indoor and outdoor onsen baths, which KI-NRT says you really should get if you can. Nobody in the thread describes the baths in any detail.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms are detached villas, which matters in Kurokawa because most buildings in the area are wood with thin sound insulation (the renowned main Yamamizuki included), so here you are assured of peace and quiet. KI-NRT calls the place quirky and says to get the C-type room with its indoor and outdoor onsen. jpit2107 found an Edo-period feel in January 2025, but the heating system whined.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Yamamizuki Bettei is the thread's top pick for a scenic, rustic stay in Kurokawa Onsen, where KI-NRT says the luxury drops off steeply after Takefue and Gosho Gekkoju but the area is full of charming and rustic ryokans. jpit2107 chose it on that basis in January 2025 and would come back only in nicer weather.

cities.text: Direct highway bus Fukuoka to Kurokawa Onsen (~2.7 hr).
Shinkansen toward Kumamoto, then ~2 hr by car up to Kurokawa Onsen.

inns.name: Ekoin
inns.summary: Ekoin is a working Buddhist temple on Koyasan that runs a single luxurious suite (a private garden, two double beds and a tatami dining room where a strictly vegan shojin dinner arrives at a fixed 5:30pm). There is no onsen, and guests are encouraged to join meditation in the afternoon and the service and fire ceremony before breakfast. Both first-hand stays enjoyed it as the closest a temple lodging gets to non-Buddhist comfort, and both agree that a single night is the right dose for Ekoin and Koyasan together.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The food is strict shojin cooking, vegan and, according to the temple's handout, without garlic or onion either, served in the room at fixed hours (dinner at 5:30pm, breakfast at 8am). Dinner arrives all at once as a spread of small dishes, with a candle burner under the one hot dish and a hot soup, and the rest cold. RichardInSF found breakfast looked more colorful and interesting than it tasted, while Buster CT1K thought the food well flavored.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at Ekoin, and no mineral water of any kind. The shower room off the main bathroom has an ordinary bath of heated tap water, so bathing is not part of the experience here.

service.label: Service
service.text: The monks who look after you speak decent English, and RichardInSF puts the service at or close to luxury level, although the temple's timetable is fixed: dinner at 5:30pm, breakfast at 8am and checkout at 10am. Guests are encouraged to attend three ceremonies, meditation in the afternoon and the regular service and the fire ceremony before breakfast. Internet is included and excellent, and there is free parking on the premises.

room.label: Room
room.text: The temple has a single luxurious suite: a living room with a mini bar and a view onto its own private garden, a large tatami room beside it where meals are served, and a bedroom with two actual double beds and a monster TV on the opposite wall. The toilet is a small room near the suite's entrance, about as far from the bedroom as it is possible to get, and the main bathroom has a single sink with a shower room and bath next to it.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Ekoin is a genuine working Buddhist temple on Koyasan that makes its revenue by running a hotel inside its grounds, and the suite looks onto its own private garden. RichardInSF says he stayed to experience temple life only "somewhat", because this sort of luxury does not go with Buddhism. Both guests enjoyed Koyasan, but Buster CT1K was blunt that one night was enough for Ekoin and the mountain together and two would have been too much.

cities.text: Osaka-Namba to Koyasan ~2h via Nankai train + cable car, then short bus/walk to Ekoin.
Kyoto to Namba ~45 min, then Nankai + cable car ~2h to Koyasan.

inns.name: Honjin Hiranoya Kachoan
inns.summary: Honjin Hiranoya Kachoan is possibly the top ryokan in the center of Takayama, a minute from the old town and far nicer than its sister property Bekkan, but KI-NRT calls it, along with the other central options, far inferior to Wanosato, with good but not amazing food and a multi-story building that has nothing like a garden to give it charm from outside. Service is a real strength, led by an attentive named butler. It is very solid luxury if you want to sleep in the historic district, and his advice is to pair it with Wanosato instead of choosing between them.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki meals were good but not amazing, and KI-NRT compares them directly with Wanosato, where the food was exceptional: here it was delicious but not memorable, run-of-the-mill for anyone whose expectations were formed at Japan's finest ryokans. Meals are served in the restaurant instead of your room, in a private room for each party. Takayama is deep in the mountains, so the kitchen leans on Hida beef, mountain vegetables and river fish.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Kachoan has no onsen, and the bath is ordinary heated water, which KI-NRT notes may be off-putting to some. If hot-spring water is something you are after, he says to look elsewhere in Takayama.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was the most impressive part of KI-NRT's two nights. Their nakai (a female butler), Yukimi, was a total sweetheart, low-key yet charming, and catered to their every whim, although they had little need of anything because they were already so well taken care of. The entire staff were gracious and polished, and you can tell they take pride in working at the top property in central Takayama. He reports no service issues at all.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT stayed in the Hanayagi no Ma, the top room, which occupies the 6th floor: 90m², clean, delightfully decorated (not too busy and not too spartan) and nicely appointed, though nothing about it struck him as particularly memorable. No room in the building has a balcony, and he does not know how far the windows open, which matters if you book to watch the Spring Festival procession pass right in front. Call and ask which rooms face the street.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Kachoan has by far the best location of any ryokan in Takayama, a minute from the main old town area with its shrines and temples (the other central luxury options are about a 30-minute walk away), and the Spring Festival procession passes right in front. It is a single, tall multi-story building, though, with no grounds and nothing like a garden to give it charm from outside, and KI-NRT found it more of a hotel than a ryokan.

cities.text: Limited Express Hida Nagoya->Takayama ~2h22 (direct), then ~20 min by car/shuttle.
Limited Express Hida Toyama->Takayama ~1h30, then ~20 min by car/shuttle.

inns.name: Katsuragi Hotel Kitanomaru
inns.summary: Katsuragi Hotel Kitanomaru is a Yamaha-founded forest hotel of the 'local luxury' school, with a great garden, a classic piano and a fusion kaiseki kitchen (a standout Omi beef course and dessert among the courses) that carried the stay. The rooms are where it falls down, since KI-NRT's booked 28-square-meter room was cramped and, at over $500 per person, poor value; most of the inventory runs small, and he says the place needs suites. He calls it worth trying once, and only once, unless a suite is available.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner was the highlight: unique, creative fusion Japanese, with small dishes such as muscat grape, Japanese turnip with mashed tofu, and crown daisy with chestnut, a combination that sounds weird but worked. The softshell turtle soup was a delight, the Omi beef steak lived up to its billing (KI-NRT puts it with the best from Kobe, Tajima and Hida), and of the four excellent desserts the Satsuma sweet potato ice cream blew him away.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the baths here; the only bathing KI-NRT describes is the combined shower and tub unit in his 28m² room.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was friendly and attentive, a little on the formal side in the old-school Japanese way, and everyone worked to cater to KI-NRT's needs with quiet efficiency. Katsuragi is a large property, much bigger than a family-run ryokan, so the slightly impersonal feel is no surprise. It caters mainly to a domestic, local Aichi clientele (golfers included), so English-speaking staff may be hard to find, though he couldn't confirm that.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT booked the Deluxe Western-style Twin, Fuji-dono, 28m², and even knowing the size he was unpleasantly surprised at how claustrophobic and unappealing it was, with small windows and a combined shower and tub unit unbefitting a luxury property at these rates. Higher categories exist but are a small share of the rooms, so good luck finding one on your dates. He would halve the room count by combining adjacent rooms into suites.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The grounds are the best part of Katsuragi: expansive, immaculately maintained and remarkably quaint, with beautiful gardens and surrounding forest you can easily spend over an hour strolling, which KI-NRT recommends. The entrance is traditional Japanese in a good way, and the lobby's floor-to-ceiling windows give commanding views over the garden, which makes the tiny rooms all the more jarring. It is a Yamaha-founded hotel in a forest in Aichi.

cities.text: Tokaido Shinkansen Kodama Nagoya->Kakegawa ~40 min, then ~25 min by car.
Tokaido Shinkansen Kodama Tokyo->Kakegawa ~1h50, then ~25 min by car.

inns.name: Matsushima Sakan Shoan
inns.summary: Sakan Shoan is an eleven-room bayside inn 45 minutes northeast of Sendai, and the setting is why you go: spectacular Matsushima Bay views from just about anywhere on the property, plus good local sashimi and abalone served in a private dining room hosted to a very high standard. It is a ryokan/hotel hybrid with no onsen at all and view suites that run small, but KI-NRT wouldn't hesitate to return, which makes it a solid Tohoku view stop, if not quite a destination inn.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Meals are served in a private dining room (not your own room), and the strength is the locally caught seafood, above all the sashimi, with the abalone another highlight. KI-NRT enjoyed the meals but was not blown away, which was fine because he never expected Sakan Shoan to be a culinary destination; a bit more ingenuity and creative flair would help the kaiseki.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen anywhere on the property. The rooms have baths but not hot-spring ones, and there is no gender-segregated communal onsen either, which surprised KI-NRT for a luxury ryokan in this part of Japan. He called the lack a real bummer given the serenity and beauty of the setting, though he notes that part of this is out of the property's control.

service.label: Service
service.text: Sakan Shoan is hosted to a very high standard. Dinner was looked after by Nana Suzuki, who was charming and proactive and explained every detail of each course to KI-NRT.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT booked Oimatsu, a B Type Japanese and Western corner room, the top category with a bay view. It had sufficient but not abundant space, a tatami sitting area and a separate bedroom with two Western beds, and is otherwise Japanese in decor and furnishings, which he found the best of both worlds. The larger Tokubetsu-shitsu suites above it have the space but no view, so if the bay matters, take a B Type.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Sakan Shoan is tucked into its own small cove about ten minutes' drive from Matsushima's centre, so it is private and serene, and the view from just about anywhere is spectacular, above all at sunset. Because the inn is on its own secluded bay you miss the whole island-studded panorama, though KI-NRT still calls it a million-dollar view. He adds that Matsushima's billing as one of Japan's three great views oversells it.

cities.text: Matsushima is roughly 40 min by car from Sendai Station, or about 25 min by JR Senseki line to Matsushima-Kaigan plus a taxi.
Tohoku Shinkansen Hayabusa from Tokyo to Sendai is about 1h30, then roughly 40 min by car to Matsushima.

inns.name: Satoumitei Kinparo Hontei
inns.summary: An eight-room seaside inn in Oarai, founded in 1888 and rebuilt in 2011, that KI-NRT chose for its location: twenty minutes from both Hitachi Seaside Park and Kairakuen, and within reach of Ashikaga's wisteria. He calls it not remotely in the league of Japan's top ryokans and no destination in itself, but the torii view, the waves and an enjoyable local dinner made a flower-season base he would use again.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is rustic countryside cooking of local seafood and Hitachi ingredients, bought from local fishmongers daily and served in Kasama-yaki pottery. KI-NRT found it enjoyable: Hitachi beef shabu-shabu, a kinmedai-broth noodle soup in place of rice and a shirasu pizza that worked shockingly well, though courses came out too fast, the next set down before the last was finished. Breakfast was much weaker (nikujaga and one fish the first morning).

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The semi-open-air bath in the Sodegaura suite is plain heated water and not onsen, because Ibaraki has no major hot-spring source, which KI-NRT found understandable, and for him the sea views more than compensated. The gender-segregated communal baths do not stock towels, so you carry your own from the room, something he noted even fairly average ryokan no longer ask of guests.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is friendly and refreshingly informal while still polite. KI-NRT enjoyed chatting with Ms. Akita, the dinner server and an Oarai local, and Ms. Nakata, an energetic young woman from Hitachinaka who handled breakfast. It fell short in the details. Dinner courses came out on top of each other, slippers had to be asked for, no sleepwear beyond yukata was provided, and the meal plan could not be varied by night without a phone call.

room.label: Room
room.text: Sodegaura, the 85 square metre end-unit suite, has separate sleeping, dining and tatami spaces, a semi-open-air bath and a seaside terrace, and gets the best angle toward the Kamiiso-no-Torii gate. KI-NRT calls it spacious and very comfortable but more rustic than luxurious: one sink, yukata but no sleepwear, and slippers only on request over floors that did not seem heated. Entry-level rooms also have a private veranda over the rocks.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The inn sits on the Oarai coast beside Oarai Isosaki Jinja, whose Kamiiso-no-Torii gate stands on the sea rocks and glows orange at dawn. The shoreline is a designated Place of Scenic Beauty, part rocky, part sandy beach, and from the rooms you watch families in the tide pools. The exterior is dated and concrete-heavy with almost no signage (KI-NRT drove past it twice), but inside it is warm and wood-heavy, with rooftop terraces over the sea.

cities.text: JR to Mito (Hitachi LEX ~1h15), transfer to Oarai-Kashima Line ~15 min, then short taxi to the inn.
Oarai-Kashima Line Mito->Oarai ~15 min plus a short taxi.

inns.name: Umioto Mari
inns.summary: A six-room seaside ryokan on Shodoshima, Japan's olive-growing island, opened in April 2019 as the modern sister property to the traditional Shimayado Mari (about 10 minutes away by car). The star attraction is a twelve-course Olive Kaiseki dinner that KI-NRT called wonderful, but there is no onsen anywhere on site, only a tub you fill yourself, cut with spring water carried over from Shimayado Mari, which is a real letdown if onsen is what you are after. Ikyu's guests love it regardless, with meals and satisfaction near the top of their marks.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The star attraction is the twelve-course Olive Kaiseki, in which just about every dish carries olive oil: celery juice with yuzu olive oil, miso-marinated olive-fed hamachi, grilled olive-fed Sanuki wagyu shank, and a milk and rosemary sorbet with olive oil frozen over it into a hard shell. KI-NRT worried about being 'olived-out' halfway through, but the olive never overpowered the other ingredients. Ikyu guests give the meals their highest mark.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen here, and no communal bath either. The owner drilled deep but never hit a spring, so the bath in your room is one you fill yourself, with onsen water carried over from Shimayado Mari and mixed with ground water, which makes it technically half onsen. KI-NRT called it nice but said that if onsen is what you are after, this isn't going to cut it.

service.label: Service
service.text: The waiters explain the olive oil in each dish the way a sommelier explains wine, down to how it was farmed, which KI-NRT found a tad overboard even for someone who loves the stories behind the food, though they had an answer to any question he asked.
