The one drawback is the meal times: dinner is at 17:30 or 19:30 and nothing else, and with half the rooms empty they still refused to shift his by 30 minutes. Ikyu guests mark the service lowest.

room.label: Room
room.text: There are six rooms in all, each with a view of the sea, and two of them are 'hanare' villas of 73 square metres. KI-NRT's villa To no Oto was adequate, but for a property that opened in 2019 he was surprised to find a single sink and vanity, and even the top category room has no separate bedroom and living room. Ikyu guests mark the rooms among the property's highest categories.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: A small, charming property by the sea on Shodoshima, with no Japanese garden but a wonderful view of the ocean from the rooms. Shimayado Mari sits in the centre of town about 10 minutes away by car, a plus or a minus depending on what you are after, and with a car KI-NRT preferred the more tranquil setting here. The island itself is a peaceful place to laze away and do some light sightseeing, though he says nothing on it is bucket-list material.

cities.text: ~1 hr ferry from Takamatsu port to Shodoshima (Tonosho or Ikeda), plus a taxi/drive across the island to Horikoshi.
~2 hr ferry from Himeji (KI-NRT's own route into Shodoshima) to Fukuda port, plus a short drive to Horikoshi.

inns.name: Mifuneyama Rakuen Onsen
inns.summary: A non-traditional art-hotel ryokan in Takeo Onsen that shares the same onsen and the magnificent Mifuneyama Rakuen garden with its luxury neighbor Chikurintei, with a dark lobby, a flashlight check-in and a colored-light show at the front desk. Nagasaki Joe's 2023 stay found pleasant meals and a much-touted spa that did not live up to its billing, at a fraction of the neighbor's price. His advice is to book Chikurintei if you can and to fall back on this decidedly non-luxury alternative when it is full.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner and breakfast were both pleasant on Nagasaki Joe's 2023 stay, though he does not single out any dish, and nobody else in the thread has eaten here.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The spa is a proper Takeo Onsen hot-spring bath with saunas and cold baths, and it gives you the same onsen experience as Chikurintei next door, which Nagasaki Joe thinks may be jointly owned. It is promoted as the number one spa in Japan, but he found it just OK and overrated.

service.label: Service
service.text: Check-in happens in a very dark lobby with no lights on at the front desk, so the staff work by flashlight. Beyond that, nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: Nobody in the thread has described the rooms. Nagasaki Joe booked the hotel as the cheaper alternative when Chikurintei had no availability, and he does not count it as a luxury ryokan.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The vast Mifuneyama Rakuen garden is right next door and free for guests. The whole area around Mt. Mifuneyama bursts with color when the azaleas bloom in April, and KI-NRT expects the momiji against the evergreens in mid to late November to be a stunning sight, with a fall illumination he says could be spectacular. Inside, the lobby is kept dark, and a vast array of colored lights near the front desk gives an artistic light show.

cities.text: Ltd exp / Nishi-Kyushu Shinkansen relay Hakata to Takeo-Onsen, then ~10 min shuttle.
Shinkansen to Shin-Tosu, transfer toward Takeo-Onsen, then ~10 min shuttle.

inns.name: Sekitei
inns.summary: A 12-room garden ryokan in mainland Hatsukaichi near the Miyajima ferry, with a hypnotic garden and an oyster-and-conger-eel kaiseki. Japanese travelers adore it (4.81 on Ikyu), but KI-NRT gave it three stars, near the bottom of anything he reviews, for the aging, under-cleaned suite and the hassle of the self-fill tub, and he calls it a convenient overnight that is not a destination ryokan in its own right. Yet five years on he still sends Miyajima-bound travelers here and still praises the food and garden; it works as a single night if you choose your room carefully.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is an extravagant full kaiseki of local Setouchi ingredients and wild mountain vegetables, served in the room in artisan ware: conger eel prepared masterfully several ways, oysters, mugwort tempura with mugwort-buckwheat soba. Breakfast in the main restaurant is a grand, creative spread. KI-NRT calls the meals exceptional, just outside his own top ten, and Japanese travelers count Sekitei among the country's ten culinary destinations.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The communal open-air onsen is the bath to use, and KI-NRT found it wonderful. Only some of the 12 rooms have onsen at all, and in Oimatsu the open-air tub is not free-flowing: you fill it yourself from a tap, which takes 20-plus minutes, then dilute it with cold non-onsen water to cool it, and he found dead skin in the bath after filling it. He does not recommend Sekitei if an in-room onsen is your main goal.

service.label: Service
service.text: Dinner is served in the room and breakfast in the main restaurant, and shoes are collected at reception when you arrive. KI-NRT told the staff about the dirty bath but does not say how they responded, and nobody in the thread has written about the service otherwise.

room.label: Room
room.text: All 12 rooms differ in space, layout, view and privacy, and the style is a mix of traditional Japanese and early-20th-century, so do your research in advance. KI-NRT's Oimatsu, a two-story suite with an open-air bath, was decent in size but chopped into too many little nooks and felt claustrophobic, aging and under-cleaned (dust, grime, dead skin in the tub), with no internet. The tatami floors were heated, a godsend in winter.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Most of the rooms face the inner garden in a U-shape, and that garden, with its views of the Seto Inland Sea and Miyajima, is what Sekitei is famous for; KI-NRT found it hypnotic. Several detached rooms farther down the hill have better privacy but inferior views. The inn is in Hatsukaichi on the mainland near the Miyajima ferry, and he would still rather stay on Miyajima itself, since Sekitei is a convenient overnight and no destination ryokan.

cities.text: Reverse of: JR back to Hiroshima (~30 min).
Shinkansen Kyoto→Hiroshima (~1h40), JR ~25 min toward Miyajimaguchi + short taxi.
Sanyo Shinkansen Nozomi Hakata→Hiroshima (~1h), change to the JR Sanyo Main Line→Ono-ura/Miyahama (~35–45 min), then a ~5-min inn shuttle/taxi (call ahead).

inns.name: Teisui
inns.summary: A rare outpost of luxury on Akita's remote Oga Peninsula, revived since 2017 by the okami Emiko Hirabayashi's investment in a new onsen source and refurbished rooms. KI-NRT calls it the most polarizing property he has experienced in Japan: breathtaking views and a soothing onsen against uneven service, food that is merely "good" and rooms he would avoid. She seemed cold at first and then warmed into an engaged host who gave them a tour of the whole property, and he says that without those conversations the stay would have ranked among his more underwhelming.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is built on good Oga ingredients served in the traditional way: the local red snow crab was excellent and so was the abalone, but they came steamed and sauteed, and the zensai ran to 16 small bites, too many for KI-NRT to savor at once. The deep-fried horsehead fish went well with the eel and Akita Komachi rice, while the matcha ice cream finale was a downer in a prefecture with no tea tradition. He calls the food merely "good".

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The onsen is a rare hazel-brown water that the okami dug for on site, at a cost of almost a million dollars, after the nearby source she depended on began to decline, and KI-NRT found it soothing. In the Nishinokaze suite the in-room bath runs straight from the source and unfiltered and comes out brown, while the public and private rental baths are treated and recirculated, which leaves them clear.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is uneven and not anticipatory. KI-NRT found the staff a bit timid, and at dinner the server could not explain many of the appetizers and called on the okami, Emiko Hirabayashi, to step in. She seemed cold and inflexible at first (she initially refused to take the meat off the crab for Mrs. KI-NRT, who had one working arm), then warmed into long, engaging conversations and a tour of the property. There are no English-speaking staff yet.

room.label: Room
room.text: Quality splits sharply by category. KI-NRT's 77m² Nishinokaze suite was clean, contemporary and comfortable, a bit tight but with an incredible balcony over the ocean and bay and its own brown onsen tub. The 92m² Kitanokaze "special room" already looks tired, with no balcony and no bath at all, and he cannot imagine anyone choosing it over Nishinokaze. Interiors are simple, with no flowers or art, and the bathrooms carry no amenities.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Teisui sits on the remote Oga Peninsula of Akita, where anything resembling luxury is remarkable, and the views from the rooms are breathtaking: an unobstructed sweep of capes, nearby reefs and a lighthouse on Tomi Island that reminded KI-NRT of Prince Edward Island and Cape Cod, like a Monet painting. The building is huge for ten rooms, with a lounge holding far more chairs than it needs and whole floors and corridors left unused.

cities.text: Teisui is roughly 1.5h by car from Akita city out toward the tip of the Oga Peninsula.
Akita Shinkansen Komachi from Tokyo to Akita is about 3h50, then roughly 1.5h by car to the Oga Peninsula.

inns.name: Ginyu
inns.summary: A Hakone ryokan with the best views in the area and its hardest reservation, which in KI-NRT's eyes is resting on its laurels, with those views wrapped in Balinese interiors that could use a refresh, impersonal hotel-like service and a recirculated onsen. 'It's still nice, but for the prices they command I'd expect a bit more,' and its claim to fame nowadays is the difficulty of booking it; he would not return. If you do go, get the highest floor you can for the view.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: KI-NRT found the food hit-and-miss, and when he steers people to Ginyu it is for the views and never for the kitchen.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The onsen water is recirculated instead of being fed continually straight from the source, which KI-NRT counts against it. Room layouts vary a lot, and in some of them the bath's barriers stand in front of the views, so the room you get matters.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is a bit impersonal and very hotel-like. When KI-NRT pulled up to the front there was nobody waiting at the entrance and he had no idea where to park, and at check-in you are seated in the lounge to enjoy the wonderful views, then called back to the front desk counter to do the formalities.

room.label: Room
room.text: The interiors are Balinese in style, and KI-NRT, who prefers either modern or well-maintained traditional Japanese, finds Ginyu is neither; the place could also use a refresh. Room layouts vary a great deal, and some put bath barriers in front of the view, so the higher the floor the better.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: For views it is no contest, the best in Hakone, and the higher the floor the better; even KI-NRT, who does not count Ginyu among his Hakone favourites, sends people here when the view is the priority. The seating area where you wait at check-in has the same wonderful views. Ginyu is one of Hakone's prominent luxury ryokans alongside Gora Kadan and Gora Hanaougi, and more centrally located than Yama no Chaya.

cities.text: Odawara Shinkansen + Hakone Tozan line/bus toward Gora ~2h12.
Tokaido Shinkansen to Odawara + Hakone Tozan line/bus ~2h15.

inns.name: Ryokan Kurashiki
inns.summary: An eight-room inn in an authentic historic building at the heart of Kurashiki's canal district, with Meiji-era antiques throughout and a spot right on the main canal by the Nakabashi Bridge, and the default luxury choice in town. KI-NRT's stand-alone Inui suite came with a service gap and a stairway that ruled out room dining, but he closed by saying he'd stay again with a different room and a better-briefed server; by 2025 he was calling it a coin toss against the newer Yoruya nearby.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinners are straightforward kaiseki, well presented though not particularly innovative, and KI-NRT enjoyed the vast majority of dishes and called them more than satisfactory. Breakfast was a bit lacking, with small portions and not the variety he is used to at other luxury ryokans. Meals are served in the rooms except in the Inui suite, whose steep stairs mean its guests eat every meal in the main restaurant, and the inn does not say so online.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen in the rooms, and the only hot spring bathing is a small onsen bath in a separate facility on the premises, which KI-NRT noted but did not describe.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was the big irritation of KI-NRT's stay. The same waiter served every meal, which would have been good had he known and cared more about his work; asked about a dish, he picked up the handwritten menu on the table and read it aloud. KI-NRT expects a top ryokan to train its servers in the intricacies of each dish and found Kurashiki does not, and a year on he told another poster that the butler service 'left a lot to be desired.'

room.label: Room
room.text: Luxury Suite Inui is in a stand-alone building across the rear garden, 63.1 square metres and the newest, most modern of the rooms, bright and airy with vaulted ceilings and light-coloured wood, though with only one sink. The steep stairs are the bigger problem, because the staff consider them a hazard and will not carry meals up, so Inui is the only room without in-room dining, and KI-NRT would pick another room next time.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Ryokan Kurashiki stands at the heart of the Kurashiki Bikan historical quarter, on the main canal by the Nakabashi Bridge, and the historic building blends in nicely with the rest of the old town, with Meiji-era antiques inside in darned good shape. Kurashiki is touristy but gorgeous, and KI-NRT found two nights the right length to see it slowly. Even after a disappointing stay he still called the inn charming and centrally located.

cities.text: Okayama Stn to Kurashiki ~15 min by JR local/rapid, then ~15 min taxi to Bikan district.
Hiroshima to Okayama ~40 min Shinkansen, transfer to Kurashiki ~15 min, then ~15 min taxi.

inns.name: Setouchi Retreat Aonagi
inns.summary: A seven-room Tadao Ando retreat above Matsuyama that appears on many 'ryokans to stay at before you die' lists, and KI-NRT is not entirely sure why. It is exclusive, with that famous pool, and the food and service draw real praise: sea bream and a spectacular Takikomi Tai Meshi at dinner, staff who got everything right. But there is no true onsen (the rentable pool, sauna and jacuzzi struck him as an artificial, party-mood dungeon), and the aging concrete is the flaw that leaves him cold, so he would sooner return to Oborozukiyo.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is built on Seto Inland Sea seafood, and the local red sea bream, Spanish mackerel and white horse head were all fantastic, with the Takikomi Tai Meshi (rice cooked with red sea bream) spectacular. The executive chef came over from sister property Iki Kairi Murakami and still brings in longtooth grouper and blackthroat seaperch from Iki. KI-NRT puts the food at very good, memorable but not top class.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen bath in the rooms or communal bath; instead Aonagi has a pool with a sauna and an onsen jacuzzi that guests rent privately. KI-NRT did not like it: a jacuzzi gives off a party atmosphere where an onsen should be calm and relaxing, and stylish as they are, the pool and jacuzzi struck him as an artificially created dungeon. He would have preferred something open-air, and the missing real bath in the room is his one nit to pick.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is attentive and prompt, and KI-NRT says everything about the property was done right. He went in unsure about the food and service, since so much of the attention goes to the architecture, and they turned out to be the definite highlights of his stay.

room.label: Room
room.text: The best of the seven rooms is the Aonagi Suite, a massive 169.6 square metre duplex, and although KI-NRT prefers single-storey rooms, the maisonette layout allows gigantic double-height windows that look over the iconic pool to the Seto Inland Sea and its islands. The decor is tastefully minimalistic, but the interior is beginning to show its age in design and maintenance. It is also the only room where meals are served in the room.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Aonagi is Tadao Ando's creation above Matsuyama, with the iconic pool as the centrepiece and a view of the Seto Inland Sea that KI-NRT calls Instagram-worthy. The architecture left him cold. There are interesting nooks and crannies, but to him it is a sea of concrete, more like a museum or a European castle than a comfortable home. It is a 25-minute drive from Dogo Onsen, and he thinks you need to be a big fan of Ando to stay more than a night.

cities.text: Setouchi Retreat Aonagi is roughly 20-30 min by car (or airport shuttle) up into the hills from central Matsuyama.
Limited Express Shiokaze from Okayama to Matsuyama is about 2h40, then roughly 20 min by car to the hilltop property.

inns.name: Hyakuna Garan
inns.summary: Hyakuna Garan is an 18-room property in Nanjo on Okinawa's main island, and its standalone Garan Annex is immense at 130 square meters, with a rooftop hot tub and a panoramic ocean view; like most Okinawa properties it has no onsen. KI-NRT's four nights there in December 2020 were enjoyable, with warm service and the Goya Champuru and desserts among the highlights, but the furnishings were dated, the local beef fell flat, and it isn't a beach destination, so his hunt for a true Okinawa luxury ryokan continues.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The food is unique and varied, built on local Okinawan produce, seafood and seaweed, and staff explain each ingredient. Some of it hit and some missed: the Goya Champuru (bitter melon with Agu pork, egg and tofu) was fantastic, as was the Okinawan soba, and each dessert brought at least five little bites. But the local beef was tough, chewy and bland with no marbling, and KI-NRT would have preferred one taste and then wagyu from elsewhere.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at Hyakuna Garan, as at the vast majority of Okinawa properties. The Garan Annex has a hot tub on its rooftop terrace with a commanding view of the ocean, but it is heated water and no hot spring.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was of generally high quality, and everyone was warm, gracious and attentive. The manner is easier than at a typical luxury Japanese hotel, though never overly familiar, which KI-NRT found right for an island resort as opposed to a buttoned-up city hotel.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Garan Annex Bekkan is a stand-alone 130m² unit plus two terraces (the rooftop one with hot tub and ocean view), and the only room that takes children. It has a bedroom with two large Western beds, two bathrooms, a kitchen and a living room with a table for eight, almost too large for its own good. But the whole resort is in so-so shape, with furnishings straight out of the 80s and cheap-looking, and KI-NRT thinks a refurbishment is overdue.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Hyakuna Garan is in Nanjo, quite a distance from Naha, which is a plus or a minus depending on your plans; for KI-NRT it was a hideaway from the city and from the cold that grips Honshu in winter. The main restaurant and the Annex rooftop look out over the ocean. With a rental car it made a good base for Okinawa World, Sefa Utaki and Gangala Valley, but it is not really a beach destination, so look elsewhere if that is what you want.

cities.text: ~30-35 min by car from central Naha to the inn.
~35 min by car from Naha Airport to the inn.

transit.note: Okinawa main island reached only by air into Naha.

inns.name: Iwaso
inns.summary: A celebrated 1854 institution in the single best spot on Miyajima, beside Itsukushima Shrine and the floating torii, and that location is most of what it has going for it. There are no onsen baths on the property, the rooms run from dated to tiny, and KI-NRT came away 'very underwhelmed,' switching rooms mid-stay and still finding little comfort. The food was decent but unexceptional, service was friendly, and a member in the newer rooms enjoyed her stay. You stay for the shrine at night and put up with the rooms.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kitchen leans on local Hiroshima ingredients, and the farmed Hiroshima oysters were the dish KI-NRT loved. The anago (conger eel) was tough and chewy and their presentation of it was not done well, and the local beef pales next to Tajima, Hida or Kobe. He called the food decent but not exceptional, some great dishes and some only so-so. Meals come to the room in the Hanare cottages, but guests in the newer wing eat in the main dining room.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There are no onsen baths anywhere on the property, and KI-NRT lists that among the things the historic setting fails to deliver. In the Senshin Tei cottage the wash basin sits by the veranda across from the bathroom and shower, and because heating is limited to the main living area, a winter visit to the bathroom or shower is even colder than the room itself.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service from the friendly staff was the one part of the stay KI-NRT praised without reservation, and when he asked to leave the freezing cottage after the first night they found him a room in the Annex the same day, even though only standard rooms were free.

room.label: Room
room.text: Honkan rooms are dated and small, the Shinkan run down and tight even in the Suites, and KI-NRT's cottage Senshin Tei was 'wonderfully Japanese, and tremendously uncomfortable': one room under 30 square metres, no closet, no insulation (freezing in November), no WiFi and curtains shut against hikers on the path opposite. After a night he took a 26 square metre Annex room, warmer but smaller, without in-room dining. peachy3 liked the newer rooms.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Iwaso has the absolute best location on Miyajima, minutes from Itsukushima Shrine and the floating torii and next to Momiji-dani park and the Mount Misen ropeway. The 1854 Honkan is as gorgeous and traditional as they come, and swarms of day-trippers come to photograph it and the maples around it, which is why the cottages lack privacy. Once the crowds have gone you have the island to yourselves, and peachy3 loved exploring Miyajima at night.

cities.text: Hiroshima Stn ~1h to Miyajima via JR + ferry, then ~3 min walk.
Kyoto to Hiroshima ~1h40 Shinkansen, then JR + ferry to Miyajima.

inns.name: Kotohira Kadan
inns.summary: A 43-room Kotohira inn built around Chouseiden, a history-steeped standalone villa once home to the local lord and hung with the original owner's art collection. KI-NRT calls the room well worth the privilege as an experience and dinner a delight, and sums it up as a good stay at a reasonable price, though the service was indifferent and the villa has no private onsen bath, only free use of the rentable one.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is served in the room, and KI-NRT calls it a delight: the kitchen makes an effort with seasonal, local dishes that give you a good taste of Kagawa, and the deep-fried pike conger with simmered vegetables in dashi broth was unique and flavorful, as was the red sea bream shabu-shabu. It is not the best ryokan meal he has had, and breakfast was varied and bountiful without anything that blew them away, which suited a morning of udon tasting.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Chouseiden villa has no onsen bath of its own, which KI-NRT counts as its one drawback, since he expects one in the top room of a top-level ryokan. Some of the standard rooms do have in-room onsen baths, which might tip some people toward them, and there is a private bath that can be rented by the hour and is free for guests in the Hanare villas. Nobody in the thread has described the water itself.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is not up to the standards of the top luxury ryokans, which KI-NRT puts down partly to the high room count and perhaps to a less refined service culture in Kagawa. There was nothing wrong with the staff, but their attitude was indifferent overall: nobody came running out to help with the bags when they pulled into the parking lot, requests were met at a leisurely pace at best, and in the thread he calls them robotic and cold.

room.label: Room
room.text: Chouseiden is the top room, a stand-alone villa once home to the local lord and hung with the original owner's art collection of screens, sliding doors and scrolls by famous artists. It has 152m² of space, but it is so old and history-laden that KI-NRT calls it scary (a famous sumo wrestler supposedly ran screaming out of its traditional second bathroom), and he thinks it needs a refurb. As an experience he found it well worth the privilege.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Kotohira Kadan is within easy walking distance of Kotohira-gu (Konpira-san), one of Shikoku's top sights, and some of the finest Sanuki udon restaurants are close by. The grounds are not massive, though there is a pretty little pond with interesting vegetation around it, and the architecture of the Hanare villas gives the property a real sense of place next to the shrine. With 43 rooms there can be a walk to reception, outdoors from Chouseiden.

cities.text: JR Dosan/Yosan line Takamatsu to Kotohira runs about 40-60 min, then the inn's free pickup is roughly 30 min by car from JR Kotohira Station.
Hourly Limited Express Nanpu covers Okayama to Kotohira in about 1h across the Seto bridge, then roughly 30 min by the inn's car from Kotohira Station.

transit.note: Asan Kotonami sits well south of Kotohira Station; times include the ~30 min inn pickup.

inns.name: Kusatsu Onsen Kei
inns.summary: Kei is the 2019-opened bid for luxury in Japan's most famous onsen town, and as of KI-NRT's November 2023 stay it isn't there yet: genuine two-source onsen and a satisfying kaiseki inside an inn that cut corners on towels, toiletries and, most damagingly, staff training, given what it charges. He left glad to have seen Kusatsu and unconvinced by Kei, and two years on he still says the town "just doesn't have an amazing place to stay."

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner, served in a private room, runs to delicacies such as fugu, suppon (soft-shelled turtle) and kobako-gani (female snow crab), each creatively prepared, artfully presented and wonderful in taste. KI-NRT has had better kaiseki, but he was satisfied with quality and quantity and doubts anyone leaves hungry or without a few memorable dishes. Breakfast was equally refined, though the variety at both meals fell a little short of the luxury norm.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Kei draws on two hot springs. Takasago and the A01 suite have open-air room baths fed from the more acidic Bandaiko Gensen, while C01 and the two indoor rental baths run on the softer Jizo Gensen, better for sensitive skin. The indoor rentals are unique and atmospheric, and Ryoku, the open-air one, is ordinary. Only three of the seven rooms have their own onsen, which KI-NRT calls inexcusable for a place sold as Kusatsu's pinnacle of luxury.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was uneven and somewhat cold. Someone is usually behind the reception counter, but not once on leaving or returning was KI-NRT greeted or welcomed back. At dinner no single waitperson is assigned to your table, and the servers, eager and charming, did not know the dishes well, so "where did this rice come from?" often got "let me find out." He left saying staff training is what stands between Kei and true destination status.

room.label: Room
room.text: The 85m² A01 Type Suite has a separate living room and bedroom (split by a partition), a two-sink bathroom with the open-air onsen, and a tatami area with a heated sunken cutout for your feet. It ticks most boxes, but the corner-cutting shows: uneven furnishings, small thin towels that barely absorb, a toilet without the one-touch seat lift, and minimal low-grade toiletries. An odd work alcove off the bedroom got nicknamed "the dungeon".

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Kusatsu Onsen town itself is the attraction: Yubatake, the hot-spring field at its centre, is lit up at night to eerily beautiful effect, and the streets are full of visitors in yukata and geta. Kei is a nondescript building a five-minute uphill walk from there, facing the small Jizo Gensen spring square. There is no garden or grounds at all, though KI-NRT doubts any ryokan near the centre has one either.

cities.text: Kusatsu-Shima LEX to Naganohara-Kusatsuguchi ~2h30, then ~25 min bus to Kusatsu Onsen.
~80 min direct bus from Karuizawa to Kusatsu Onsen.

inns.name: Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan
inns.summary: Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan is a 37-room hot-spring inn in the Yamanashi mountains, founded in 705 AD and run by 52 generations of one family, and KI-NRT went out of his way to visit for that history. Guinness World Records lists it as the oldest hotel in the world. The onsen was sublime and the top suite impressed him, but a typhoon erased the old buildings decades ago and maglev-tunnel construction dusts up the approach, and he closes by naming smaller, more polished, better-located ryokans he would pick first. The record and the water justify the detour, and the surroundings add nothing.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Meals come to your room only if you book one of the handful of special suites such as Kitadake, which KI-NRT enjoyed, and the food itself exceeded his expectations. He calls it good, and he notes that many smaller, more intimate ryokans offer great food as well.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The water is natural hot spring, free-flowing into the open-air bath of the Kitadake suite and into quite a few public baths on site, a scale only a handful of much smaller luxury ryokans can match, and KI-NRT found both the in-room and the communal baths sublime, wonderful even by Japan's high standards. The one drawback is the showers, since the public baths have none and the suite's own shower is outdoors.

service.label: Service
service.text: The same family has run the inn for 52 generations. KI-NRT says little about the current staff beyond a room attendant who explained the maglev works in the valley, and when he lists what many smaller ryokans do better, more polished service is on the list.

room.label: Room
room.text: Book the special room Kitadake if you go, a top-floor corner suite with its own free-flowing open-air onsen that had KI-NRT giddy before he arrived and proved plenty spacious once he did, and one of the few rooms where meals are served in the suite. The building around it is a single large block of 37 rooms put up in 1997 with zero historic charm, which he calls bland, and the in-room shower is oddly outdoors, though the wifi is fast.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Keiunkan sits deep in the Hayakawa mountains of Yamanashi, an area KI-NRT found super remote but not uniquely beautiful, with nothing to see or do within a 30-minute drive (Minobusan's temple, half an hour away, is not a must-do). The road in follows a dusty river lined with quarries and gravel trucks, and road works for the maglev tunnel continue until at least 2027. A typhoon destroyed the original inn, a few miles downriver, some 60 years ago.

cities.text: Azusa LEX Shinjuku->Kofu ~1h30, then ~1.5h by car into the Hayakawa valley.
~1.5h by car from Kofu to the remote Hayakawa mountain site.

inns.name: Bettei Yaeno
inns.summary: A four-room, family-run villa ryokan in Minakami, ten minutes from the better-known Bettei Senjuan, and on KI-NRT's stay it was not quite on Senjuan's level. He calls it perfectly adequate, with good but not spectacular kaiseki, trucked-in onsen water and nothing at all to do outside your room. He would be hard pressed to recommend the arduous detour just to stay here, and points anyone passing through Minakami to Senjuan instead.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki is mountain-interior cooking, heavy on wild vegetables and freshwater fish, from a chef who has been here since the inn opened in 2006, and KI-NRT found it good but not spectacular, well short of Senjuan's. Two dishes stood out: iwana (white-spotted char) as sashimi, a very rare treat because it must be prepared just before serving, and charcoal-grilled Masuda beef, a little-known grass-fed Gunma breed, flavorful and well marbled.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The bath is in your room, and it becomes a semi-open-air onsen when you slide the glass windows open. The water is trucked in, because Yaeno has no onsen source of its own, so it is not gensen kakenagashi, which KI-NRT counts as another drawback next to Bettei Senjuan (it matters to him somewhat). There is no communal or rental bath anywhere on the property, so the room tub is all the bathing there is.

service.label: Service
service.text: The staff are three people, the owner (the GM), his wife the proprietress and Ms. Shimada, who has been there for 15 years, and you see little of them because you spend nearly all your time in your room, where meals are served. KI-NRT found the service fine and no more; Ms. Shimada was polite but somewhat impersonal, and being locally born and raised she probably does not speak much English.

room.label: Room
room.text: All four rooms are villa-type units, two of 60m² and two of 70m². KI-NRT took Yamaboushi, a 70m² unit with a separate bedroom, living room and dining room, a patio and light, warm, comfy futons, and called it perfectly adequate. They were last renovated in 2009, but the classic Japanese style is reasonably well maintained and it did not feel old. There is only one sink, though, and the button on the two-generations-old toilet seat did not work.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Minakami is a sleepy, pretty little town flanked by the photogenic Mt. Tanigawa, and the drive in from Niigata is beautiful, but Yaeno itself gives you almost none of it. Arriving is not wow-inducing, you are ushered straight from the car to your room, and there is no lobby, lounge, gift shop, garden or exhibit; the only space outside the room is a small glass-enclosed private lounge with two chairs looking onto the nondescript inner courtyard.

cities.text: Joetsu Shinkansen Tokyo->Jomo-Kogen ~1h15, then ~25 min bus + ~10 min taxi to Minakami.
Joetsu Shinkansen Niigata->Jomo-Kogen ~40 min, then bus + taxi to Minakami.

inns.name: Sakurayu Sanshuyu
inns.summary: Sakurayu Sanshuyu is a seven-room ryokan in Akayu's onsen town in Yamagata, in a nondescript building along the main highway with no real garden, though it has in-room dining and special rooms like the 79m² Oyama Renge with its own open-air onsen bath. KI-NRT finds this famous Tohoku name overrated, a good property and quite cheap by luxury-ryokan standards but not worth visiting the area just to stay at. One other guest, Michaeljinnyc, called his stay completely unforgettable. It makes sense only if Akayu is already on your route.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner runs to 12 courses and is served in your room. KI-NRT has nothing in particular to say about it, and he finds that Yamagata The Takinami, a five-minute walk away in Nanyo town, has a vastly more interesting cuisine.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Oyama Renge special room has its own open-air onsen bath, so you get Akayu's hot-spring water in private. KI-NRT lists the bath as a feature of the room and says nothing more about it, good or bad, and nobody in the thread has written about the inn's other baths.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: Oyama Renge, one of the Tokubetsu-shitsu special rooms, gives you 79.3 square metres with an open-air onsen bath and both meals served in the room, and KI-NRT calls the property good overall. The one drawback is the room's own yard, which was poorly maintained if it was maintained at all, with shabby weeds all over the place.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The inn is a nondescript building on the main highway through Nanyo, street-facing in the middle of Akayu's onsen town with no real garden to speak of, and KI-NRT calls this famous Tohoku name overrated, starting with the setting. The area itself has more to offer, though, since Osteria Sincerita is here and Akayu lies near the heart of Yamagata's cherry-growing regions, which brought him back a third time one June.

cities.text: Yamagata Shinkansen / Ou line from Yamagata to Akayu is about 20 min, then roughly 7 min by taxi to the inn.
Yamagata Shinkansen Tsubasa from Tokyo to Akayu is about 2h50, then roughly 7 min by taxi.

inns.name: Naoshima Ryokan Roka
inns.summary: Roka is Naoshima's first true luxury ryokan (opened 2022), from the family behind Kifu no Sato, modern and artsy, and on KI-NRT's 2023 stay still a work in progress: no onsen, corporate service, rigid meal times and thin amenities around a good island kaiseki. Next time on Naoshima he would take a suite at Benesse House, which he doesn't think is a major compromise and costs a fraction of what Roka charges. Roka is worth a stay for the art island more than for the inn itself.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is a kaiseki built on the bounty of Naoshima and the Seto Inland Sea, carefully crafted and presented with care. KI-NRT left plenty satisfied, but the later, larger courses could have used more imagination: the miso-glazed amberjack is a dish found all over Japan, and the yuzu-soy Spanish mackerel was bland. Dinner at Umioto Mari was the more memorable meal. Menus come in Japanese and English, though curiously there is none for breakfast.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen at Roka. The bath is an ordinary one, and to make up for it the inn supplies a large jar of onsen concentrate from Yunogo Onsen (where Kifu no Sato is) to add to the water, which KI-NRT calls better than nothing. He knew going in, but the lack of hot spring was the big bummer of his stay, and he would have thought the heir to Kifu no Sato could have found a way to get some onsen here.

service.label: Service
service.text: Everyone was friendly and accommodating, but KI-NRT found the service too corporate for an 11-room inn: black uniforms, check-in in a lounge next to the kitchen, no butler and no private dining. Dinner is at 18:00 or 18:30 and breakfast at 08:00 or 08:30, and servers described each course by the book, so asking whether the fugu was local got "let me check with the chef". Bilingual menus and many non-Japanese staff suit foreign guests.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Roka Suite is the only one of its kind, 106m² with a tatami room, a Western living room, a bar counter, a semi-kitchen, a bedroom and a separate bath, which is spacious for two. The other ten rooms are smaller, and all eleven face a small hill that is not much to look at; there is no TV. The toiletries are very limited for a luxury ryokan: only a toothbrush, toner and razor, with no moisturizer, cotton swabs or shaving foam.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Roka is about as secluded as a place on Naoshima can be, a 10-minute walk from the Honmura district and its Art House Projects, with not much else around. KI-NRT spent most of his time at the museums around Benesse House, a 25-minute walk or an hourly shuttle away for non-guests. Roka itself is modern and stylish but the grounds are not huge: a rock garden out front and an outdoor hearth where a bonfire is lit for nightcaps.

cities.text: Ferry from Takamatsu port to Naoshima (Miyanoura) takes about 50 min, plus transfer to the port and a short island ride.
JR Uno line Okayama to Uno port is about 50 min, then a 15-20 min ferry to Naoshima plus a short island ride.

inns.name: Fufu Kyu-Karuizawa
inns.summary: Fufu Kyu-Karuizawa is a Fufu-brand hot-spring hotel in old Karuizawa, and the one member who has stayed, OWHKG2016, arriving straight from Fufu Nikko, called it a big letdown and would not go back. The restaurant is good and Kumoba Pond is at the doorstep, but poorly trained staff and a zoo-like courtyard layout spoiled the stay. That single one-night stay is all anyone in the thread has written about it, so treat it as a warning and no more.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The restaurant was the best part of OWHKG2016's one-night stay, with food and service they called great, though the tables are placed close together and the dining room looks onto the same small inner courtyard as the rooms, so you watch other guests come and go while you eat.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the baths or the water here.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was the real letdown of OWHKG2016's stay. The staff were mostly quite young and not really well trained, and they call the result extremely unacceptable: the front desk was unmanned and reception ignored them when they came back in. This is the stay they would not repeat, and a year later they placed Fufu Kyoto alongside Kyu-Karuizawa at the opposite end of the brand from Fufu Nikko.

room.label: Room
room.text: The hotel is nicely decorated, but the rooms, the lounge and the restaurant all face the same small inner courtyard, so everyone can see you going in and out of your room, which struck OWHKG2016 as pretty much a zoo. Nobody in the thread has described the rooms themselves.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The hotel stands in old Karuizawa, a good base for Kumoba Pond's autumn foliage, and like the streets and buildings around it it has a much smaller footprint than Fufu Nikko, with the whole compound built around a single small inner courtyard. OWHKG2016, who came straight from Nikko, found the contrast a big letdown.

cities.text: Hokuriku Shinkansen Tokyo->Karuizawa ~1h5, then ~5 min by car.
Hokuriku Shinkansen Nagano->Karuizawa ~30 min, then ~5 min by car.

inns.name: Sanso Kannawaen
inns.summary: A 30-room Beppu stalwart behind a grand thatched gate, with a lovely Noh-stage garden attached to a big-box building. KI-NRT was not quite impressed on his 2022 stay, which fell mid-renovation, and later downgraded his advice to calling it solid while recommending Yufuin instead, where the ryokans are superior, and the member who followed his original recommendation in 2024 was openly unhappy. The renovation may have changed the building since, but nobody has stayed to say so.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The Kaede restaurant serves teppanyaki, which is rare among Kyushu ryokans, and KI-NRT names Kannawaen when asked where to find grill dining in the south. Nobody in the thread has written about the food itself.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the baths here, though Beppu supposedly produces more hot-spring water than anywhere else in Japan, with steam rising all over the city.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT booked the top room, Special Room Shun, and was told only at check-in that the whole floor was closed for renovation and the room unavailable. Michaeljinnyc, who booked on his recommendation in 2024, wrote from the property that they were not too happy with it.

room.label: Room
room.text: The 30 rooms are in a building that looks like a big-box hotel. As of KI-NRT's 2022 stay the facilities were decent but could stand to be renovated, and a renovation was under way, so his impressions may no longer apply. The top room, Special Room Shun on the top floor, is a 143 square metre suite where meals can be served in the room, but its floor was closed for the renovation when he stayed.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: An impressive thatched-roof entrance gate leads to a wonderful garden with a Noh stage, a tea house and a koi pond, which gives the big-box building a decent atmosphere. Steam rises all over Beppu and you can smell the sulfur, but KI-NRT says in the end it is just another city, with the touristy Beppu Hells a bit fabricated, and he recommends Yufuin instead. Michaeljinnyc ranks Beppu among the least enjoyable places he has been in Japan.

cities.text: Ltd exp Sonic Hakata to Beppu (~2h10), then ~15 min taxi to the inn.
Shinkansen to Kokura, Sonic down to Beppu, then ~15 min taxi; no direct link.

inns.name: Hazu Gassho
inns.summary: A five-room Meiji-era ryokan in the forest near Nagoya, its thatched-roof buildings recalling Shirakawa-go, but the shared, thin-walled building undermines the seclusion: a note in the room admitted the "authentic" construction has little sound-deadening, and KI-NRT heard the neighbors talking and the guests overhead walking about. Food was good, if unmemorable, and his in-room bath ran too cold to bother heating, while dining in a shared hall was the other letdown. He would explore other options before returning.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The food is good and appropriate, built on seasonal local produce plus local beef, duck and river fish, which KI-NRT says gave them an education in the area's traditional ingredients, and ayu (sweetfish) lightly salted and grilled to perfection. Nothing was unique or mind-blowing, but he was satisfied with the quality of the meals. Dinner is served in an open dining area and not in your room, which he found inexcusable for a five-room property.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen here: neither of the two communal baths is hot-spring water, and the alternative is a courtesy shuttle to an onsen facility nearby, which KI-NRT finds pointless when he would expect every room in a small high-end ryokan to have its own spring. Two of the five rooms have an open-air hinoki tub, his among them, but at 5°C in December the water was not warm enough and he did not bother topping it up, so he used the communal bath.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has written about the service here.

room.label: Room
room.text: All five rooms share one two-storey building with little sound insulation, so KI-NRT heard the neighbors talking next door and the guests above walking in their room, and a note in the room asks guests to keep the noise down at night. His 50m² suite was reasonably comfortable, with a tatami room where the futons go out during dinner and a second room with a large kotatsu. With five rooms on a large footprint, he argues each should be detached.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Hazu Gassho sits in a secluded spot surrounded by forest, with a tranquil river flowing behind the ryokan, and the thatched roof of the Meiji-era main building, which gives the place its name, reminded KI-NRT of the farmhouses at Shirakawa-go. Inside, the furnishings and the structure itself are charming in an old-country-home way and take you back a century or more. It is one of very few luxury properties within an hour of Nagoya.

cities.text: JR to Toyohashi ~30 min, then ~50 min by car to Yuya Onsen.
~50 min by car from Toyohashi Stn to Yuya Onsen.

inns.name: Ginrinsou
inns.summary: Ginrinsou is the most famous address in Otaru, an 18-room historic ryokan on a hillside above the town with perhaps the finest suite in Hokkaido, and KI-NRT still swore he will never patronize it again, after average kaiseki, staff so full of themselves that they think guests should feel privileged to be there, and a cold-handed checkout that cost him hundreds of dollars. It is about as harsh a judgment as he has published, and the treatment outside the room outweighs the magnificent Tsuru suite, which is why the property ends up far below what the room and the setting alone would suggest.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki was decidedly average on KI-NRT's stay, and he asks how a top property on the coast of Hokkaido can serve "ok" food. There is also a French restaurant on site, which he did not try.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Tsuru suite has its own in-room onsen bath. Nobody in the thread has written about the bathing itself or about the communal baths.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is why KI-NRT will never go back. The style is old-school snobbery, with staff who think guests should feel privileged, a nakai-san who talked down to him about etiquette and a butleress without warmth. Checkout was the bombshell, since Ginrinsou left the Go To Travel discount paperwork to its guests and said so too late, which cost him hundreds of dollars with no apology, unlike Gora Kadan or Kayotei, where your problem becomes theirs.

room.label: Room
room.text: Tsuru, the top-floor suite in the new wing, is 118.6 square metres of bright, airy, functionally modern space with every amenity, an in-room onsen bath and a 270-degree view of Otaru and the bay, and KI-NRT calls it one of the more inspiring ryokan suites he has ever stayed in; he lamented booking only two nights. The rest of the 18-room house is semi-traditional inside and very well maintained.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Ginrinsou is a distinguished, historic property on a hillside overlooking the charming town of Otaru and the Sea of Japan, and its exterior architecture is old-school Japanese, in a good way. It is widely regarded as the most historic and luxurious ryokan in Otaru, if not in all of Hokkaido.

cities.text: ~40 min by car or JR rapid from Sapporo, then ~15 min by car from Otaru Station.
~1.5 hr by car from New Chitose Airport (CTS) to Otaru.

inns.name: Okutsuso
inns.summary: An eight-room 1927 ryokan on the Yoshii River in Okutsu Onsen, prized by Japanese connoisseurs for its water and food. On KI-NRT's stay he was the only guest, with a green, short-staffed team, and dinner was the real letdown (the house specialty, a steamed-yam custard, was incredibly bland), though he found the indoor baths very nice. He closes calling it "still a pretty good place", just not one that beat out other top ryokans for a return visit.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner was the lowlight of KI-NRT's stay. The ingredients were largely local and the plates had a spring theme (hinasushi for Girls' Day), but none of it was memorable, and the house specialty joyomushi, a mountain-yam custard steamed at the hot-spring source, was incredibly bland. He calls the meal decent, and says decent does not cut it in Japan, and wonders whether the kitchen had turned over, since they were the only guests.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The water is free-flowing and sourced nearby, supposedly among the best in Japan, though KI-NRT could not tell the difference. Two indoor gender-separated baths, Kagiyu and Tachiyu, are lined with large rocks from the Yoshii River for a rough, natural feel, which he found very nice, and two more can be rented free, and only Kawa-no-yu is semi-open-air, its river view blocked by railings. The indoor baths feel cramped with two others in them.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was warm and welcoming but lacked the polish KI-NRT has had at other ryokans. Of the three staff they mainly dealt with, one was a trainee, one an intern and the veteran had been there about a year, with no knowledge of the ryokan's history or the area. The okami was nowhere to be found, and the waka-okami (the future proprietress) seemed indifferent and not particularly engaging. He suspects COVID cost the inn its experienced staff.

room.label: Room
room.text: Seikantei, one of two detached Hanare villas among the eight rooms, is a cabin with a separate bedroom and living room and an onsen bath on its deck, reasonably spacious, with a bit more privacy and space than the main-building rooms. As at other old properties there is no shower, so guests would get into the onsen unwashed, only one sink, and the hallway to the deck gets very cold on winter nights, as only the bedroom and living room are heated.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Okutsuso is a small family-owned ryokan founded in 1927 in the heart of Okutsu town, on the banks of the Yoshii River, and the main building and its interior are well preserved, traditional and charming. The footprint is very small and there are no grounds at all, no garden and no pond. Okutsu is one of Okayama's three famous onsen towns and far sleepier than Kinosaki or Kusatsu, which KI-NRT says is a plus or a minus depending on taste.

cities.text: ~1.5 hr by car from Okayama to Okutsu Onsen.
Hiroshima to Okayama ~40 min Shinkansen, then ~1.5 hr by car to Okutsu.

inns.name: Hoshino Resorts Kai Tsugaru
inns.summary: A 40-room Hoshino KAI property in Owani, Aomori, billed as a luxury onsen ryokan, which KI-NRT found to be anything but that: no greeting, no welcome tea, Western uniforms, carpeted rooms and an unattractive building, compounded by rigid two-seating dining and no laundry service. Above-average food and a shamisen performance were the only pluses, and unless there is a reason to be in the area he sees zero reason to stay again, after one stay in 2021.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The food quality exceeded KI-NRT's expectations, and they put effort into the dining. The quantity is much less than at many luxury ryokans, though: you will not go hungry, yet the sheer number of dishes that is part of a ryokan meal's appeal comes up short, at breakfast too. Dinner is in the restaurant at 5:45 or 7:30 only, with no in-room or private-room option, and after dinner a well-known shamisen player performed and explained its history.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The bath is a communal natural hot-spring bath, one for men and one for women, which KI-NRT calls decent, and that is all there is: no room has its own onsen, and there are no baths that couples or families can book for private use, unlike at some luxury ryokans.

service.label: Service
service.text: KI-NRT says nothing about the service suggested a luxury ryokan. Nobody was outside to greet them or help with luggage, the entrance was deserted every time they came and went, and the staff stay behind the front desk, which left him cold. There was no welcome tea or sweets at check-in, no room attendant is assigned to you, the server changes from meal to meal, and there is no laundry service. There were no major mishaps, just nothing personal.

room.label: Room
room.text: The rooms are Western-style and carpeted, and shoes stay on even in the room, which KI-NRT finds unsanitary in a self-styled luxury ryokan. His 50m² room (category TC2) was comfortable but too small and constricting to want to stay in, the same complaint he has about Hoshinoya Tokyo, and the only suite was being remodeled and unbookable. Guests get samue instead of yukata, and the toiletries are substandard, with not even a moisturizer.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The main building is depressingly unattractive as you pull up, the grounds are very small, and KI-NRT found the property bland, a place that could be anywhere in Japan. Behind the building is a man-made pond, seen from the lobby, restaurant and most rooms, with lanterns along the walkway and in the water lit at night, which he calls cute but a cheap way to spruce up a bland backyard. Inside is a Neputa art exhibit from the nearby artisan village.

cities.text: Ou line from Shin-Aomori toward Hirosaki and Owani-Onsen is about 50 min, then a 5-10 min inn shuttle.
Tohoku Shinkansen Hayabusa Tokyo to Shin-Aomori is about 3h, then roughly 50 min by Ou line to Owani-Onsen plus a short shuttle.

inns.name: Satoyama no Auberge Maki No Oto
inns.summary: A three-room auberge in the farmland of rural Toyama, where the setting is pretty and calming and almost everything else disappointed KI-NRT, who came away 'unimpressed in almost all aspects': the best of the three rooms is basic and its bathroom puts toilet, shower and sink in one space, and the French-Japanese food was only good. He would neither return nor recommend it, and the scenery alone does not justify the trip out.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Maki no Oto is known among Japanese travelers for its French-Japanese fusion cooking, and the food is what disappointed KI-NRT most. He found it only 'good', with no dish that stood out: the grilled red tilefish with vermouth sauce was just okay, the cutlass fish with kogashi butter likewise, and the grilled ayu over vegetable terrine only adequate. He expected more umami from Sea of Japan seafood and would not drive out just to eat here.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: There is no onsen. The bath in the room is an ordinary tub with jacuzzi functionality, and the bathroom is where the property feels most dated: green wall tiles that look 1980s (though the building went up in 2005), a single sink, and the shower and toilet sharing one space, which KI-NRT despises.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service was not particularly proactive on KI-NRT's stay, and the arrival set the tone. The entrance is unassuming and narrow enough to mistake for someone's small home, they had to go inside and call for someone, and were then pointed to a parking structure about a quarter of a mile away with no offer to park the car for them. He felt the inn never managed the special vibe that other luxury ryokans pull off, though nothing was a big fail.

room.label: Room
room.text: KI-NRT booked the best of the three rooms, the executive room that takes up the whole second floor, and even that felt smaller than its listed 57 square metres. The bedroom is only partly cut off from the living room by a glass wall that stops short of the walls, and its sheer curtain gives neither privacy nor darkness. The furnishings are 'fine' and basic, going for a country vibe, and a raised tatami corner crowds the living room.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The auberge sits in remote farmland in Nanto, a satoyama landscape of fields that is pretty and serene though not jaw-dropping, a 15 minute drive from Ainokura, so there is major sightseeing nearby. The fields are the calming influence, so a garden is no loss, yet on the property there is nothing to do: one building holds the lounge, restaurant and three rooms, with no talk or performance to give a sense of place, which KI-NRT counts against it.

cities.text: ~40 min by car from Shin-Takaoka Stn to Nanto.
Via Kanazawa/Shin-Takaoka (Hida LEX or Thunderbird + Hokuriku Shinkansen) ~2.5h, then ~40 min by car.

inns.name: Uoshizu
inns.summary: A Yugawara ryokan that is a cautionary tale about the bottom of the price range. At roughly 30,000 yen for two with kaiseki half-board, benihana320 found the service lacking and the building a little run-down, and KI-NRT's response was blunt: you cannot expect awesomeness at that price. The one stay in the thread ended in disappointment and benihana320 would not return.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: The kaiseki meals are the one part of benihana320's May 2025 stay that drew no complaint: the food was not too bad, which is as far as the praise goes, and no dish is named.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Uoshizu is in Yugawara, a hot-spring town, but nobody in the thread has written about the baths here, so the water situation is unknown.

service.label: Service
service.text: The quality of service was lacking on benihana320's May 2025 stay, and that was the main disappointment. benihana320 had not thought of Uoshizu as a cheap pick and left asking the thread what the price floor now is for excellent service in a well-kept building; KI-NRT's answer was that at Uoshizu's rate for two, half board included, you cannot expect awesomeness.

room.label: Room
room.text: The building seemed a little run-down to benihana320 in May 2025, and that is the extent of it; nobody in the thread describes the rooms themselves.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Uoshizu is in Yugawara, but nobody in the thread has written about the location or the grounds here.

cities.text: JR Tokaido Line / Odoriko LEX Tokyo->Yugawara ~1h20, then ~15 min by car.
JR Odawara->Yugawara ~15 min, then ~15 min by car.

inns.name: Gora Karaku
inns.summary: A 70-room Orix-run onsen hotel in Gora that photographs like a modern ryokan but runs like a business hotel. stargold's one-night stay was not good, with dinner and its service the failure, and KI-NRT later told a poster weighing it to pass, even while granting it gets decent crowd reviews. stargold's group concluded that the Hotel Indigo, where they stayed the next night for half the cost, was a far better experience overall.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner was the absolute low point of stargold's stay, served in the restaurant with little privacy and no explanation of the courses beyond the scant description on the menu. The menu said the rice was cooked to order, but the pot was never presented and it did not taste freshly made, and he thought the food was ordinary at best and nowhere near ryokan standard. The paid upsells for the fish and meat courses felt like a cheap money-grab.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The rooms have their own outdoor onsen baths, and stargold found his pleasant, one of the few things in the room that worked. Nobody in the thread has written about the water itself or any other bathing here.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service at dinner was absolutely atrocious: inexperienced, inelegant and clumsy staff with no experience of a luxury setting. At one point the server dropped a plate of tsukemono onto the tray, put the pickles back with a fork and his fingers, and tried to serve it without seeing any need for a new one. stargold summed the place up as a typical Japanese hotel with none of the character, history and service levels you expect from a ryokan.

room.label: Room
room.text: The bed was comfortable, but otherwise the room was a slightly nicer version of the soulless dark grey wood decor you find in a typical modern business hotel. There are more than 70 rooms and they are basically identical, differing only by east wing (mountain views) or west wing.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Gora Karaku is a large modern building in Gora, which has easy access to most of Hakone's sights, and its public areas have been done up to be very Instagrammable, with decent decor. The other choices in Gora are Gora Kadan, Gora Byakudan, Gen Hakone (opened 2021), Gora Hanaougi and Gora Hanaougi Madoka no Mori, and KI-NRT would pass on Karaku in favour of those.

cities.text: Odawara Shinkansen + Hakone Tozan line/bus to Gora ~2h12.
Tokaido Shinkansen to Odawara + Hakone Tozan line/bus to Gora ~2h15.

inns.name: Akariya Geihanro
inns.summary: Inuyama's oldest inn, founded in 1919 on the Kiso River and rebuilt in 2017 as a ten-room house with a semi-open-air onsen bath in every room and the National Treasure castle keep on the bluff above the water. Ikyu's crowd gives it 4.87 across 155 reviews and ranks it first in all of Tokai, with bathing (4.89) and hospitality (4.88) its strongest marks and cooking (4.83) its softest. The house takes no children below elementary age, and it is about thirty minutes out of Nagoya.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is seasonal Japanese cooking built on river and Ise Bay catch (ayu sweetfish, flathead, sakura shrimp) and beef grilled long and low, and the head chef comes out to the table to check the seasoning. Ikyu guests put meals at 4.83, which is the softest of the inn's six marks and still a high one, and the quibbles that do surface are about texture and nothing bigger.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: The Inuyama Onsen 'Hakutei no Yu' spring feeds a semi-open-air bath in all ten rooms, and several are angled so that the castle keep or the Kiso River sits in the opening. There is a bookable private bath below. Ikyu guests put bathing at 4.89, the inn's top mark, and repeat guests write specifically about how much closer the castle looks from the water.

service.label: Service
service.text: Guests write about the staff more than anything else: they hold luggage after checkout, arrange rides to the station, and are remembered by the shift they worked. Guests describe the proprietress photographing them against the castle and bowing until they were out of sight. Ikyu guests put hospitality at 4.88, and the number of return visitors backs that up.

room.label: Room
room.text: There are ten rooms only, rebuilt in 2017, each with a semi-open-air bath, wood-battened ceilings and a river-facing wall of glass onto a private terrace, and the Kiso Premium Suite runs 75 m² in a Japanese-Western layout. Ikyu guests put the rooms at 4.88. No children below elementary school age stay in the house, which is a large part of why guests describe it as quiet.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Geihanro stands directly on the bank of the Kiso River in old Inuyama, with the keep of National Treasure Inuyama Castle (one of Japan's twelve surviving original towers) on the bluff above. The castle town and the Urakuen tea garden are a walk away, cormorant-fishing boats work the river in season, and Meitetsu Nagoya is about thirty minutes down the line.

cities.text: Reverse of: Meitetsu Inuyama→Meitetsu-Nagoya (~30 min), a ~10-min walk across to JR Nagoya, the Ltd Exp 'Shirasagi' Nagoya→Tsuruga (~1h40), then the Hokuriku Shinkansen 'Tsurugi' Tsuruga→Kanazawa (~43 min). Two changes, both timetabled connections. (Via Nozomi to Kyoto + 'Thunderbird' to Tsuruga lands within ~15 min of the same total, with one more change — take whichever departure fits.)
Reverse of: Meitetsu Inuyama→Meitetsu-Nagoya (~30 min), a ~10-min walk across to JR Nagoya, then a Tōkaidō 'Nozomi' Nagoya→Tokyo (~1h40). One change; both legs run several times an hour.

Reverse of: Meitetsu Inuyama→Meitetsu-Nagoya (~30 min), a ~10-min walk across to JR Nagoya, then a Tōkaidō 'Nozomi'/'Hikari' Nagoya→Kyoto (~35 min). One change and the shortest hop on the hokuriku board — Inuyama is effectively a Nagoya suburb with a castle.

inns.name: Akazawa Geihinkan
inns.summary: Akazawa Geihinkan is a 15-room sukiya hideaway on 1,000-plus tsubo above the Akazawa coast at Izu Kōgen, with Ajiro-woven ceilings and a private open-air bath in every room. Its signature is deep-sea water, drawn from about 800 m offshore and run through the room baths, the public baths and the cooking, and there is no hot spring, though guests get the adjoining Akazawa resort's sea-view day-bath, spa and sauna free. Ikyu guests put it near 4.73 over about 81 stays, with the baths and facilities their high marks.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is seasonal kaiseki built on the Izu coastal catch and served in private dining rooms, and guests praise the chef's technique and generous portions. Ikyu guests put the meals near 4.63, below the baths, and the occasional chipped clay pot or piece of tableware has been noted since the change of ownership.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Unusually, there is no hot spring here. Every room's open-air bath, the two public baths, a deep-sea-water pool and a barrel sauna all run on deep-sea water drawn from about 800 m off the Akazawa coast, prized for its buoyancy, and guests also get the neighbouring Akazawa resort's sea-view day-onsen, spa and sauna free. Ikyu guests put the baths near 4.84, among the top marks.

service.label: Service
service.text: Warm, smiling welcomes and smooth escorting to the room draw repeat praise, and anniversary guests leave delighted, but Ikyu guests put the service near 4.59, the softest of the marks, and the recurring friction is meal explanations from international staff that some guests found hard to follow.

room.label: Room
room.text: The fifteen Japanese-style rooms run about 68 square metres, up to a 150-square-metre detached villa, and each opens onto a private open-air deep-sea-water bath framed by garden or landscape; some detached villas add a private sauna. Ikyu guests put the rooms near 4.77 and call them bright, clean and relaxing, with the bird-song garden views a repeated highlight.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The inn is a 1,000-tsubo sukiya estate above Sagami Bay at Izu Kōgen, with Ajiro-woven ceilings, Juraku-plaster walls and a broad Japanese garden, and guests have free run of the Akazawa onsen resort next door: spa, bowling and sea-view day-bath, plus a games lounge with free drinks. Ikyu guests put the facilities near 4.86, among the strongest marks, and call them strong value.

cities.text: JR Ltd Exp 'Odoriko' Tokyo→Izu-Kōgen (~2h, one seat) — or Shinkansen Tokyo→Atami (~40 min) + Izukyū Line — then the inn's free shuttle (~6–15 min, reserve).
Reverse of: Izukyū Izu-Kōgen→Atami (~50 min), then 'Hikari' Atami→Kyoto (~2h; 'Nozomi' skips Atami).

inns.name: Amane Resort Seikai
inns.summary: Seikai is the larger, original half of Beppu's two-inn Amane pair, and it holds the complex's big communal onsens, the French dinner restaurant and the buffet breakfast, which makes it the family-friendly counterweight to Gahama next door. Jalan guests rate it 4.8 across nearly 1,600 stays. KI-NRT has only crossed over from a stay at Gahama for its restaurant and breakfast, and nobody in the thread has written up a stay at Seikai itself.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner at Seikai is French, while the kaiseki table is at its sister Gahama, and guests at either inn can eat at both. KI-NRT, staying two nights at Gahama, wanted to try both kitchens, and he called Seikai's breakfast buffet wonderful and a big hit with his kids. Jalan guests give dinner and breakfast 4.7 each and describe a tasty French dinner and a breakfast they enjoy.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Seikai has the pair's large communal onsens, which Gahama lacks, and KI-NRT found them unnecessary for adults but great fun for kids. An ocean-view sauna was added in 2023. Jalan guests give the bath 4.7 and repeatedly praise how clean the baths are kept.

service.label: Service
service.text: A complimentary golf cart runs on demand between Seikai and its sister Gahama, a one-minute ride, and guests at either inn can use the facilities and restaurants of the other, which KI-NRT counted as a requirement. Nobody in the thread has written about the service here. Jalan guests give it 4.5, their lowest mark, and describe friendly staff in aloha shirts; many are marking an occasion, and how the staff handle it decides the review.

room.label: Room
room.text: Seikai is the larger, original half of the two-inn complex, and some rooms have their own open-air bath. Nobody in the thread has described a room here. Jalan guests give the rooms 4.8, their highest mark, and clean rooms are a recurring note.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Seikai stands in Beppu, where hot-spring steam rises from the ground all over the city and you can smell the sulfur, which KI-NRT calls an awe-inspiring sight, though in the end he finds Beppu just another city, pleasant but no more, and the famous Hells very touristy and a bit fabricated. The property shares a parking lot with a big Nitori furniture store, and its sister Gahama is a five-minute walk across it.

cities.text: Ltd exp Sonic Hakata to Beppu (~2h10), then ~15 min taxi to the inn.
Shinkansen to Kokura, Sonic down to Beppu, then ~15 min taxi; no direct link.

inns.name: Amanojyaku
inns.summary: A small suite ryokan on Maejima in the Amakusa archipelago, built around in-room onsen baths behind motorized window-walls that open the whole room to the sea. Ikyu guests put it at 4.78 across roughly 170 stays and single out the rooms and the bathing as its strongest points, but the dissent is consistent: dinner is their lowest mark, and recent reviewers describe an over-worked kitchen. Nobody in the thread has stayed yet, though KI-NRT had booked the top suite for December 2025 before Tayuta lured him away.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is a sushi-centred omakase of about twelve courses from a Ginza-trained chef at a ten-seat counter that takes only about five groups a night, so ask for it on your first night. Amakusa's purple sea urchin is famous. Food is nonetheless the lowest Ikyu mark (4.64), and the recurring complaint in recent reviews is a kitchen that over-works its ingredients and a breakfast below the class of the inn, with portions running light.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Every room has an onsen bath, which KI-NRT calls a huge advantage over the sister inn Tenku no Fune, with water straight from the source. In the Junior Suites the bath is indoors behind a motorized window-wall: closed, it is a hot indoor bath with the whole sea view, and opened fully it is a semi-open-air soak. The top suites add a terrace rotenburo, a sauna and a cold plunge. Ikyu guests put the bathing at 4.84, just behind the rooms.

service.label: Service
service.text: Nobody in the thread has stayed here, though KI-NRT found the service first-rate at Amakusa Tenku no Fune, the older sister inn under the same owners. Free pickup is from Matsushima Port or the bus stop only, with no airport pickup, and cancellation penalties start 61 days out. Ikyu guests put service at 4.81, close behind the rooms and the bath, and recent complaints are about the food, none of them touching the staff.

room.label: Room
room.text: The Junior Suites run 78 square metres plus a 26 square metre terrace, with the onsen bath at the window; the top suites reach 115 square metres with a terrace rotenburo, sauna and plunge. Rooms draw the highest Ikyu mark (4.87), and the space of the suites, with glass walls that retract fully toward the sea, is what their reviews praise.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: Amanojyaku stands on Maejima in the Amakusa archipelago, and everything faces the water. KI-NRT calls Amakusa breathtakingly scenic, more beautiful even than Matsushima, with small islands dotting the bay, and the sushi counter hangs over an infinity basin with the early-January sun setting around 5:25 in view. The one car-free excursion is the dolphin-watching boats two minutes away, and Amakusa is a remote place to reach.

cities.text: Reverse of: Inn-arranged car Tayuta→JR Kumamoto ~1h (per Tayuta's own access chart) via the Five Bridges + Misumi — coastal, snow-proof — then Kyushu Shinkansen 'Sakura'/'Mizuho' Kumamoto→Hakata (~33 min, every 20-30 min). Rail alt: 20-min taxi/boat→Misumi + JR Misumi line 50 min→Kumamoto (+1 change).

Kyushu Shinkansen 'Sakura' Kagoshima-Chūō→Kumamoto (~48 min), change to the JR Misumi line (~50 min — ⚠ 14-18/day, plan the connection), then the 20-min taxi/boat Misumi→Tayuta (the inn's own access chart; inn-synced Takarajima boat where sailing — Iruka 1/2 suspended Dec–Mar, 3-5 sailings remain). Carless, coastal, snow-proof.

Reverse of: Carless via the Misumi corridor: inn-synced 15–20-min boat/taxi to Misumi, Misumi Line→Kumamoto (~50–60 min), then Shinkansen→Shin-Tosu + Relay Kamome→Kamome to Nagasaki (~2h) — all-rail, snow-proof. Drivers' variant (the ferry drive): ~45 min to Oniike Port, Shimatetsu car ferry→Kuchinotsu (30 min, ~every 45), then ~1h45 down the Shimabara peninsula with Sakitsu Church and the Unzen jigoku en route (~3.5h; winter gales occasionally cancel the strait ferry).

Reverse of: By car ~1h10 via the Five Bridges, Misumi and R57 — coastal and effectively snow-proof. Carless parity (~1¼h): 15-min Takarajima-Line boat Matsushima Port⇄Misumi port (+2-min walk to the station) or 20-min taxi, then Misumi Line⇄Kumamoto ~50–60 min — both Tayuta and Amanojyaku sync pickups. ('Amakusa-gō' rapid bus Matsushima→Sakuramachi BT ~1h20, ~9/day, no reservation.)

No Tokyo→Amakusa flight exists. Fly via Kumamoto: Tokyo→Haneda (~30 min), HND→Aso-Kumamoto (KMJ) ~2h, then ~1.5h taxi/arranged car SW across the Amakusa bridges to Matsushima — Tayuta's official access figure; the inns arrange transfers. Rail-purist alt: KMJ limousine bus→Kumamoto Stn (~1h) + Misumi Line (~50 min) + 15–20-min boat/taxi ≈ same door-to-door. (Connecting via Fukuoka to tiny Amakusa Airport works too but isn't faster.)

inns.name: Ancient Hotel Asama Karuizawa
inns.summary: Ancient Hotel Asama is a 13-room design boutique in the Karuizawa woods with jewel-box rooms and pleasant local cooking, and at $400–650 a night it sits well below what its peers charge. Ikyu guests adore it, marking it 4.9 across 41 stays and praising warm, attentive staff, with only minor gripes breaking the consensus. KI-NRT has 'yet to find a Karuizawa stay worth its salt', and this is the affordable design pick more than a connoisseur's destination.

cuisine.label: Food
cuisine.text: Dinner is a creative kaiseki on local, seasonal ingredients, comfortable cooking and no destination kitchen, and breakfast gets as much praise as dinner in the reviews. Draft beer flows free with the stay, with no time limit, and the guests who come back or say they want to name the food alongside the staff as the reason. Ikyu guests put the food at 4.88, level with the rooms and just behind the service.

onsen.label: Bath
onsen.text: Bathing is an indoor mineral hot-spring bath plus a private family bath that you reserve, and there is no in-room onsen, so the private slot is the route for anyone with tattoos. It shares Karuizawa's usual caveat of imported onsen water. Ikyu guests put the bath at 4.88.

service.label: Service
service.text: Service is the strongest part of this inn, and the hotel sends a free car to Karuizawa Station. Ikyu guests describe warm, at-home hospitality, with staff who arrange surprises for birthdays and Christmas down to the detail, greet repeat guests like family and look after small practical things in the mountain weather, from warming shoes on a snowy morning to lending boots for the waterfall walk. They put service at 4.95.

room.label: Room
room.text: There are thirteen rooms, each named for a natural stone and done in jewel tones, and one suite has a rotating central fireplace. Guests describe them as comfortable, with a balcony, though there is no shower in the room and no TV. Ikyu guests put the rooms at 4.88.

setting.label: Place
setting.text: The hotel sits in the Karuizawa woods at Nagakura, and TripAdvisor ranks it first of 53 places to stay in town. It is easy to reach, but it shares Karuizawa's light snow and near-Tokyo resort character, so there is no deep-country atmosphere. Guests praise the location, and the inn lends boots and bear bells for the walk to the waterfall nearby.

cities.text: Hokuriku Shinkansen 'Asama' Tokyo→Karuizawa (~1h06–1h16), then ~15 min by taxi (free hotel pickup) — the easiest access on the whole corridor. For the Hiramatsu (Miyota), ride one stop on to Sakudaira + a ~20-min taxi (~1.9h total).
Hokuriku Shinkansen 'Hakutaka' Kanazawa→Karuizawa direct (~1h50; the faster 'Kagayaki' skips Karuizawa), then ~15 min by taxi. The Hiramatsu adds ~15–20 min to Miyota via Sakudaira (~2.4h).

inns.name: Araya Totoan
inns.summary: An 18-generation Yamashiro Onsen inn where Rosanjin lived for a year, with source-fed cypress rotenburo in most rooms and his art on the walls. Ikyu guests mark it 4.58 across 70 reviews and repeatedly praise the bathing and the crab-course dinner, calling the house Michelin-1-Key quality, though more than one flags service and amenities as below what the price should buy. Nobody in the thread has stayed since the renovation that began in 2018, which leaves it a historically compelling unknown.
